title: cuRoboV2-Fast: Fast Torque-Limited Collision-Free Motion Planning
authors: Balakumar Sundaralingam,Adithyavairavan Murali,Stan Birchfield
abstract:
We present cuRoboV2-Fast, a GPU-accelerated planner that reduces both planning
latency and execution time for collision-free, payload-aware, torque-limited
motions. B-spline trajectory optimization reduces the required iterations,
while accelerated robot computations and differentiable inverse dynamics reduce
refinement cost and accommodate changing payloads. TimeOpt optimizes traversal
speed along the fixed path under sampled velocity, acceleration, jerk, and torque
constraints, exploiting local spline support to solve banded Newton systems
efficiently on the GPU. With a 3 kg payload, cuRoboV2-Fast achieves
4.4 ms mean planning time on RTX 5090, 14.7×14.7\times faster than cuRoboV2. Our method
on Jetson AGX Orin plans faster than cuRoboV1 + TOPPRA
on RTX 5090. A stereo-camera-based
deployment on YAM achieves 5.93 s mean completed pick-and-drop cycles,
34.6% shorter than cuRoboV2.
Code (Apache 2.0): github.com/NVlabs/curobo.
Project Page: research.nvidia.com/labs/lpr/curobov2-fast/.
introduction:
Fast manipulation requires motions that are both quick to plan and quick to
execute. Motion planning has made substantial progress in finding collision-free
paths through cluttered environments [1]. Executing these
paths requires timing that respects velocity, acceleration, and actuator torque
limits. Carried payloads change the dynamics and can render an otherwise feasible
motion infeasible. Moreover, geometric path length alone does not determine
execution time: a shorter path can require slower motion under actuator
constraints. Efficient motion planning must therefore consider both the
computational cost of generating a trajectory and the time required to execute it.

Prior work establishes the benefits of parallel planning, smooth trajectory
representations, and efficient robot
computations [2, 3, 4].
Planning executable motions nevertheless requires repeated collision and dynamics
evaluations during trajectory optimization. Reducing this cost requires both
fewer optimization iterations and cheaper computations within each iteration.
Execution time presents a complementary challenge: uniformly rescaling the
timestep cannot redistribute time along a path whose limiting actuator
constraints vary with configuration. Efficient payload-aware planning therefore
requires flexible optimization of trajectory geometry and timing alongside
fast constraint evaluation.

We present cuRoboV2-Fast, a single-GPU planner for collision-free, torque-limited
motions that reduces both planning latency and execution time. B-spline
trajectory optimization refines geometry with fewer iterations, while TimeOpt
optimizes traversal speed along the resulting fixed path. The timing spline’s
local support yields banded systems for efficient GPU optimization. A parallel
GPU RRT provides route initialization when needed, and accelerated robot
computations reduce the cost of refinement. Differentiable inverse dynamics
incorporates payload-dependent torque limits and supports runtime inertial
updates as carried objects change.
We make six contributions toward fast, executable motion planning:

We use B-splines for collision-free, payload-aware, torque-limited
trajectory optimization, matching the success of cuRoboV1 [2]
with 25 versus 125 initial iterations in our convergence benchmark.

We introduce GPU-accelerated TimeOpt with banded Newton systems and
a primal–dual predictor–corrector solver for fixed-path timing under
sampled velocity, acceleration, jerk, and torque bounds. It reduces mean
motion duration by 15.7% beyond uniform timestep refinement and averages
0.28 ms on valid 100 g benchmark queries on RTX 5090.

We accelerate robot computations and differentiable inverse dynamics,
supporting payload updates without recompilation. Trajectory optimization iterations are 2.7×2.7\times faster than cuRoboV2 [5]
on RTX 5090 and 2.6×2.6\times faster on Jetson AGX Orin.

We achieve sub-millisecond route initialization with a parallel
GPU RRT: 0.305 ms on average, 43×43\times faster than
cuRoboV1 PRM [2] and 1.48×1.48\times faster than
pRRTC [6] under coarse collision checks.
Separating constraint validation from tree growth enables additional
checks without changing growth kernels.

Our integrated pipeline achieves 4.4 ms mean motion-planning time
with a 3 kg payload on RTX 5090, 14.7×14.7\times faster than
cuRoboV2 [5] while maintaining similar success.
cuRoboV2-Fast on Jetson AGX Orin also plans faster than
cuRoboV1 [2] +
TOPPRA [7] on RTX 5090.

We demonstrate a stereo-camera-based pick-and-drop pipeline on YAM,
integrating perception, grasp generation, and motion planning on a single
GPU. Mean completed cycle time is 5.93 s, 34.6% shorter than cuRoboV2,
with planning accounting for only 1.0% of cycle time.

We have open sourced the cuRoboV2-Fast implementation under the Apache 2.0
license at github.com/NVlabs/curobo.

title: Perceptive Humanoid Motion from Simulation
authors: Siyuan Hu,Abulikemu Abuduweili,Yue Meng,Shipeng Liu,Quentin Leboutet,Chen Chen,Matthias Müller,Vladlen Koltun
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
comment: Code and videos at:this https URL
abstract:
Humanoid robots have the potential to automate a wide range of physical tasks. Progress toward generalist humanoid autonomy, however, remains constrained by a data bottleneck: mapping pixels and free-form language to low-level joint commands requires paired supervision, and no corpus of such data exists at sufficiently large scale.
Some approaches rely on human teleoperation and wearable capture devices, which require at least an hour of human time to produce an hour of data.
We present HALO, a humanoid autonomy system powered by a pipeline that synthesizes vision-language-motion data across a thousand procedurally generated homes. The corpus scales with compute rather than human labor.
HALO acquires a repertoire of physical skills, including sitting on chairs, navigating to named objects, stepping sideways through half-open doors, crouching and crawling beneath tables, and pushing boxes. It orchestrates these skills to solve composite, long-horizon tasks. Without ever seeing a real home during training, HALO transfers zero-shot to the physical world, achieving a 91% success rate across 360 trials in six unmapped real-world environments. See https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-halo/ for code and videos.
introduction:
Humanoid robots can somersault, dance, and run. Yet none of them can be invited into an unfamiliar living room and asked to sit down. They are agile but blind: a backflip is choreographed in advance and executed against geometry the robot never has to perceive. The tasks that would make a humanoid useful are not like this. They take place in rooms nobody has scanned, among furniture nobody has annotated, and the robot has to find the chair before it can sit on it. Perception enters twice, and at two levels of abstraction. It is semantic, deciding what to do: which of the objects around me does the instruction refer to? And it is physical, deciding how to move: the seat has to be met where it actually is, and the robot’s weight transferred onto it without losing balance.
Neither level is supervised the way a backflip is. A backflip requires only a reference motion clip and a tracker to follow it. Mapping pixels and free-form language to joint commands, however, demands paired supervision: an egocentric image, an instruction, and the precise whole-body trajectory that satisfies it.

In natural language processing, broad generalization has been unlocked by massive data volume [1]. But while text and video are abundant, as a byproduct of people writing and filming, whole-body motion with paired context is not. Every single episode must be deliberately produced. Teleoperation systems such as ALOHA [2] and TWIST [3], or wearable capture devices such as UMI [4], can generate these demonstrations, but they couple data generation with physical labor. Because a person must manually act out every episode, an hour of data costs at least an hour of human time.

In this paper, we introduce HALO (Humanoid Autonomy, Learned in simulation, running Onboard), a humanoid autonomy system powered by a data generation pipeline that produces egocentric vision-language-motion data entirely in simulation. The resulting policy runs fully onboard the physical robot. Simulation unshackles data generation from human labor. A scene can be generated, a motion synthesized, and the corresponding egocentric video rendered with no human intervention. What would have taken hours (and days, and years) of human time can instead proceed autonomously and in parallel, bounded only by compute.
To create a training episode, a motion diffusion model generates the whole-body humanoid motion, a procedural generator supplies the environment, and the simulator situates the motion in the environment to render the robot’s sensory inputs. Our training corpus comprises 300300 hours of episodes across a thousand procedurally generated homes, none of which anyone has had to visit or scan. Data scales with compute rather than human time. Quality is maintained by automated verifiers.

The HALO autonomy stack has three layers, illustrated in Fig. 2. An orchestrator (an off-the-shelf vision-language model invoked every two seconds) decomposes a free-form language request into a sequence of subtasks, each identifying one skill and the object it applies to. A motion generator running at 3 Hz combines a VLM-based encoder with a DiT-based decoder and maps an egocentric RGB observation and the subtask to a whole-body kinematic motion plan: five seconds of joint angles and pelvis poses. Finally, a 50 Hz motion tracker takes this motion plan in conjunction with onboard depth and proprioception, and drives the robot via joint-level actuator commands. The motion tracker is trained by large-scale reinforcement learning to follow motion plans while respecting balance, contact, and actuator limits. The first two layers settle the semantic half of the problem (which chair?); the tracker settles the physical half (meeting the seat where it actually is).

With this stack, HALO autonomously performs perceptive whole-body skills: sitting on chairs, navigating to named objects, stepping sideways through half-open doors, crouching and crawling beneath tables, and pushing boxes. It also orchestrates them into longer multi-step sequences in response to free-form natural-language requests (Fig. 1).

This paper makes three contributions:

Data generation pipeline. HALO produces egocentric vision-language-motion episodes in simulation, with no teleoperation, no capture suit, and no scan of the deployment environment. Data volume is decoupled from human effort and is bounded only by compute. We train across a thousand procedurally generated home environments.

Onboard autonomy stack. A high-level orchestrator determines the next semantic subtask. A mid-level generator then solves this task from the current egocentric view, emitting a five-second whole-body motion plan. A low-level tracker grounds this plan in the physical world, executing the trajectory using onboard depth and proprioceptive feedback. No prior system pairs a perceptive low-level controller with a whole-body motion plan produced by a generative model running entirely onboard.

Whole-body autonomy demonstrated in previously unseen physical environments. Deployed on the physical robot, HALO achieves a 91% success rate over 360 trials across six real-world home environments that were neither seen during training nor scanned or mapped. The system transfers directly from simulation to novel physical environments, with no preparatory scanning of the target environment.

title: VABAR: A Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics
authors: Shuangyu Xie,Kaiyuan Chen,Uksang Yoo,Xinyue Zhu,Meadow Shen,Jaimyn Drake,Eugen Solowjow,Lionel Gulich,Alexander Millane,Rafael Cathomen,Tuur Stuyck,Sangeeta Subramanian,Yichao Pan,Bruce McGowan,Michael Benedict,Linxi Fan,Yuke Zhu,Spencer Huang,Ken Goldberg
abstract:
For robots to operate reliably in commercial and industrial applications, they must persistently perform specific tasks with known variations in object shape and pose.
We call this Variational Automation (VA) to differentiate these settings from fixed automation.
Inspired by recent papers on Agentic Robotics, where pretrained LLM and VLM coding agents combine interpretable robot programming with the open-world adaptability of model free policies,
we propose a general set of agentic robotics benchmark design criteria that includes accessibility, repeatability, diversity, relevance to agentic robotics and practical applications, physical realizability, resistance to benchmark saturation, and computational efficiency.
We instantiate these principles in six manipulation task classes spanning industrial, medical, and infrastructure applications: tool sorting, tool hanging, gear meshing, syringe packing, cable insertion, and cable routing.
We introduce the Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics (VABAR), an open, easily replicable, simulation-based manipulation benchmark to systematically evaluating agentic robotics systems.
Built fully on open-source tools, VABAR features detailed implementations using the Newton physics engine, standardized task variations, difficulty tiers, success metrics, and a library of 33 generalizable skills with human-authored programmatic reference solutions.
We provide initial baseline evaluations using an open agentic manipulation harness, Graph-as-Policy (GaP), and Isaac Lab Arena.
introduction:
For robots to operate reliably in commercial and industrial applications, they must solve
Variational Automation (VA) tasks,
where operational objectives and workspace persist with structured variations in objects, layouts, task parameters, and execution conditions across instances.
In fixed automation, robots repeatedly execute carefully engineered programs in highly structured environments, often achieving high reliability and throughput but requiring substantial human effort to design, deploy, and retune when conditions change [1].
In comparison, generalist robotics aims to perform a broad range of open-ended tasks, but current model-free end-to-end approaches struggle to achieve the speed and reliability required for commercial and industrial adoption.
VA tasks lie between fixed automation and fully generalist robotics.

Recent advances in agentic robotics provide a promising approach to implementing VA by combining the reliability and interpretability of classical robot programming with the adaptability of learned policies.
Rather than directly mapping observations to low-level actions through a monolithic model-free policy, agentic robotic systems use multiple LLM agents to reason about task instances, generate and modify executable robot programs, and invoke perception, planning, and control modules named skills.

Existing robot manipulation benchmarks (e.g., LIBERO [2], ManiSkill [3], and SimplerEnv [4]) evaluate the robustness and generalization of language-conditioned deep visuomotor policies by offering simulation environments, human-teleoperated training episodes, and success metrics across new scene configurations.
Many of these have recently been saturated by systems that achieve very high success rates and they primarily focus on household pick-and-place tasks.

We introduce VABAR, a Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics. VABAR provides six application-oriented manipulation task classes spanning industrial, medical, and infrastructure settings: tool sorting, tool hanging, gear meshing, syringe packing, cable insertion, and cable routing.
Each task is defined with a set of instances with explicit variation axes, difficulty levels, and success conditions. For each task, we provide a physics and photorealistic simulation environment, a set of generalizable skills to facilitate execution, and a human-authored reference solution expressed as a computation graph over the same skill library. The reference solution is executed with the same perception, planning, and execution stack available to coding agents.

We evaluate VABAR using GaP, an open agentic manipulation baseline [5], and with Isaac Lab Arena to establish baselines and to study how performance scales with task difficulty and structured variation.

This paper makes 5 contributions:

Variational Automation task formulation. We introduce and formalize Variational Automation, a manipulation class between fixed automation and unconstrained general-purpose manipulation, in which persistent operational objectives must be achieved across a structured distribution of task instances.

Design principles for agentic robotics benchmarks. We define practical criteria for evaluating agentic systems, emphasizing accessibility, repeatability, controlled diversity, application relevance, physical realizability, resistance to saturation, and computational efficiency.

VABAR task definition We instantiate these principles in six application-oriented manipulation task classes—(1) tool sorting, (2) tool hanging, (3) gear meshing, (4) syringe packing, (5) cable insertion, and (6) cable routing—with standardized task variations, difficulty levels, success metrics, and support for single-arm Franka and bimanual YAM embodiments.

VABAR simulation, Agentic Skills and Human-authored solutions For each task, we provide a photorealistic simulation environment, 33 generalizable skills that facilitate solving the tasks, and a human-authored code solution.

Initial agentic manipulation baselines. We provide initial baseline evaluations using an open agentic robotic system and characterize performance as task complexity and instance variation increase, establishing reference results and identifying remaining challenges for agentic manipulation.

2. Design principles for agentic robotics benchmarks. We define practical criteria for evaluating agentic systems, emphasizing accessibility, repeatability, controlled diversity, application relevance, physical realizability, resistance to saturation, and computational efficiency.

3. VABAR task definition We instantiate these principles in six application-oriented manipulation task classes—(1) tool sorting, (2) tool hanging, (3) gear meshing, (4) syringe packing, (5) cable insertion, and (6) cable routing—with standardized task variations, difficulty levels, success metrics, and support for single-arm Franka and bimanual YAM embodiments.

4. VABAR simulation, Agentic Skills and Human-authored solutions For each task, we provide a photorealistic simulation environment, 33 generalizable skills that facilitate solving the tasks, and a human-authored code solution.

title: Rethinking Self-Repair in Code-as-Policy Agents: What Drives Retry Success?
authors: Siddharth Aphale,Ayushman Singh
comment: Accepted to the CoRL 2026 Learn@Deploy workshop
abstract: Code-as-policy agents often use execution feedback to retry failed programs. Additional sampling and task guidance can also improve success, leaving the contribution of failure-specific feedback unclear. We study this question in simulated robot manipulation. A fixed lookup selects feedback templates using failure labels and the API variant. A frozen code model generates a fresh program after each scene reset. On the same 252 initial failures, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B recovers 85.3% within five retries, compared with 68.3% for resampling with the same retry cap. The advantage persists under fixed total-token budgets. Feedback from other episodes and fixed task guidance yield similar recovery point estimates, with no detected benefit from matching the coarse failure label. In a separate study, a fixed guided prompt used from the first attempt achieves an observed overall success rate similar to that of template-based feedback. Template-based feedback also lowers recovery on a nut-insertion task requiring a rim grasp, consistent with an incompatible center-grasp instruction. Evaluations of robot self-repair should include resampling, mismatched feedback, and concise, task-compatible static guidance as baselines.
introduction:
Code-as-policy agents translate language instructions into executable robot programs [1]. Their failures often follow clear patterns: a program may skip the grasp, release an object after lifting, or place it away from the target. A common response is iterative self-reflection. The model reads its failed program and execution trace, writes a critique, and tries again [2, 3, 4]. Retry success can reflect additional sampling, concise task instructions, feedback about the current failure, or editing the previous program. We ask whether feedback after failure improves recovery over guidance available from the first attempt.

We study this question with frozen Qwen2.5-Coder-3B/7B models in a reset-and-retry setting. Each retry starts from the original scene. Our main conditions generate a fresh program with the failed program omitted from the prompt. We use template-based feedback to study which information improves retry success. A fixed lookup selects instructions using the failure label and API variant, such as “MUST grasp the object before lifting.” We call this condition Compiled. The lookup lets us replace matched feedback with another episode’s feedback, hold the guidance fixed, or remove it while keeping the retry loop unchanged (Figure 1). Separate editing conditions expose the previous program and request a revision. All conditions restart the original scene. We do not test recovery from the physical state left by failure.

Compiled recovers 85.3% of the 252 initial failures within five retries, compared with 68.3% for resampling with the same retry cap. The gain persists under fixed total-token budgets. Feedback from other episodes and one fixed template per task produce similar point estimates. We detect no benefit from matching the coarse failure label to the current episode. The confidence intervals still allow differences between conditions. In a separate study, a fixed guided prompt used from the first attempt achieves an observed overall success rate similar to Compiled’s, with fewer tokens per solved episode. That comparison changes initial guidance and the generation instruction together. Their individual contributions remain unresolved.

We compare feedback content and program-generation strategies under matched retry budgets to test how additional sampling, reusable task guidance, and failure-label matching affect recovery. Evaluations of robot self-repair should include static guidance as a baseline for adaptive feedback.

title: ConDR: Conservative Reachability through Neural Hamilton-Jacobi Subsolutions
authors: Kendra Givens,Taylor T. Johnson,Bryan C. Ward,Thomas Beckers
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) Reachability identifies the unsafe states of a dynamical system from which it can be forced into failure under worst-case disturbance. However, classical grid-based solvers scale exponentially with state dimension. DeepReach improves scalability by replacing the grid with a neural value function trained on the HJ-Isaacs (HJI) variational inequality (VI), but penalizes both sides of the residual equally. This allows the learned value to lie above the true one and unsafe states to be misclassified as safe. We propose Conservative DeepReach (ConDR) which aims to learn a subsolution of the HJI VI such that the learned unsafe set contains the true one. ConDR enforces the obstacle branch and terminal condition by construction, pushes the HJI residual to a safety margin ϵ\epsilon below zero with a one-sided loss, and prevents the degenerate solution of classifying everything as unsafe. We prove that the exact solution of the margin-shifted VI that ConDR trains toward is a subsolution of the original VI so its unsafe set contains the true one and its value lies within ϵ​τ\epsilon\tau of the true value function. We compare against DeepReach and MADR in the established systems of Air3D, Air6D, a 9D multi-vehicle system, and a 13D quadrotor. ConDR reports the lowest rate of unsafe state misclassified and the lowest closed-loop collision rates with at most a small increase in intervention. On Air3D and Air6D, ConDR tolerates model mismatch that scales with ϵ\epsilon. At matched false-negative rates, ConDR’s unsafe sets are smaller than the baselines showing the safety is not obtained by trivial over-approximation.
introduction:
As more complex and autonomous systems are deployed in safety-critical settings, verifying their behavior becomes increasingly important. These systems often have nonlinear dynamics, operate under control and state constraints, and may be affected by external or even adversarial disturbances. Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability provides worst-case safety guarantees under exactly these conditions. By solving for the value function, HJ reachability identifies the backward reachable tube (BRT), which represents the set of states from which the system can be forced into the target set, a chosen unsafe set of states, within the time horizon under worst-case disturbance. The value function can be used to recover the optimal control policy.

However, HJ reachability suffers from the curse of dimensionality. Classical HJ solvers use level-set methods on a discretized grid [1] where both memory and runtime grow exponentially with the dimension of the system state. Exact methods can extend beyond low-dimensional systems, but require the system to decompose into coupled subsystems [2]. Recently, neural approaches have improved the scalability. DeepReach [3] overcomes this limitation by representing the value function by an implicit neural representation (INR) [4] instead of a grid, which avoids direct dependence on spatial discretizations and makes higher-dimensional problems more tractable. The ExactBC [5] variant removes the terminal condition by construction. MPC-guided Adversarial DeepReach (MADR) [6] expands on DeepReach and ExactBC by augmenting the loss with a self-generated signal from model predictive control (MPC) rollouts, which improves convergence. The learned value function is then used as a least-restrictive safety filter in closed loop rollouts [7], [8]. Control barrier functions [9] provide an alternative safety filter, but require the barrier function to be provided or learned beforehand, whereas HJ reachability only requires the dynamics.

Despite the scalability benefits, neural HJ approaches recover the exact value function only in the limit of a vanishing residual over the whole domain [10]. However, this is never achieved in practice, as the residual is typically nonzero at most points. As a result, the sign of the residual matters, i.e., a positive residual pushes the learned value function above the true one and results in higher false negatives (FNs) where unsafe states are classified as safe. A negative residual only enlarges the learned unsafe set resulting in higher false positives (FPs). Since both sides are penalized equally, FNs can be as frequent as FPs. Deploying a learned value function in a real control system requires some protection against the FNs. There exist methods that can bound the error of the model training [11], [12], but they inflate the volume of the level-set by the size of the worst violation. Additionally, neither changes the training objective that produced the violation.

We propose Conservative DeepReach (ConDR), a neural HJ reachability method that trains towards a subsolution of the HJI VI, such that the target BRT overapproximates the true one. We enforce the obstacle branch [13] and terminal condition of the HJI VI at all times by construction, using a one-sided L1 loss to push the residual to the safe side with safety margin ϵ\epsilon, and add a complementarity loss term to prevent the degenerate solution of declaring everything as unsafe. This results in smaller post-training corrections, which in turn yield a tighter tube volume and fewer collisions during closed-loop safety-filtering rollouts, while tolerating model mismatch up to ϵ\epsilon.

Contributions
Our key contributions are

ConDR: a conservative neural HJ reachability model that uses an easy to implement margin-shifted one-sided loss, trains toward a subsolution of the HJI VI, and composes with MADR.

Guarantees that the BRT of the exact margin-shifted VI solution contains the true BRT, overapproximated by at most ϵ​τ\epsilon\tau, and that a value function whose residual is at most −ϵ-\epsilon remains a subsolution under model mismatch up to ϵ\epsilon.

Evaluation against DeepReach and MADR under matched experimental setups on Air3D, Air6D, a 9D multi-vehicle system, and a 13D quadrotor where ConDR has the lowest FN, subsolution violations, and collision rates in every setting tested.

A tunable safety margin i.e. sweeping ϵ\epsilon on Air3D and Air6D shows the tolerated model mismatch scales with ϵ\epsilon with a linear accuracy cost in ϵ\epsilon.

title: PyRUA-REAL: Robot Exploration and Adaptive Learning through RSI in the Real World
authors: Qiang Wang,Jianxin Bi,Shulong Jiang,Ruiyang Si,Wenbo Huang,Kaiqi Chen,Jiaxin Li,Liyun Li,Xuanyi Li,Daquan Zhou
abstract:
Coding agents powered by models such as GPT-6-Astra connect spatial reasoning with executable robot behavior, raising the question of how such agents can produce lasting improvements in robot capabilities from physical interaction.
In this work, we study embodied recursive self-improvement (RSI) through
real-world exploration, code refinement, and deployment using PyRUA-REAL,
a framework in which coding agents retain interaction experience as
persistent memory and reusable executable skills that inform subsequent
exploration and improvement.
Our empirical study places physical manipulation at the center of the improvement process, examining how agents collaborate, what kinds of execution feedback support effective code refinement, and how task specifications and previously acquired skills influence robustness and task transfer.
We further investigate the efficiency and capability of the resulting programs when deployed without involving an online agent for decision-making.
Across eight real-world tasks, PyRUA-REAL achieves an average success rate of 91.1%.
In complementary evaluation on 42 tasks from the RoboDojo benchmark, it achieves an average success rate of 84.4%.
This study provides empirical guidance for turning physical exploration
into reusable robot skills that support continued improvement and
robust, efficient deployment.
introduction:
Large language models can translate task instructions into robot programs
that combine perception, spatial reasoning, and feedback
control [11, 6]. Coding agents powered by
models such as GPT-6-Astra extend this interaction by executing code,
inspecting observations, and adapting subsequent actions through execution
feedback [16]. These capabilities make code a practical
interface between high-level reasoning and physical behavior. They also
raise a question beyond completing an individual task:
How can coding agents turn physical interaction experience into
robot capabilities that persist and improve across successive attempts?

Experience-based adaptation and iterative code modification offer ways
to improve agents while keeping foundation model parameters
fixed [15, 24]. In robotics, recent work
has explored skill and agent-harness evolution in
simulation [18], simulation-based practice followed by
physical deployment [20], and policy improvement through
direct robot interaction [22, 19]. Building on
these developments, we study embodied recursive self-improvement (RSI)
as a process in which execution experience informs code revisions and is
retained as memory and reusable skills for subsequent exploration.
Our focus is an empirical account of this process in real-world
manipulation, tracing how capabilities are acquired, refined beyond first
success, and converted into programs for deployment.

Physical exploration presents challenges at several levels. Agents must
decide which experiments to run, which implementation details to revise,
and when to reconsider the underlying approach. Repeated local changes
may leave an unsuitable perception or control strategy intact. Execution
feedback is also ambiguous: an apparent task failure can originate in
motion, perception, or the procedure used to verify success. Moreover,
success under one configuration does not establish robustness to changes
in object positions, orientations, or task requirements. Retaining a
successful implementation therefore raises further questions about its
reuse on new tasks and its ability to operate without repeated online
agent decisions. Understanding embodied RSI requires examining these
aspects of the improvement process alongside task success.

We present PyRUA-REAL (Python-based Robot-Use Agent for Robot Exploration and Adaptive Learning) as an embodied RSI framework for this study (Figure 1). A researcher
agent selects experimental objectives and technical approaches, while an
engineer agent implements programs, executes robot trials, and diagnoses
failures. Their interaction connects local code improvement with task-level
reassessment. A persistent repository records environmental facts,
attempted approaches, execution outcomes, and reusable implementations,
allowing later experiments to build on earlier experience while model
parameters remain fixed. For deployment, the resulting code can be frozen
and executed without runtime language-model calls, while still responding
to live observations through its perception, control, and recovery routines.
This separation enables us to study both the process of developing robot
capabilities and the behavior of the programs that retain them.

Our experiments cover eight manipulation tasks on a dual-arm Franka
platform, spanning reasoning, long-horizon execution, precise contact,
deformable objects, and bimanual coordination. Recorded development success
averages 91.1% across tasks. These rates aggregate attempts across code revisions; frozen-program
performance is evaluated separately. Complementary evaluation on 42 RoboDojo
tasks yields 84.82% success, averaged equally over five capability groups,
compared with reported results of 50.35% for PyRUA-Lean and 22.48% for
GPT-6-Astra. Our main contributions can be summarized as:

An empirical study of skill acquisition and
continued improvement through real-world interaction.
Across eight physical manipulation tasks, we trace how coding
agents turn exploration experience into executable robot skills
and improve them beyond first successful rollout, documenting gains and
trade-offs in task completion, execution time, and placement
precision across program revisions.

An empirical study of skill acquisition and
continued improvement through real-world interaction.
Across eight physical manipulation tasks, we trace how coding
agents turn exploration experience into executable robot skills
and improve them beyond first successful rollout, documenting gains and
trade-offs in task completion, execution time, and placement
precision across program revisions.

Case studies on the factors shaping embodied RSI.
Through comparative experiments and diagnostic case studies,
we examine how agent coordination, execution feedback, explicit
task requirements, and previously acquired skills affect
revision efficiency, robustness, and transfer to new tasks.

An evaluation of the resulting robot capabilities
and their deployment costs.
Real-world evaluations compare frozen programs with online agent
execution, quantifying execution-time benefits and identifying
situations that still require online assistance.
Complementary evaluation on 42 RoboDojo tasks measures performance
across five capability groups against reported baselines.

title: Dexterous Robotic Hands in the Foundation-Model Era: A Full-Stack Survey of Hardware, Data, Cross-Embodiment Transfer, Learning, and Evaluation
authors: Ji Pei
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
comment: . Structured narrative review of hardware, data, cross-embodiment transfer, foundation models, tactile sensing, and evaluation for dexterous robotic hands
abstract: Dexterous robotic hands are increasingly coupled to large-scale human data and foundation models, yet progress in hardware, representation learning and evaluation is often assessed separately. This survey reviews work from January 2024 to early November 2026, with earlier studies included to establish technical lineages. We organize the literature into five interdependent layers: hardware; data collection and curation; cross-embodiment transfer; learning and foundation models; and evaluation and applications. Human hand–object understanding and tactile sensing provide two cross-cutting perspectives. A system-level architecture, comparative tables and five case analyses connect design choices across these layers. We distinguish within-study experimental comparisons from heterogeneous corpus statistics, vendor specifications and company-reported results. Three conclusions emerge. First, the value of human data depends on kinematic, visual and contact alignment, not recording volume alone. Second, shared action representations and foundation policies do not remove embodiment-specific constraints on force, latency and contact. Third, task completion is insufficient to establish physical correctness or deployment readiness. Evidence remains limited for zero-shot transfer of contact-rich skills between morphologically different hands, long-duration reliability, and cross-sensor tactile generalization. We identify eleven open problems and propose reporting interfaces and controlled comparisons that can make full-stack progress more measurable. The review is a structured narrative synthesis rather than a pooled performance ranking or an exhaustive systematic review.
introduction:
The human hand is the interface through which most of the built world is operated: tools, containers, fasteners, cables, keyboards and laboratory glassware are all designed around five fingers, opposable thumbs and a sense of touch. Building robot hands that can use this world without redesigning it has been a goal of robotics for decades [1, 2, 3, 4]. For most of that time, progress was limited on three fronts at once. Anthropomorphic hands were expensive, fragile and hard to maintain (the Shadow Dexterous Hand [5] costs more than US$100k); data for multi-fingered manipulation were scarce because teleoperating 20 joints is slow and lacks force feedback; and learning methods for high-DoF hands were largely confined to single tasks trained with reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation [6, 7, 8, 9].

Between 2024 and 2026 all three constraints loosened at the same time. On the hardware side, a 22-DoF hand became available for about US$6.5k [10], a six-DoF linkage hand for under US$1k [11], and open-source hands for a few hundred dollars [12, 13]; Chinese market trackers report shipments growing from about 19k units in 2025 to a forecast of 70k in 2026 [14]. On the data side, collection moved away from teleoperating a robot towards capturing humans directly: wearable exoskeletons and gloves that are kinematically matched to the robot hand [15, 16, 17, 18], and egocentric video with 3D hand tracking at the scale of 10310^{3}–10510^{5} hours [19, 20, 21, 22]. Industrial players report even larger corpora, with press reports of 270k to more than 500k hours of wearable data [23, 24] and about ten million glove episodes collected in homes [25]. On the learning side, generalist VLA models [26, 27, 28, 29, 30] and world-action models [31, 32] began to target high-DoF hands, with hierarchical systems that add a dedicated high-frequency contact layer below the policy [33, 34].

These developments are tightly coupled. A hand whose kinematics and camera placement mirror a human’s can reuse human data with little retargeting error; data collected with a hand-specific exoskeleton usually require additional retargeting for reuse with a different hand; whether a unified action space is needed depends on how many embodiments a model must serve; and benchmark results only transfer if hardware, sensing and evaluation protocols are comparable. Recent evidence makes this coupling explicit. EgoScale reports a log-linear relation between human-pretraining hours and validation loss, alongside improved downstream completion [20]; Liber-0 reports that, under identical post-training, 10k hours of glove data outperform 2M hours of web video, and that a more human-like robot benefits more from the same human data [35]; DexWild finds that too much human data relative to robot data (1:5) hurts performance compared with 1:2 [17]. None of these findings can be understood from the data layer alone.

Figure 2 groups selected milestones by year and layer.

Figure 1 gives the complementary systems view: the survey follows the forward path from human or robot data to deployment, while treating failures, contact signals and benchmark results as feedback into the next design cycle.

Classical surveys cover the mechanics of robot hands [2, 3], dexterous manipulation in general [1, 4], or a single learning paradigm such as RL [36], in-hand manipulation [37] or imitation learning [38]. A recent survey organizes embodied data into a “pyramid” [39] without focusing on hands. In contrast, we treat the dexterous hand as a full stack and survey how its layers co-evolve. We focus on work released between January 2024 and early November 2026, and include earlier work where it defines a lineage (e.g., Dactyl [6] for sim-to-real in-hand reorientation, DexPilot [40] for vision-based retargeting).

This is a structured narrative review of sources released between January 2024 and 4 November 2026, with earlier work included for foundational methods. The source collection covers arXiv, major robotics, learning and vision venues, project pages, company technical blogs and trade press. Core studies concern multi-fingered hands; adjacent gripper and whole-body studies are included when they motivate a transferable component and are identified as such. Although reference-checking notes accompany the source collection, a complete search log, screening counts and an independent dual-review record are not available. We therefore do not claim exhaustive coverage or systematic-review completeness. Publication, language, company-disclosure and positive-result biases may affect the synthesis.

We separate the source of a claim (paper/preprint, company technical report, or secondary press) from the setting in which it was measured (simulation, real robot, or deployment). Within-study ablations support local comparisons, whereas cross-paper plots summarize reported scale or cost and are not leaderboards. Recommended architectures, maturity assessments and the kitchen design are explicitly our synthesis, not independently validated deployments.

title: Where Is VLA Inference Time Spent? Bottlenecks and Optimization Interactions Across GPUs
authors: Muhammad Danish Waseem,Ahmed Ali-Eldin Hassan
abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models map camera observations and language instructions to robot actions.
However, their large backbones and repeated action generation can make inference take longer than the robot real-time requirements for its next action.
To reduce the load of VLA computations, researchers have proposed multiple optimization approaches, including quantization and pruning. These optimizations can be combined with other general optimizations such as better kernel compilation or using CUDA graphs instead of the eager mode. However, most of these optimization results are usually reported on a single GPU type, typically for a few VLA models, with no analysis on what are the real bottlenecks for a model on a particular hardware or how these optimization would generalize beyond the reported results.
In this paper, we provide a comprehensive measurement study of seven families of inference optimization methods, from CUDA graphs and compilation to token pruning and quantization, on seven state-of-the-art VLAs evaluated on four GPU families ranging from a datacenter H100 to an embedded Jetson Thor. We analyse how CPU launch overhead, memory bandwidth and kernel efficiency jointly shape optimization gains, and how applying one method changes the benefit of another.
From this analysis, we derive VLA-Triage, guidelines for stacking optimizations under latency budgets.
The guidelines identify which stages can provide the required saving and which combinations need testing in the deployed execution mode.
introduction:
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) are multimodal models that enable robots to translate visual observations and natural-language instructions into executable actions, such as moving an arm or opening a gripper.
They typically build on pretrained vision-language models that are trained on robot demonstrations, connecting visual and semantic knowledge with the physical skills needed to perform tasks Zitkovich and others (2023).

VLAs aim to support general-purpose robots that can follow diverse instructions and generalize to unfamiliar objects and environments Kim et al. (2024); Intelligence et al. (2025).

Internally, VLAs typically run a VLM with millions or billions
of parameters to generate the robot’s control steps. This limits the reaction time of a robot by the inference latency of the VLA. At each policy inference step, a typical VLA receives a natural-language instruction, represented as text, and image observations from one or more cameras. In a common architecture, a vision encoder converts camera images into visual embeddings, which are projected into the language model’s embedding space and processed jointly with the instruction tokens by a transformer backbone. The resulting representations condition the prediction of a robot action or a short sequence of actions with the action generations performed using an action-head.

VLAs need to be real-time, providing a robot with a sufficient number of actions such that the robot does not stall. Robots typically operate with strictly bounded latencies to maintain a continuous, closed-loop feedback cycle. In addition, if a VLA is too slow, it acts on stale visual data, i.e., by the time the model computes and outputs a command, the physical world has already changed leading to dropped objects, collisions, or unstable movement. This is challenging, especially when the VLA is running on the limited on-robot hardware.
One approach to reduce the computational time of VLAs is to use optimization methods such as, token pruning, quantization, compilation, or CUDA graphs. However, our study of 25 published paper (Appendix E) reveals that most of these approaches do not consider the intricacies of the different VLA architectures and the hardware they run on.

VLAs today vary in architecture, backbone size, visual token count and action path.
These choices decide which stage dominates latency and therefore which optimization can help.
The backbone size sets how many weight bytes every pass must read, so a large model could spend most of its time reading the model weights, whereas a smaller model could spend its time in the denoising loop of action head. In addition, previous work on VLA optimizations does not consider the inherent bottlenecks of the underlying hardware platform projecting generality of the results while only evaluating the work on a limited set of hardware. For example, many previous works evaluate the optimizations on GPUs such as NVIDIA RTX 4090s, a GPU that has a heavy weight and high power draw—it is neither designed for running on a robot platform nor is available on most clouds, hence, not supporting a cloud-robotic deployment.

In this work, we provide a comprehensive study of VLA optimization performance. We start by analyzing seven families of inference optimization methods, namely; CUDA graphs, compilation, fused attention, batching, reducing the denoising steps, token pruning and quantization. We evaluate these optimizations on seven VLAs, namely; OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, LLaVA-VLA, CogACT, π0.5\pi_{0.5}, GR00T, and SmolVLA, with four kinds of action head (token decoding, parallel decoding, diffusion, flow matching). These combinations are then tested on four different GPU families; a datacenter grade
H100, a cloud A10G, a consumer RTX 4090, and an embedded Jetson Thor.

Our evaluations focus on the latency gains of these optimizations, showing that the optimization results are non-uniform. Gains
differ between GPUs in magnitude, in sign and in rank.

For example, compiling GR00T with CUDA graphs makes it faster on the H100 and slower on the Thor, and storing
CogACT’s weights in 8 bits makes it faster on the A10G and slower on the H100. In addition, we find that the choice of baseline to compare an optimization method to can be misleading, e.g.,
FastV Chen et al. (2024) and several other token pruning methods (Appendix E) select the visual tokens to prune by their attention weights, so it is typically
evaluated and compared to running with unfused attention. However, VLAs in production are often deployed with fused attention kernels such as FlashAttention-2 Dao (2024), which never write attention weights to memory. Measured against unfused attention, FastV at 5050% pruning saves 21.421.4% of OpenVLA-OFT’s inference time on an H100. Measured against FlashAttention-2, the same run saves 6.96.9%, because the selector reads attention weights and forces the slower kernel (Table 5).

Our analysis also shows that each stage of inference is limited by either the GPU compute power, its memory bandwidth, or the CPU that
launches the GPU kernels. This means that the same stage can be subject to a different bottleneck on different GPUs. Therefore, a proposed optimization method’s benefit may not extend beyond the platform it is tested on.

In addition, optimization methods can be combined, or stacked. Hence, running multiple optimizations in sequence means that later VLA optimizations act on the inference stages that are left by previous optimizations. Hence, the total gains from a later method depends on the methods applied before it. Based on the above observations, we formalize VLA-Triage, a systematic approach for evaluating the expected gains of multiple VLA optimization methods on a given hardware. To summarize, our paper has three connected contributions:

Characterisation: paired measurements of inference-stage costs and optimization benefits across seven VLAs and four GPU-host platforms, including cases where a method helps on one platform and hurts on another.

Interactions: We show how graphs, compilation and pruning change the gains for later applied methods, and how reusing standalone gains can change latency-budget decisions.

Guidelines: A measurement-based workflow for choosing an execution mode, checking feasibility under stated assumptions, and validating method combinations to be used in deployment.

1. Characterisation: paired measurements of inference-stage costs and optimization benefits across seven VLAs and four GPU-host platforms, including cases where a method helps on one platform and hurts on another.

2. Interactions: We show how graphs, compilation and pruning change the gains for later applied methods, and how reusing standalone gains can change latency-budget decisions.

3. Guidelines: A measurement-based workflow for choosing an execution mode, checking feasibility under stated assumptions, and validating method combinations to be used in deployment.

title: When to Ask for Help: Uncertainty-Triggered Aerial Refinement for Off-Road Navigation
authors: Pranay Samineni,Adam Thorpe,John Chubick,Anand Balakrishnan,Christian Ellis,Swarat Chaudhuri,Ufuk Topcu
comment: Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Heterogeneous air–ground teams can use aerial sensing to address the limited range and viewpoint of ground-vehicle sensors, but deciding when the UGV needs assistance and what information the UAV should collect remains a challenge.
This paper presents a planner-conditioned air–ground assistance method that evaluates how uncertain map information affects the UGV’s current MPPI rollouts.
When navigation remains degraded, we score the same rollouts under resolved map hypotheses, select the map layer with the largest useful improvement, request the corresponding aerial measurement, fuse the returned information, and replan.
Unlike approaches driven by fixed support roles, task structure, or uncertainty alone, our method conditions assistance on whether resolving uncertainty improves predicted ground navigation.
Across 180 simulation trials on three off-road routes, the method achieves 98.9% goal attainment while reducing mean UAV flight time by 87.7% relative to continuous greedy aerial mapping.
Aggregated across the routes, each second of estimated UAV flight time saves 2.94 s of UGV navigation time.
Field experiments spanning approximately 2 km of UGV operation demonstrate uncertainty resolution and successful navigation recovery. Project page: https://anonymous.4open.science/w/when-to-ask-for-help/.
introduction:
Ground vehicles operating alone in outdoor, unstructured environments are limited by their sensing perspective, mobility, and onboard perception.
Ground-level sensors have limited range, suffer from occlusion, and can provide incomplete or ambiguous information about terrain, obstacles, and vehicle state.
An unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) may therefore fail to complete an otherwise achievable mission because it cannot obtain the information needed to navigate safely and reliably.
Heterogeneous robot teams address this by combining complementary sensing and mobility.
An unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) can observe the environment and the ground vehicle from viewpoints unavailable to the UGV and provide information that improves the ground robot’s navigation state.
However, UAV assistance is limited by flight endurance and cannot be used continuously throughout long missions.
The key problem is therefore deciding when the UGV needs assistance and what information the UAV should provide.

This paper presents a heterogeneous air–ground teaming approach for recovering degraded UGV navigation caused by incomplete or uncertain information in off-road environments.
The UGV maintains separate navigation map layers together with their associated uncertainty.
When navigation degrades, we evaluate the current MPPI rollout population [1] against counterfactual versions of these map layers and score how the resulting map changes affect predicted ground motion.
We then select the corresponding UAV sensing action for the map layer with the largest useful improvement.
The UAV collects the requested aerial information, such as an elevation map or semantic map, and communicates it to the UGV. The UGV fuses the information into its navigation maps, updates the planner representation, and replans.

Existing air-ground systems use heterogeneous sensing for cooperative localization, mapping, exploration, and navigation.
Many approaches assign the UAV a fixed support role, invoke aerial sensing according to predefined task logic, or trigger additional sensing from uncertainty in a perception output [2].
These sensing criteria do not directly determine whether the uncertainty affects the UGV’s current navigation decision.
Uncertainty can be large in regions that have no effect on the current route, while localized uncertainty can prevent the UGV from identifying or executing a safe path.
We therefore evaluate uncertainty through its effect on ground navigation and request UAV assistance only when resolving uncertainty is predicted to improve the UGV’s ability to make progress.

Our main contribution, illustrated in Figure 1, is a planner-conditioned air–ground assistance method that determines when the UAV should sense by evaluating resolved map hypotheses against current UGV rollouts and selecting an aerial sensing action based on the change in navigation score.
Across 180 simulation trials, our method achieves 98.9% goal attainment with 87.7% less mean UAV flight time than continuous greedy mapping.
Across three routes, each estimated UAV flight second saves 2.94​s2.94\,\mathrm{s} of UGV navigation time.
Field experiments spanning approximately 2 km of autonomous UGV operation through unstructured routes demonstrate repeated resolution of map uncertainty and resumed navigation following aerial assistance.

title: Cognitive and Behavioural Effects of Haptic Feedback for ROV Teleoperation in Hazardous Environments
authors: Joshua Brown,Ildar Farkhatdinov,Michael Jenkin
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
comment: Accepted for IEEE Telepresence 2026
abstract: Teleoperating a Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV) in complex underwater environments presents unique challenges. Dynamic, three dimensional obstacles and unseen water currents pose real risks to expensive robotic hardware in environments in which recovery can be next to impossible. This paper explores the cognitive effects of haptic feedback to improve vehicle safety in such environments. An in-water study is analysed with a ROV exposed to controlled cross-currents, with environmental information presented via a soft and vibrating haptic touchpad.
introduction:
Teleoperating a robot underwater carries significant and unique challenges. Unlike ground robots, ROVs can encounter dynamic hazards from any direction in 3D space, which may or may not be visible to onboard sensors or cameras. Unlike drones, visibility underwater is notoriously poor, with inconsistent lighting, high turbidity, and visual distortions among the many problems associated with operating in this environment [1, 2]. Haptic feedback has been proposed as a means of delivering denser spatial information to the operators of remote robots, however the effects of this additional information on cognitive load and confidence remain broadly unexplored.

Haptic communication of environmental and robot state information is an increasingly well-investigated area. It is known that force feedback can be used to provide directional cues to warn of hazards [3, 4] or stimulate flight instability [5]. Haptic feedback has also been used to enhance communication between humans and robots in shared control paradigms, particularly in underwater environments [6]. Other examples of haptic feedback being used to enhance underwater teleoperation include use of force feedback to restrict access to hazardous ‘keep-out’ zones [7] and mitigate the effects of satellite delay in long-distance teleoperation [8].
For a full and recent review of the applications of haptic feedback to robot teleoperation, see [9].

In a recent in-water study, we showed that multimodal haptic feedback comprising vibration and softness-change can improve the quantitative positioning accuracy, and path efficiency of operators of ROVs in the presence of invisible cross-currents [10]. This paper extends these previously published quantitative performance indicators with a new exploration of the effect of haptic feedback on operator confidence and the specific components of cognitive load. We present a controlled, in-water study investigating the behavioural and cognitive effects of haptic feedback during hazardous teleoperation scenarios.

title: Compounding Physical RSI: Turning Execution Failure into Inherited Capability
authors: Yixuan Yang,Qiang Chen,Run Shao,Shuwei Dong,Wenhao Li,Yunpeng Wang,Wenhan Fang,Haomiao Wu,Xingyu Wang,Lichen Man,Rong Zhang,Xuezhi Cui,Yuan Liu,Bingyan Lu,Jiawei Ma,Xiaoyang Ma,Zhemin Sun,Zhuorui Yao,Yutong Dong,Yuxuan Zhao,Yichong Mu,Jiabao Jiang,Wenxuan Deng,Junling Zhou,Yi Chen,Deyu Zhang,Yiming Yan,Yige Yuan,Shan You,Fei Wang,Haifeng Li,Hongyan Xu,Yichao Cao,Xiu Su
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have substantially advanced generalist robot manipulation by unifying visual perception, language grounding, and action generation within a single policy [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Recent efforts have extended this paradigm across diverse embodiments [6, 7, 8], refined spatial representations and fine-tuning efficiency [9, 10], and scaled pre-training to over 100K hours of real-world trajectories [11]. Yet despite these advances in pre-training scale, a generalist policy still encounters many of its fundamental capability limits only after static training has ended and closed-loop physical execution begins.

This limitation stems from the sequential, stage-gated nature of manipulation. A robot must approach an object before grasping it, and must establish a stable grasp before transporting or placing it. Consequently, a deficiency in a downstream stage remains masked until the policy reliably passes all preceding stages: a policy that fails during grasping never reveals how it would fail during transport, because its rollouts never reach that state. Moreover, the failure modes encountered during transport depend directly on the contact configuration produced by the grasp, as each policy induces its own closed-loop state distribution [12]. We define the earliest task stage that a policy cannot yet pass reliably as its capability frontier. Because behavior beyond this frontier remains unobserved during execution, a fixed dataset cannot anticipate how the evolving policy will fail once it crosses the current barrier. Each successful fix advances the capability frontier and exposes the next latent failure mode.

A moving capability frontier naturally motivates Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) for embodied intelligence. Rooted in classical formulations of self-referential learning [13, 14] and renewed in modern foundation-model research [15], RSI recognizes that when a policy’s next bottleneck becomes visible only after the current one is resolved, improvement cannot be reduced to a single static training run. Instead, the robot must iteratively execute, diagnose its own failures, learn from them, and execute again so that each generation uncovers the empirical evidence required by the next. Physical RSI formalizes this paradigm for embodied systems, where contact-rich physical experience drives persistent policy evolution [16, 17]. Recent studies have explored key facets of embodied self-improvement, including inference-time self-correction and subtask backtracking [18], deployment-time adaptation and memory consolidation [19, 20], and iterative policy updates via autonomous data collection or residual reinforcement learning [8, 21, 22, 23].

While these efforts show that a robot policy can improve over a single update or within narrow task settings, the central open question is whether such improvements can compound across generations. The potential for compounding follows directly from the staged structure of manipulation. Because a task succeeds only when every constituent stage succeeds, overall task completion behaves like a product of stage-level pass rates. In such a product, stage-level gains multiply: stabilizing a grasp not only lifts the completion rate of every subsequent stage, but also sends a larger fraction of rollouts across the capability frontier, generating richer downstream evidence for the next generation. A recursive loop can therefore achieve super-additive progress across rounds, provided that each generation builds reliably upon the verified gains of its predecessor.

However, making Physical RSI compound in practice is hindered by three fundamental bottlenecks that mirror the lifecycle of a policy update. First, execution feedback suffers from opaque temporal credit assignment [24]: a terminal failure flag indicates that a trial failed, but rarely localizes which stage broke, as visible failure often manifests long after the erroneous action that caused it. Second, failed rollouts lack corrective supervision: even a precisely localized failure shows what went wrong without specifying the counterfactual action the policy should have executed. Third, multi-task gains are fragile under shared weights: because a generalist policy encodes all skills in one parameter set, an unconstrained update that repairs one failure stage can silently degrade previously mastered tasks [25]. Under the same multiplicative structure that amplifies stage-level gains, such cross-task regressions multiply losses, causing naive recursive loops to accumulate policy churn rather than lasting capability.

We argue that the core challenge of Physical RSI is therefore achieving compounding—ensuring that every generation diagnoses its active frontier, resolves it effectively, and inherits verified capabilities without regression. To this end, we propose Compounding Physical RSI, a three-stage self-evolving policy framework, and evaluate the resulting generalist policy, CSU-AI-07, across all 42 tasks of RoboDojo-Sim. Our main contributions are:

Formulating compounding as the central problem of Physical RSI. We show how the stage-gated structure of manipulation necessitates recursive improvement and establish a formal structural definition of compounding across policy generations.

A closed-loop Diagnosis–Remedy–Retention framework. We couple stage-level capability-gap diagnosis with objective-conditioned offline reinforcement learning (remedy) and evaluation-guided weight-space consolidation (retention), ensuring that targeted frontier fixes are absorbed without eroding prior skills.

State-of-the-art generalist benchmark performance. Across the 42 tasks of RoboDojo-Sim, CSU-AI-07 ranks first on the overall leaderboard in both Overall Score (26.15) and Success Rate (20.70%), outperforming thirteen public generalist policies by substantial margins.

1. Formulating compounding as the central problem of Physical RSI. We show how the stage-gated structure of manipulation necessitates recursive improvement and establish a formal structural definition of compounding across policy generations.

2. A closed-loop Diagnosis–Remedy–Retention framework. We couple stage-level capability-gap diagnosis with objective-conditioned offline reinforcement learning (remedy) and evaluation-guided weight-space consolidation (retention), ensuring that targeted frontier fixes are absorbed without eroding prior skills.

3. State-of-the-art generalist benchmark performance. Across the 42 tasks of RoboDojo-Sim, CSU-AI-07 ranks first on the overall leaderboard in both Overall Score (26.15) and Success Rate (20.70%), outperforming thirteen public generalist policies by substantial margins.

title: Detecting Silent Action-Interface Mismatch with Calibrated Relational World Models
authors: Rui Zhu,Xurui Li,Haixu Tang
comment: Accepted at the CoRL 2026 Workshop on Modeling Uncertainty in Robotic World Models (UncertainWM). including of supplementary material
abstract:
A robot action can satisfy shape and range constraints yet carry the wrong
semantics: axes may be permuted, signs inverted, rotations rescaled, or gripper
polarity reversed. We study learned state–action–effect relations as offline
contracts for detecting these mismatches and ranking their likely fields. Clean
held-out transitions calibrate alarms; a fixed inverse vocabulary supports
closed-set localization. On ten LIBERO Spatial tasks comprising 432 source
episodes, a capacity-controlled comparison at 2.5% empirical clean false-positive
rate gives 46.1% recall for a ridge forward residual, 61.0% for a four-component
joint Gaussian mixture, and 65.7% for the exact conditional of that same mixture.
The joint score retains a 14.9 percentage-point advantage over ridge, while
conditioning improves recall by a further 4.7 points. Joint scoring instead has
higher localization: 95.8% versus 94.6%. These matched-rate comparisons are
retrospective diagnostics, not deployment calibration guarantees. Earlier
Object/Goal results broaden tasks within the LIBERO convention; DROID, all three
HYDRA tasks, short temporal faults, small offsets, exact repair, and simulated
mitigation fail their respective gates, while xArm contributes one task only.
The evidence supports a bounded offline diagnostic and a detection–localization
tradeoff, rather than joint-density superiority or cross-robot safety.
introduction:
World models usually predict dynamics or support planning. At a controller
boundary, they can also ask whether an action’s semantics agree with the observed
transition. A seven-dimensional action vector may mix normalized translation,
axis-angle rotation and gripper commands. Components can agree on shape and bounds
while disagreeing about scale, axes, signs, rotation units or polarity. Such a
command is numerically legal but inconsistent with the recorded state change.

We study whether recorded state–action–next-state tuples can supply an
executable contract for this failure class. A detector is trained on clean
transitions, a disjoint clean split fixes its alarm threshold, and in-range semantic
mutations are applied only after that calibration is frozen. After an alarm, the
system evaluates a declared set of inverse transformations and reports the one that
best restores relational consistency. This separates two questions that aggregate
anomaly scores often conflate: whether the transition should be inspected and
which contract field is the most plausible explanation.

The diagnostic addresses interface semantics, not perception, planning, contact or
task progress. Replay supplies the factual next state of the original action, not
the physical outcome of executing a corrupted action. We evaluate offline alarms
and closed-set localization; they do not measure task success or safe correction.

The study separates three sources of apparent advantage: using the observed
transition, representing multimodal clean behavior, and choosing an alarm operating
point. The original joint-mixture comparison outperformed a ridge forward residual,
but those methods had different achieved false-positive rates. A post-decision
capacity-controlled analysis addresses both confounds. At matched empirical clean
FPR, the exact conditional of the fitted mixture has higher detection recall than
the joint score; the joint score retains better closed-set localization. We report
that reversal alongside episode-level uncertainty and the external and closed-loop
failures that bound the method’s use.

title: SCRUB: Contact-Based Surface-Frame Estimation for Force-Motion Control with an Armless Quadruped
authors: Sourav Selvaraj,Juan Pablo Espinosa Chessal,Mahdi Agheli
abstract:
Wiping, sanding, and inspection robots press a sliding tool on a surface with
controlled force. Controlling that force needs the surface normal,
which is unknown on real-world, unmapped surfaces. Surface-normal estimators can help estimate the surface normal, but they either need a friction model or assume that the instantaneous tool velocity lies along the surface; however, walking violates this assumption.
We propose SCRUB, a contact-based surface-frame estimator, which lets an armless quadruped slide a
body-mounted tool along near-vertical surfaces in the absence of known, axis-aligned, or vision-predicted normals. SCRUB’s predictive
controller presses and slides the tool using a Kalman-filter estimate of
the normal from two cues: 1) A force cue measures the estimate’s tilt
across the motion. If friction directly opposes the motion, the cue is
zero exactly when that tilt is zero, for any friction coefficient.
However, if the cue’s sliding direction is wrong, friction appears as a
false tilt. 2) A velocity cue measures tilt along the motion. Walking
and pressing move the tool in and out. SCRUB therefore subtracts the commanded
press rate from the tool velocity, averages the result over each gait
cycle, and treats this mean as lying along the surface. On
Unitree Go1 hardware at nominal speed and load, SCRUB completed every
wall traverse and column orbit. No orbit completed with
either cue removed, without gait averaging, or with a fixed normal.
introduction:
Robotic wiping and sanding need force–motion control: the robot presses a tool along the surface normal while sliding it along the surface [1, 2, 3]. The controller therefore needs the local surface frame: the normal and two directions in the surface [4]. We study force–motion control on an armless quadruped that slides a trunk-mounted tool along a flat wall and around a curved column (Fig. 1). Without an arm, the robot saves mass and cost, but its trunk and stance feet must move the tool, resist the contact force, and keep the robot balanced [5, 6]. Hence, a frame error makes the tool slide in the wrong direction and changes the contact wrench the legs must balance.

On an unmapped curved surface like the column of Fig. 1, the frame is unknown and rotates as the tool slides, and deformation of the tool’s soft silicone bumper shifts the effective normal [7]. Since the bumper also hides the contact patch from vision, we estimate the frame from contact. Contact-based estimation faces two problems. First, friction tilts the force off the normal, and correcting that tilt needs a friction model [7, 8]. Second, the controller moves the tool in and out to hold the force, and the gait compresses and releases the bumper (gait ripple). The tool velocity is therefore not always tangent.

Hybrid and operational-space controllers take the frame as given [1, 2], whereas constraint-based task specification estimates uncertain geometry within a known task model [9]. Estimators recover constraints from force [8], from force and motion on robot arms [10], or by touch with a leg [11]. Three others need no known friction coefficient. One takes the normal perpendicular to the tool velocity [12]; another places it in the plane of the contact force and sliding direction [13]; and a third subtracts friction drag with a coefficient fitted online [14]. However, each assumes that the instantaneous tool velocity is tangent, an assumption that is violated with walking gait.

Legged robots learn end-effector force control [15] and plan or learn interaction forces with an arm [16], a leg [17], multiple contacts [18], or the body [19]. Mahmud et al. [20] slide a body-mounted structure, as extra support for an arm, on planes with known normals. Zeng et al. [21] regulate wiping force on a wheeled-legged robot with the normal aligned to a controller axis, and humanoids wipe walls in a calibrated frame [22] or along normals predicted from vision [23]. Focchi et al. [13] estimate the normal under a sliding foot, but none of these robots estimates the surface frame from contact for a sliding tool.

To estimate the rotating frame without a surface map, we propose Surface Contact Regulation Using the Body (SCRUB) as shown in Fig. 2. A Kalman filter corrects its normal estimate using two cues, called measurement rows, including force and velocity rows (Fig. 3), which measure the estimate’s tilt across and along the slide. If friction acts exactly opposite to the motion, the force lies in the sliding plane of the true normal and sliding direction [13]. The force row therefore measures cross-slide tilt from the force component perpendicular to the estimated sliding plane. As along-slide tilt barely affects the force row, the velocity row measures it from the tool velocity [12, 13]. This row averages the tool velocity minus the commanded press rate over each gait cycle. Since most gait ripple cancels in this mean, the row treats the mean as tangent. Using the estimate, centroidal model predictive control (MPC) [5, 24, 25] plans body motion, foot forces, and the tool reaction force. Whole-body control (WBC) turns the plan into joint torques [26]. Our contributions are:

A contact-based surface-frame estimator for a walking robot’s sliding tool,
with a gait-averaged velocity row and a force row that extends the
sliding-plane cue of [13] (Secs. III-A–III-D). Ideally, the force row is zero exactly when the cross-slide tilt is zero, for any friction coefficient and even when the tool velocity has a normal component (Proposition 1).

An interaction-wrench
MPC [6, 18, 27]
adapted to an armless quadruped’s trunk-mounted tool. The MPC plans the tool
reaction with a first-order lag, a drag cost, and a cap on the binormal force
(Secs. IV-A–IV-C).

In horizontal slides on Unitree Go1 hardware (Sec. V), SCRUB completed 5/5 flat-wall traverses, 5/5 orbits of a constant-curvature column, and 89 of 90 trials in a speed and load sweep on both surfaces. With each condition tuned individually (Sec. V-A), no orbit completed with a fixed normal, our reimplementation of the friction-compensated normal [14], either row removed, a velocity row without gait averaging, or the MPC’s tool reaction removed. An MPC that plans only the normal part of the tool reaction completed 2/5 orbits.

title: Dynamic Shape Control of Soft Trunk Robots
authors: Hehui Zheng,Marc Stampanoni,Roshan S. Kaundinya,Ronan Hinchet,George Haller,Robert K. Katzschmann
abstract: Controlling the shape profile of soft trunk robots extends their reach into complex regions of the workspace and enhances their use in practical applications. Recent advances in soft robot design have enabled soft trunk robots to achieve greater flexibility in conforming to complex shapes. Specifically, trunk robots whose geometries are designed as helicoids have been shown to enable extreme shape-changing capabilities. Their compliance makes them highly nonlinear, which in turn makes shape control difficult. On similar tendon-driven trunk robots, model-based controllers based on the theory of adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs) have achieved high accuracy in closed-loop end-effector tracking. We extend this approach by learning an aSSM model of the full body of a trimmed-helicoid soft trunk robot from data and use this in a model predictive control (MPC) scheme to demonstrate a range of shape control tasks on hardware. On closed-loop dynamic shape regulation, our method outperforms the available linear baselines by a factor of 10. In human-in-the-loop interactive demos, our method completes section-by-section shaping and balances a tennis ball for over 25 s25\text{\,}\mathrm{s}, while the linear baselines fall short. A model-free reinforcement learning policy trained for 12 h12\text{\,}\mathrm{h} on hardware fails on the same balancing task. These results establish aSSM-based MPC as a practical route to full-body shape control on real soft hardware.
