title: FOSCo-Net: Ego-centric Voxel Completion for Forest LiDAR Occlusions
authors: Iman Esfandiyar,Dominik Belter
comment: accepted for presentation at ACIVS 2026 (23rd Advanced Concepts for Intelligent Vision Systems) Okinawa, Japan
abstract: Ground robots operating in temperate forests suffer from systematic LiDAR occlusions caused by tree trunks, creating persistent blind regions that degrade traversability estimation. In this paper, we propose FOSCo-Net, a self-supervised voxel completion framework that learns to reconstruct occluded geometry from a single scan using temporally accumulated observations as automatic supervision, and we evaluate cylindrical and Cartesian ego-centric grids with multiple decoder designs. FOSCo-Net consistently improves reconstruction quality and traversal safety, with a gated skip decoder achieving the most reliable performance and significantly reducing false obstacle predictions compared to baselines.
introduction:
Autonomous robots operating in forests must maintain accurate
traversability estimates to navigate safely around trees and undergrowth.
Spinning LiDAR sensors are the primary exteroceptive sensor for this
task, but they suffer from persistent occlusion shadows: every
trunk blocks the sensor rays behind it, leaving wedge-shaped unobserved
volumes that are recorded as unknown space in occupancy maps.
Unlike random sensor noise, these shadows are systematic: the same trunk consistently blocks the same angular sector relative to the sensor heading.

Occlusion shadows have safety-critical consequences for motion planning. Planners typically treat unknown space as either free (risking collision with hidden obstacles) or occupied (blocking traversable corridors behind trunks) [9]. In dense forests, the conservative policy fragments the free-space map into disconnected islands, often preventing the planner from finding any path. By predicting occluded geometry before planning, the proposed FOSCo-Net converts unknown voxels into confident occupancy or free estimates, giving the planner a complete local map for safe routing through the corridor behind each trunk.

Semantic scene completion (SSC) aims to infer full 3D geometry from partial observations, originally targeting camera-based inputs with large annotated datasets. LMSCNet [9] extends SSC to single-frame LiDAR using a coarse-to-fine voxel decoding strategy. More recent generative approaches such as DiffSSC [2] use denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) to iteratively corrupt and reconstruct data, enabling high-quality scene completion from noise. In parallel, S3CNet [3] combines sparse 2D bird’s-eye-view (BEV) and 3D voxel representations with dedicated completion networks and BEV-guided voxel fusion.

Other methods [10, 1] improve sparse LiDAR depth using overlapping camera views to obtain denser reconstructions and better free-space estimates, but they rely on visible or multi-view cues and do not explicitly reconstruct regions occluded by foreground obstacles. Self-supervised alternatives reduce annotation requirements by exploiting temporal consistency: Vizzo et al. [11] use accumulated scans as pseudo-ground truth for TSDF-based completion, but their formulation is world-centric and less suited for pose-invariant online inference. More recently, implicit neural map representations reconstruct large-scale scenes from full posed scan sequences: SHINE-Mapping [14] fits a sparse hierarchical feature grid to a scan sequence offline, and 4dNDF [15] extends this formulation with a time-dependent TSDF that additionally separates dynamic objects. These approaches deliver accurate reconstructions of observed space, but they require the complete sequence and per-scene test-time optimization, and they cannot infer geometry in regions never covered by any sensor ray. Our task is complementary: predicting unobserved, occluded space from a single scan in one forward pass of a network trained once, which rules out such sequence-based mapping methods as direct baselines. In contrast, world-frame representations support large-scale mapping [13] but are computationally heavier, while ego-centric representations are more efficient for local control [5], including BEV fusion [8] and top-view prediction [4]. Finally, sparse convolutional networks [12] enable efficient processing by operating only on occupied voxels, while learned skip-gating mechanisms [16] reduce false positives by suppressing unreliable features. These ideas motivate our design, including a sparse encoder and σ\sigma-gated skip connections that explicitly handle unobserved regions.

To the best of our knowledge, no prior work addresses the systematic trunk
occlusions of forest environments with a completion network that is simultaneously
(i) self-supervised, with supervision derived from robot motion alone and no manual
labels, (ii) ego-centric, hence pose-invariant and applicable per scan without a
persistent world map, and (iii) evaluated on traversability safety rather than
reconstruction quality alone: camera-based SSC relies on annotated datasets,
LMSCNet-style LiDAR completion is trained against world-frame ground truth, and the
self-supervision of Vizzo et al. is world-centric and map-bound. FOSCo-Net closes
this gap.

Our contribution can be summarized as follows:

to our knowledge, the first self-supervised, ego-centric
occlusion-completion framework for forest LiDAR, in which the supervision target
(Eq. 1) is derived automatically from robot motion, with no
annotations and no world map at inference,

a new traversability-oriented evaluation metric, SFPR, which measures
false obstacles in the occluded corridor behind each trunk, the region that
determines whether a planner can route through the corridor at all,

an asymmetric σ\sigma-gated skip decoder whose gates vanish exactly at
unobserved positions, anchoring predictions to observed surfaces, validated by a
controlled ablation of four decoders on two ego-centric grids (cylindrical and
Cartesian) which shows that decoder design, not grid choice, drives performance.

1. to our knowledge, the first self-supervised, ego-centric
occlusion-completion framework for forest LiDAR, in which the supervision target
(Eq. 1) is derived automatically from robot motion, with no
annotations and no world map at inference,

2. a new traversability-oriented evaluation metric, SFPR, which measures
false obstacles in the occluded corridor behind each trunk, the region that
determines whether a planner can route through the corridor at all,

3. an asymmetric σ\sigma-gated skip decoder whose gates vanish exactly at
unobserved positions, anchoring predictions to observed surfaces, validated by a
controlled ablation of four decoders on two ego-centric grids (cylindrical and
Cartesian) which shows that decoder design, not grid choice, drives performance.

title: Playing Soccer Like Humans Do: Learning Versatile and Agile Humanoid Soccer via Latent Motion Priors
authors: Haoyu Shao,Yunshen Wang,Jingze Zhang,Shaohang Zhu,Yong-Lu Li,Tianzhu Zhang,Baoxiong Jia,Siyuan Huang
abstract: Humanoid soccer requires a robot to seamlessly combine agile locomotion, ball manipulation, and impact-rich contact dynamics across a continuous, dynamic behavioral spectrum. Yet existing approaches either cover only a limited set of skills, or forego motion priors entirely and produce unnatural behaviors, leaving the combination of a unified skill set and human-like motion quality unaddressed. We present SoccerBot, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that resolves both limitations through a structured latent motion prior distilled from large-scale human soccer motion capture data. By constraining policy learning within this dynamically plausible motion manifold, a single skill-conditioned policy naturally learns to perform moving, dribbling, trapping, and kicking in a unified formulation, while inherently producing human-like motion and fluid transitions during commanded skill switching. Augmented by robustness-oriented simulation design, SoccerBot transfers zero-shot to the Unitree G1 humanoid robot, demonstrating agile, natural, and robust execution of the full soccer skill repertoire under real-world conditions.
introduction:
Soccer stands apart from sports such as table tennis [19, 17] and tennis [28] as a uniquely demanding benchmark for humanoid robots: rather than isolating upper-body dexterity, it demands the inseparable coupling of agile whole-body locomotion and non-prehensile ball manipulation across a rich, continuous behavioral spectrum. Humans master this spectrum with remarkable fluency: sprinting, trapping, dribbling, and kicking compose seamlessly into a continuous, expressive behavioral repertoire. This fluency emerges from decades of motor learning that endows human motion with natural coordination, dynamic stability, and graceful skill transitions. Replicating such fluency on a humanoid robot is far from trivial: the robot must not only master a diverse set of highly dynamic skills, but also execute smooth, natural transitions across the full behavioral spectrum. Humanoid soccer thus emerges as a compelling platform for studying unified whole-body control, simultaneously demanding agile locomotion, non-prehensile object manipulation, impact-rich contact dynamics, and human-like motion quality within a single, coherent control problem.

Despite recent progress in reinforcement learning for humanoid locomotion [16, 14, 15] and motor skill acquisition [13, 12, 8, 4, 7, 26, 21, 3], existing approaches to humanoid soccer remain fundamentally limited along two orthogonal axes. On one axis, existing methods lack a unified skill repertoire: most prior works address only a narrow subset of soccer behaviors [6, 22, 23], such as directed kicking, dribbling, or locomotion-only control, and even multi-skill systems rely on decoupled, independently trained controllers that cannot naturally bridge the dynamics between different actions [5]. Multi-skill soccer built on human motion priors has so far been demonstrated only for simulated characters [9, 5]. The result is a fragmented behavioral space where inter-skill transitions are inherently discontinuous and unnatural, as evidenced by the jarring switches between running and trapping, or dribbling and kicking. On the other axis, many existing methods rely solely on task-reward-driven reinforcement learning without any motion prior [3], leaving motion naturalness entirely unaddressed. Without structural regularization grounded in human motion, such policies produce erratic, mechanically unnatural behaviors that are both visually implausible and brittle under the contact-rich dynamics of real soccer interaction. Together, these two axes define a clear gap in the literature: the combination of human-like coordination and a complete, unified soccer skill set has never been simultaneously achieved in a single humanoid soccer system.

To close this gap, we propose SoccerBot, a hierarchical learning framework that addresses both limitations through a unified mechanism: a structured latent motion prior distilled from large-scale human soccer motion capture data. Building on recent advances in physics-based motion imitation [10], we first distill a motion tracking policy into a compact latent action space that encodes a rich, dynamically plausible manifold of human-like whole-body motion. A unified skill-conditioned policy then operates within this latent space via residual control, learning to perform dribbling, trapping, kicking, and moving under a shared control formulation. By grounding all skills within the same motion prior, SoccerBot inherently produces natural, human-like motion across the full behavioral spectrum, and produces fluid, natural inter-skill transitions during commanded skill switching. To further support reliable real-world deployment, we incorporate robustness-oriented simulation design including ball dynamics modeling, domain randomization, and observation perturbation, enabling zero-shot sim-to-real transfer to the Unitree G1 humanoid robot.

We evaluate SoccerBot in both simulation and real-world settings, demonstrating that a single unified policy can execute the full spectrum of soccer skills with agility and naturalness under real-world conditions. The main contributions of this work are as follows:

We present SoccerBot, to our knowledge the first real-world humanoid soccer system that jointly achieves a complete skill repertoire and human-like motion quality, learning moving, dribbling, trapping, and kicking within a single unified policy.

We present SoccerBot, to our knowledge the first real-world humanoid soccer system that jointly achieves a complete skill repertoire and human-like motion quality, learning moving, dribbling, trapping, and kicking within a single unified policy.

We propose a hierarchical latent motion prior framework with transition state initialization (TSI), grounding unified soccer skill learning within a structured motion manifold and enabling agile, human-like behaviors, fluid inter-skill transitions, and robust cross-skill composition without explicit state machines or separate controllers.

We conduct extensive simulation benchmarks and real-world experiments on the Unitree G1, demonstrating strong task performance across all four skills, structured latent skill-space organization, and reliable zero-shot sim-to-real transfer with minimal performance degradation.

authors: Xuemin Hu,Kaixin Li,Qingqing Xia,Yuxin Wang,Wei Xie,Bo Tang,Long Chen

introduction:
Coordinated whole-body control (WBC) is a major challenge in achieving highly human-like movement for humanoid robot (HR) research [1]. The current mainstream methods are based on imitation learning and have achieved remarkable results  [2, 3]. However, these methods require a large amount of labeled data through motion capture systems or teleoperation, resulting in high training costs. Moreover, some marginal data, such as actions in complex and dangerous industrial and outer space operations, are difficult to collect, limiting the application of these methods [4]. Reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods [5] mainly involve single-agent RL methods, which can complete motions such as walking and running in simulators without a large amount of data and exhibit good coordination capabilities for HRs with low degrees of freedom (DoF) [6, 7], but these methods struggle to achieve precise coordination across joints with numerous joints and high DoF.

To address these issues, some researchers introduce multi-agent reinforcement (MARL), where joints or limbs are treated as multiple homogeneous agents [8, 9], as shown in Fig. 1(a). However, in fact, various joints in the human body exhibit obvious differences in muscle composition, movement directions, dimensions, and coupling [10]. For HRs, their hip joints (high torque and heavy load) and elbow joints (high sensitivity and light load) also exhibit fundamental physical heterogeneity in dynamic characteristics, DoF, and roles in whole-body balance [10]. Existing homogeneous MARL-based methods overlook heterogeneous attributes in joint and limbs and fail to learn effective actions for different agents with the same objectives but different decisions, generating incongruous motions.

Regarding the structure of the control model, some researchers adopt the end-to-end framework that directly maps observations and proprioceptions to control actions [10, 2, 11]. These methods are simple and effective for humanoid robots with low DoF, but struggle to train an effective model in state-action spaces for HRs with high DoF. Other researchers employ a hierarchical model [12] that separates high-level task planning from low-level joint control, where the high-level model often uses a large model combined imitation learning and the low-level model typically employs terminal controllers to perform planning. Nevertheless, these methods often decouple the learning of the high-level planning model and the low-level control models, often leading to insufficient coordination between high- and low-level models and stiff motions. In addition, the large model used in the high-level model often leads to a long inference time and poor real-time performance.

To address these issues, we propose a hierarchical heterogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning (H2MARL) for coordinating humanoid whole-body control, which offers the following three contributions: 1) We propose a JDoF-level physical-heterogeneity-aware policy factorization. The humanoid whole-body control is formulated as a cooperative heterogeneous multi-agent problem at the joint-degree-of-freedom (JDoF) level, where each torque-actuated JDoF is conditioned on an explicit physical descriptor containing its actuation, kinematic, and dynamic properties, as shown in Fig. 1(b), providing a fine-grained inductive bias that enables different JDoFs to learn specialized control behaviors while maintaining coordination through centralized training. 2) We develop a hierarchical policy–executor coupling mechanism in which the JDoF-level pose planner and joint executor interact with the environment through the same closed-loop trajectory and are iteratively optimized rather than trained independently, preventing the distribution mismatch caused by freezing the executor. 3) Extensive experiments conducted in the MuJoCo and Isaac Gym simulator demonstrate that H2MARL outperforms state-of-the-art methods in metrics for measuring coordination and human-like qualities. Through controlled comparisons of agent granularity, heterogeneous conditioning, and closed-loop collaborative optimization, we also isolate the contribution of each design and demonstrate that performance improvement comes from the proposed JDoF-level policy factorization and policy–executor coupling rather than from directly combining existing HAPPO, HST, and conventional PD components.

title: Robocasa-Mem: Benchmarking Environment and Process Memory in Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation
authors: Sihang Chen,Chen Ye,Wei Chen,Xiaohan Lei,Zhipeng Tang,Sha Zhang,Yuan Zhang,Zixuan Chen,Jiajun Deng,Houqiang Li,Yanyong Zhang
abstract:
In the real world, mobile manipulation robots must perform complex object interactions and make multi-step decisions, often relying on task-relevant information that is no longer observable. However, existing benchmarks provide limited evaluation of such memory-dependent decision-making in mobile manipulation.
To address this gap, we introduce RoboCasa-Mem, a new benchmark comprising nine mobile manipulation tasks that require agents to use interaction history at key decision points.
Specifically, the tasks are grouped into two categories of memory: One is environment memory, which captures spatial locations, object attributes, and object relationships. The other is process memory, which captures single-task progress and multi-task scheduling.
Particularly, we introduce Behavior-Conditioned Evaluation. For tasks with multiple valid execution paths, instead of fixing a single target or trajectory, the evaluator derives later task constraints from the robot’s earlier actions. This allows us to evaluate whether later behavior is consistent with the robot’s own interaction history while reducing shortcuts based on fixed target assignments.
We provide 1,800 successful demonstrations for policy training. We also develop a baseline on our benchmark, namely Hierarchical Memory-Augmented Policy (HMAP). Its high-level planner uses structured entity and process memories to generate subtasks. Its low-level VLA controller uses subgoal-conditioned queries to incorporate VGGT-Ω\Omega geometry into action generation. Together, RoboCasa-Mem and HMAP baseline support systematic evaluation of memory-dependent behavior and the development of memory-aware mobile manipulation policies.
introduction:
Mobile manipulation requires robots to navigate between locations and interact with objects (Szot et al., 2021; Nasiriany et al., 2024). While tabletop manipulation often concentrates task-relevant information within a fixed workspace, mobile manipulation extends interactions across different work areas. As the robot moves and interacts with the environment, previously observed information may become inaccessible yet remain essential for subsequent decisions. For example, when cooking, a robot may need to remember whether it has already added salt to the pot after the salt has dissolved and is no longer visually distinguishable. Such situations motivate maintaining historical information about both the environment and task execution, beyond what is available in the current observation (Torne et al., 2026).
Memory dependence is not equivalent to long-horizon manipulation. A task may involve multiple sequential steps without requiring historical information, provided that the current observation is sufficient for decision-making. Conversely, even a short task may require memory when critical information is no longer observable. From a partially observable decision-making perspective, historical information is needed when different interaction histories yield indistinguishable current observations but require different subsequent decisions (Kaelbling et al., 1998). We therefore evaluate memory based on the necessity of historical information for correct decision-making, rather than task length or execution complexity alone.

Existing mobile-manipulation benchmarks, such as RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2024), RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2026), MS-HAB (Shukla et al., 2025), BEHAVIOR-1K (Li et al., 2024), and the suite of works based on Habitat (Puig et al., 2024; Szot et al., 2021; Savva et al., 2019), primarily evaluate task execution, long-horizon control, generalization, and policy learning, without explicitly isolating decisions that require historical information. In parallel, robotic memory benchmarks such as RMBench (Chen et al., 2026), RoboMME (Dai et al., 2026), RoboMemArena (Lei et al., 2026), and RoboTwin-MeM (Yang et al., 2026) study history-dependent manipulation, predominantly in tabletop or fixed-base settings.
Mobile manipulation brings these memory demands into settings where robots move between work areas, lose visual access to previously observed entities, and must resume unfinished activities. Two requirements are particularly relevant: retaining object states established through earlier interactions but no longer visually distinguishable, and tracking progress and pending actions across interleaved activities in different regions. Although neither requirement is unique to mobile manipulation, their joint evaluation under changing viewpoints and cross-region execution remains limited.

To systematically characterize these requirements, we organize memory into two complementary dimensions: Environment Memory and Process Memory.
Environment Memory captures information about the physical environment that cannot be reliably recovered from the current observation, encompassing Spatial Memory, Attribute Memory, and Relational Memory.
Process Memory tracks task execution states and information needed to determine subsequent actions, encompassing Single-Task Progress and Multi-Task Scheduling.
This taxonomy explicitly accounts for visually unobservable object attribute changes and the scheduling of interleaved tasks, providing a systematic characterization of memory requirements in mobile manipulation.

Based on this taxonomy, we introduce RoboCasa-Mem, a benchmark for memory in mobile manipulation.
RoboCasa-Mem contains nine mobile-manipulation tasks covering the five memory categories above.
Each task is designed to introduce observation-insufficient decision points, where the current observation alone cannot determine the appropriate action, requiring the robot to retrieve and utilize information from its interaction history.
This design explicitly evaluates memory dependence rather than relying on task horizon as its proxy.
For tasks with multiple valid execution paths, we introduce Behavior-Conditioned Evaluation, which derives later constraints from the policy’s own earlier interactions rather than fixing a target in advance. This allows history-consistent behavior to be evaluated without prescribing a single execution trajectory.

To provide a baseline, we develop a Hierarchical Memory-Augmented Policy (HMAP) that combines structured memory for planning with geometry-augmented control. A high-level planner maintains Entity Memory and Process Memory to track environment states, execution progress, and pending actions, and generates executable subgoals. A low-level VLA controller executes these subgoals using current observations and multi-view geometric features extracted by VGGT-Ω\Omega (Wang et al., 2026), which are incorporated through task-conditioned queries and action modulation. Across the nine tasks, HMAP improves average success from 16.2% to 24.2% over π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025), with gains concentrated in hidden-attribute recall. Improvements on process-memory tasks remain inconsistent, highlighting challenges in progress tracking and interleaved execution.

Our contributions are threefold:

Benchmark and dataset. We introduce RoboCasa-Mem, comprising nine mobile-manipulation tasks organized into five memory categories across environment-state and task-state memory, together with 1,800 successful demonstration trajectories for policy training.

Evaluation protocol. We introduce Behavior-Conditioned Evaluation, which derives subsequent semantic constraints from the robot’s actual interactions to assess history-consistent behavior across multiple valid execution paths. We report both final task success and stage-level completion.

Baseline and findings. We develop Hierarchical Memory-Augmented Policy (HMAP) that combines structured semantic memory for planning with 3D geometric feature for control. Our experiments reveal gains concentrated in hidden-attribute recall and identify persistent challenges in task-progress tracking and interleaved multi-task execution.

1. Benchmark and dataset. We introduce RoboCasa-Mem, comprising nine mobile-manipulation tasks organized into five memory categories across environment-state and task-state memory, together with 1,800 successful demonstration trajectories for policy training.

2. Evaluation protocol. We introduce Behavior-Conditioned Evaluation, which derives subsequent semantic constraints from the robot’s actual interactions to assess history-consistent behavior across multiple valid execution paths. We report both final task success and stage-level completion.

3. Baseline and findings. We develop Hierarchical Memory-Augmented Policy (HMAP) that combines structured semantic memory for planning with 3D geometric feature for control. Our experiments reveal gains concentrated in hidden-attribute recall and identify persistent challenges in task-progress tracking and interleaved multi-task execution.

title: Beyond Infraction Scores: Failure-Boundary Profiles for Closed-Loop Evaluation of Driving and Robot Navigation Agents
authors: Milan Bulat,Gino Ardelean,Ellington Kirby
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Software Engineering (cs.SE)

abstract:
Closed-loop driving benchmarks in CARLA rank agents by a driving score that
multiplies route completion by an infraction penalty. This score does not
distinguish an agent that stops in front of an obstacle from one that
pushes past it. In a corridor closed by two parked cars, for example, one
agent that drives through with contact averages
52.2 on the blocked widths,
while the agents that stop average between
37.8 and
40.6. We propose
failure-boundary profiles, an evaluation in which each scenario family varies
one measured factor, such as corridor width or the time gap in oncoming
traffic, and each variant is certified from measurement as one where the agent
should proceed or one where it should stop. Along this axis we estimate two
curves per agent, commitment (the probability of attempting the passage) and
competence (the probability of passing without contact), and locate where each
crosses one half, with intervals that account for the simulator’s run-to-run
variance. The certified labels also give a summary metric, decision accuracy,
which credits clean passes on passable variants and stops on blocked ones. We
evaluate seven driving agents on seven CARLA families. The rule-based expert
reaches a decision accuracy of 0.74
and TFv6, the highest-scoring learned agent,
0.60. Agents with similar driving
scores fail in different ways, and agents that reliably stop at a blocked
corridor still rarely wait for a gap in oncoming traffic. We also apply the
method, unchanged, to a warehouse robot in Isaac Sim. The navigation policy we
test stops at blocked gaps in only one of three families, and two fine-tuned
versions of it pass more gaps cleanly but no longer stop at all.
introduction:
Recent CARLA-based benchmarks such as Bench2Drive and
Fail2Drive [10, 7] evaluate agents with the Driving
Score (DS), which multiplies an agent’s route completion by an infraction
penalty. The route is predefined for each scenario, and the infractions cover
collisions, traffic-rule violations and blocking. The intent is that a
single number captures good driving.

These benchmarks probe a wide range of behaviors through scenario
construction: merging, obeying traffic signals, and deviating from the
usual route geometry. Bench2Drive observed that long routes entangle
different failure modes and make aggregate metrics hard to interpret, and
moved to short routes with one scenario each. We argue that even a
per-scenario driving score cannot explain why two agents differ, because it
mixes two separate questions: whether the agent attempts a maneuver, and
whether it carries it out without contact.

We therefore evaluate agents along controlled axes instead of fixed
routes. A scenario family varies one measured factor, such as the
free width of a corridor or the time gap in oncoming traffic, and holds the
rest of the scene constant. Each variant is certified from measurement: a
corridor is passable or blocked according to its geometry, and a gap in
oncoming traffic is usable or one to wait for according to the traffic
that actually occurs. Along each axis we estimate two curves per agent.
Commitment is the probability that the agent attempts the passage,
and competence is the probability that it passes without contact.
The point where a curve crosses one half is a failure boundary,
which we report with an interval reflecting the simulator’s run-to-run
variance. Where commitment is higher than competence, the agent keeps
attempting a passage it can no longer complete, and the width of that
region differs from agent to agent. Since every variant carries a label,
each run can also be scored as right or wrong, a clean pass where passage
is possible and a stop where it is not. We call the resulting summary
decision accuracy. We apply this to seven driving agents on seven
families, producing curves that show each agent’s commitment-competence
gap, and we analyze the failures behind it.

The same curves and the same decision accuracy carry over to robot
navigation without modification. We test a world-model-based navigation
policy in simulation, producing similar failure-boundary curves, and
demonstrate the effects of a simple fine-tuning strategy.

Our contributions are:

a pipeline that turns natural-language requests into scenario
families whose variants differ in one measured factor and are
certified passable or blocked, with the spawned geometry checked in
the simulator;

failure-boundary profiles, i.e. commitment and competence curves
along a certified axis, with boundaries and intervals that account
for the simulator’s run-to-run nondeterminism;

decision accuracy, a summary metric that credits a clean pass on
variants certified passable and a stop on variants certified
blocked;

an evaluation of seven driving agents on seven CARLA families and
of a warehouse robot on three Isaac Sim families. Agents with
similar driving scores fail in different ways, within a family the
driving score can rank an agent that never stops above agents that
stop correctly, and learned agents rarely wait for a gap in
oncoming traffic, including those that stop at a blocked corridor.

the ten scenario families, the measurement chain and the records of
all seventeen campaigns in a
public repository,
and the simulator evidence the scores were based on in a
dataset on the Hugging Face Hub.

title: $A^3$-VLA: Automatic Perception-Guided Attention Alignment for Robot Manipulation
authors: Shengzhe Zhang,Qi Zhang,Dazhong Shen,Chao Wang,Shaopeng Zhai,Hui Xiong
abstract:
Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) enable robots to perform manipulation tasks by leveraging Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to process visual observations and language instructions.
However, the action prediction objective itself lacks fine-grained task-specific perceptual supervision, making it prone to relying on task-irrelevant visual shortcuts, leading attention away from target objects and key interaction areas, thereby limiting its operational performance and generalization ability.
To address this, we propose Automatic Perception-Guided Attention Alignment for Robot Manipulation (A3\text{A}^{3}-VLA), a framework that derives task-specific visual guidance from the manipulation process itself. Specifically, A3\text{A}^{3}-VLA first generates heuristic candidate regions for target objects and the robot from interaction-induced visual changes, and refines them with a visual segmentation model offline. These regions serve as explicit perceptual guidance through two complementary objectives: an attention allocation loss that encourages sufficient focus on task-critical regions when language or robot state tokens query the visual input, and a contrastive learning loss that aligns the representations of candidate target regions with language instructions while separating them from task-irrelevant regions. Extensive experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that A3\text{A}^{3}-VLA consistently improves multiple VLA backbones, with an average success rate gain of 6.5% - 25.2% across benchmarks.
introduction:
Embodied manipulation aims to enable robots to interact with the environment through learned policies to complete manipulation tasks Chi et al. (2025); Aldaco et al. (2024).
A core challenge is enabling robots to understand both what to manipulate (from language instructions) and how to manipulate (from visual observations).
Recently, Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable success in aligning visual and linguistic representations, demonstrating strong capabilities in tasks such as visual question answering and cross-modal reasoning Xu et al. (2021); Beyer et al. (2024); Zeng et al. (2023); Yang et al. (2026).
Building upon these advances, Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) Zitkovich et al. (2023); Team et al. (2024); Black et al. (2024) extend VLMs to robot control by directly generating action sequences conditioned on visual observations and language instructions Shi et al. (2025); Bu et al. (2025); Song et al. (2025); Zhan et al. (2025).

Early works on VLAs primarily focus on accurate action generation, pioneered by tokenization-based Team et al. (2024); Kim et al. (2025b) and flow-matching-based Black et al. (2024); Pertsch et al. (2025) paradigms.
Despite this progress in action learning, the visual perception capability of these models, including their ability to attend to regions specified by language instructions, remains fragile. As shown in Figure 1, these cases reveal a key failure mode that is often overlooked in VLA research: the model fails because the VLM backbone’s attention mechanism fails to focus on the task-relevant regions specified by the language instruction, rather than being solely attributable to action generation errors. Thus, the VLA learns to “memorize” specific action trajectories from the training data, rather than connecting the instructions with the observation of the target objects. To break this pattern, VLAs need explicit signals about where to look, raising a natural question: can we obtain such task-specific guidance from the manipulation process itself?

We argue that the above limitation reveals two deeper issues with how VLAs currently handle visual perception. First, the fine-tuning process provides no explicit signal indicating which image regions are critical for the given task. The flow-matching or autoregressive objective only supervises action accuracy Zhang et al. (2025b); Goyal et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2024); whether the model’s visual attention aligns with task-relevant regions is never directly evaluated or encouraged. As a result, the VLM backbone’s pretrained ability to discriminatively attend to semantically meaningful regions can gradually drift during fine-tuning Wang et al. (2026); Meng et al. (2026); Zhai et al. (2025). Second, prior works attempt to enhance perception in different ways, such as CoT-VLA Zhao et al. (2025) with visual chain-of-thought reasoning, π0.5\pi_{0.5} Intelligence et al. (2025) and Gemini Robotics Team et al. (2025) with open-world knowledge. The guidance they provide remains either indirect (reasoning over the entire scene) or task-agnostic (general knowledge from heterogeneous data).
These motivate a different perspective: the manipulation process itself encodes rich information about what matters visually. The moment of physical interaction, the trajectory of the robot end-effector, and the target object being acted upon all carry signals about which image regions deserve focused attention. If we obtain these signals and utilize them as explicit perceptual guidance, the task-oriented visual perception capability may be preserved during fine-tuning, rather than being overwritten by the action learning objective.

To address these challenges, we propose Automatic Perception-Guided Attention Alignment for Robot Manipulation (A3\text{A}^{3}-VLA), a framework that provides explicit visual perception guidance during VLA fine-tuning. The key insight of A3\text{A}^{3}-VLA is that interaction moments in the manipulation process naturally reveal the locations of task-critical regions. Based on this, A3\text{A}^{3}-VLA consists of two stages. First, a heuristic region proposal and temporal refinement stage extracts noisy candidate regions from interaction-induced visual changes and refines them with SAM2 into temporally consistent pseudo regions for target objects and the robot. Second, a perception-guided fine-tuning stage incorporates these pseudo regions via two complementary objectives: (i) an attention allocation loss that encourages the model to focus sufficient attention on the heuristic regions of target objects or the robot when language or robot state tokens query the visual input respectively, and (ii) a contrastive learning loss that aligns the representations of target object regions with language instructions while pushing away those of task-irrelevant regions. Together, these objectives help the VLA maintain task-focused visual attention throughout fine-tuning, rather than allowing it to drift toward task-irrelevant regions.
Overall, our contributions are as follows:

We propose A3\text{A}^{3}-VLA, a framework that derives task-specific visual guidance from the manipulation process itself, eliminating manual annotation.

We design two auxiliary training objectives, attention allocation and contrastive representation alignment, that explicitly steer VLA visual focus toward task-relevant regions.

Extensive experiments on both simulation and real-world settings demonstrate that A3\text{A}^{3}-VLA consistently improves multiple VLA backbones across diverse manipulation tasks.

1. We propose A3\text{A}^{3}-VLA, a framework that derives task-specific visual guidance from the manipulation process itself, eliminating manual annotation.

2. We design two auxiliary training objectives, attention allocation and contrastive representation alignment, that explicitly steer VLA visual focus toward task-relevant regions.

3. Extensive experiments on both simulation and real-world settings demonstrate that A3\text{A}^{3}-VLA consistently improves multiple VLA backbones across diverse manipulation tasks.

title: TwinBridge: Digital Twin-Driven Policy and Reward Transfer for Real-World Reinforcement Learning in Laboratory Robotics
authors: Shu'ang Sun,Yibo Qiu,Haoliang Ye,Zan Huang,Ao Tian,Kan Ding,Ronald Xu,Mingzhai Sun
abstract: Online reinforcement learning offers an effective approach to precise laboratory manipulation, yet costly real-world demonstrations and limited access to dense process rewards hinder its practical application. We present TwinBridge, a digital twin-driven framework that supplies policy initialization and dense visual rewards for real-world online learning. We construct digital twins by combining 3D Gaussian splatting with physics simulation. Here, simulator states provide task events and geometric progress under physical prerequisites and ordering constraints, yielding rewards for policy pretraining with simulated demonstrations and reinforcement learning. We distill this supervision into a visual reward model. During real-world interaction, its predictions are combined with execution history to compute dense rewards for human-in-the-loop policy refinement. Across five real-world laboratory tasks, TwinBridge achieves a final mean autonomous success rate of 98% with at most 25 minutes of real-world interaction per task. Experiments show that dense rewards improve interaction efficiency over sparse rewards, and simulation-based policy initialization further accelerates learning.
introduction:
Laboratory manipulation requires precise motion while satisfying physical dependencies between successive actions. A centrifuge tube must be securely grasped before transport, and a lid must be separated from its container before relocation. Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve these skills through interaction, but efficient learning on a physical robot requires both useful initial behavior and feedback that identifies valid intermediate progress.

Human-in-the-loop methods such as HIL-SERL and HIL-ConRFT have demonstrated precise manipulation by combining demonstrations, human corrections, and reinforcement learning [1, 2]. For multi-stage laboratory tasks, collecting demonstrations that cover successive operations requires skilled human effort. Sparse outcome feedback further leaves the learner to discover which intermediate actions advance the procedure.

Digital twins allow useful behavior to be learned before real-world interaction. SplatSim and GSWorld combine Gaussian splatting with physics simulation to support visual policy transfer [3, 4]. SimLauncher and TwinRL further use simulation experience to guide subsequent real-world RL [5, 6]. Simulation thus supports both policy preparation and continued learning after transfer. We focus on a complementary opportunity: transferring the task-progress information available in simulation alongside the policy, so that the twin supplies both initial behavior and feedback for real-world improvement.

Visual reward modeling provides a way to deliver such feedback from camera observations. SARM models task stages and within-stage progress [7], Robo-Dopamine uses visual process rewards for RL [8], and keyframe-guided structured rewards exploit task order in laboratory manipulation [9]. In precision manipulation, progress also depends on physical prerequisites: moving the gripper toward a holder advances tube loading only after a grasp is secured. A digital twin exposes contact, alignment, and insertion states, allowing valid events and geometric progress to be labeled automatically. The central challenge is to transfer this supervision to visual predictions while retaining event order and execution history in the deployed reward computation.

We propose TwinBridge, a digital twin-driven framework that supplies pretrained policies and dense visual process rewards for real-world online learning (Fig. 1). We combine 3D Gaussian splatting with physics simulation to construct digital twins, where simulator states provide task events and geometric progress under physical prerequisites and ordering constraints. These signals define rewards for visual policy pretraining with simulated demonstrations and RL, and provide supervision aligned with simulated images. We combine this supervision with a small set of real visual annotations to train a visual reward model. During real-world interaction, its event and progress predictions are combined with execution history to compute dense rewards, guiding human-in-the-loop online refinement of the transferred policy. An execution-history ledger credits each event once and rewards new valid progress records.

We evaluate TwinBridge on five laboratory tasks: centrifuge tube pickup, Petri dish lid removal, centrifuge tube loading, pipette tip attachment, and pipetting. TwinBridge achieves a final mean autonomous success rate of 98% with at most 25 minutes of real-world interaction per task. Dense visual rewards improve interaction efficiency over sparse outcome feedback, while simulation-based initialization further accelerates real-world learning.

The main contributions of this work are:

A digital twin-driven framework that jointly transfers visual manipulation policies and process reward supervision to support efficient human-in-the-loop real-world RL.

A physically grounded reward construction and visual distillation method that combines ordered event credit and valid progress records with execution history to provide dense feedback from real-world images.

Evaluation on five real-world laboratory tasks, including comparisons of policy initialization and reward-transfer configurations and episode-level validation of visual event and progress prediction.

1. A digital twin-driven framework that jointly transfers visual manipulation policies and process reward supervision to support efficient human-in-the-loop real-world RL.

2. A physically grounded reward construction and visual distillation method that combines ordered event credit and valid progress records with execution history to provide dense feedback from real-world images.

3. Evaluation on five real-world laboratory tasks, including comparisons of policy initialization and reward-transfer configurations and episode-level validation of visual event and progress prediction.

title: UniLoop: Unified Loop Closure Detection from Retrieval to Geometric Verification and Relative Pose Estimation
authors: Jingwen Yu,Pengyu Wang,Jin Wu,Weinan Chen,Ping Tan,Hong Zhang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Loop closure detection conventionally cascades separate models for global
retrieval, geometric verification, and relative pose estimation, leading to
redundant computation and disconnected visual representations. We propose
UniLoop, a unified framework that reuses the hierarchical representations of
the pretrained geometric foundation model throughout this pipeline.
A shared image encoder produces features for compact global descriptors; the
same features are passed to the cross-view decoder for pairwise verification;
and the original geometric predictions provide relative camera constraints for
pose-graph optimization. Experiments on place recognition, loop verification,
and relative pose estimation show that UniLoop improves loop-closure
robustness and accuracy while reducing redundant backbone computation relative
to modular pipelines. UniLoop achieves the best Recall@10 on MSLS (96.6) and
Pitts30k (99.3) among the compared methods, while its verification branch
reaches 95.63 AP and 96.29 ROC-AUC, surpassing the existing geometric verification baselines.
introduction:
Loop closure detection lets a robot recognize previously visited
places, correct accumulated odometry drift, and build a globally
consistent map over long-term operation.
Despite its central role in Simultaneous Localization And Mapping
(SLAM), it is still commonly implemented as a multi-stage cascade of
separate visual models, as shown in Fig. 1.
A visual place recognition model retrieves candidate matches, a
geometric verification (e.g., local feature image matching model) module checks their consistency, and a relative pose module recovers
the camera pose between the query and its top candidate, which is
finally fed as a constraint into pose graph optimization.
Although effective, this design duplicates image encoding, prevents intermediate representation sharing, and yields independently optimized modules whose objectives are only loosely aligned with the final
loop closure decision.

Recent geometric foundation models (GFMs) offer a different opportunity.
MASt3R [1] contains a natural hierarchy of 3D-aware
visual representations, where its image encoder produces single-view features, its cross-view decoder constructs pair-conditioned representations, and its geometric heads predict dense 3D structure and matching cues.
This hierarchy aligns with the stages of loop closure detection: global
representations serve retrieval, while patch-level representations support
verification and relative pose estimation.

Motivated by this observation, we introduce UniLoop, a unified loop-closure framework that reuses a single GFM backbone, MASt3R, for retrieval,
verification, and relative pose estimation. We attach a
SALAD aggregator [2] to the MASt3R encoder and train
the resulting global descriptors with contrastive learning. For verification,
we build on the pairwise reasoning paradigm of
Doppelgangers++ [3] to classify retrieved pairs from
intermediate MASt3R decoder states. Finally, we retain MASt3R’s dense outputs
and convert them into relative camera constraints for the downstream pose-graph
optimization.

A key design principle of UniLoop is that the three tasks do not merely
coexist as independent heads: the same image encoding is reused across
retrieval and pairwise decoding, avoiding redundant backbone inference.
Training is staged rather than fully joint—we first train the SALAD
retrieval branch, then freeze it and supervise the verification head on
hard negatives mined from the trained retrieval branch.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose UniLoop, a unified loop-closure detection framework
that maps the hierarchical representations of a 3D geometric
foundation model onto the retrieval, verification, and relative pose
estimation stages, sharing a single backbone across all three.

We instantiate this design through (i) a MASt3R-encoder
retrieval branch that aggregates encoder tokens into compact global
place descriptors without a separate image backbone, (ii) a
lightweight verification transformer that classifies retrieved pairs
from pair-conditioned MASt3R decoder states, and (iii) the retained
MASt3R geometric predictions, converted into relative camera
constraints for pose-graph optimization.

We establish a staged training and evaluation protocol that
measures both module-level performance and end-to-end
retrieval-conditioned loop-closure quality.

1. We propose UniLoop, a unified loop-closure detection framework
that maps the hierarchical representations of a 3D geometric
foundation model onto the retrieval, verification, and relative pose
estimation stages, sharing a single backbone across all three.

2. We instantiate this design through (i) a MASt3R-encoder
retrieval branch that aggregates encoder tokens into compact global
place descriptors without a separate image backbone, (ii) a
lightweight verification transformer that classifies retrieved pairs
from pair-conditioned MASt3R decoder states, and (iii) the retained
MASt3R geometric predictions, converted into relative camera
constraints for pose-graph optimization.

3. We establish a staged training and evaluation protocol that
measures both module-level performance and end-to-end
retrieval-conditioned loop-closure quality.

title: Vortex-Induced Torque in Grasping Soft Objects: Influence of Geometry and Pneumatic Parameters
authors: Roman Mykhailyshyn,Tomohiro Motoda,Ivan Virgala,Ann Majewicz Fey,Yukiyasu Domae
comment: Accepted for the SII
abstract: Vortex grippers are commonly integrated into automated systems for handling objects with complex geometries in packaging, sorting, and assembling. However, their interaction with compliant objects remains difficult to predict, particularly with respect to the vortex-induced torque transmitted during grasping. This study investigates vortex-induced torque during the grasping of compliant objects and quantifies the coupled effects of supply pressure, tangential nozzle diameter, surface geometry, and curvature. The results show that increasing the tangential nozzle diameter primarily enhances the sensitivity of the generated torque to supply pressure rather than producing a uniformly higher torque. Surface geometry also strongly influences the rotational interaction, with dome-concave surfaces generally producing substantially greater torque than corresponding dome-convex surfaces, whereas the difference between cylindrical concave and convex surfaces is comparatively small. The strongest and most repeatable response was observed for a dome-concave surface exhibiting favorable object-gripper geometric matching. Among the evaluated machine-learning regression methods, Gaussian Process Regression provided the best overall predictive performance under repeated cross-validation, demonstrating that vortex-induced torque can be estimated from combined pneumatic and geometric parameters. These findings provide a basis for predicting and utilizing vortex-induced torque in the dexterous manipulation of soft objects.
introduction:
Pneumatic gripping devices are very easy to integrate into robotic automation processes due to their predictability and ease of use [1, 2]. This is a general statement that is only partially true. There are many different subtypes of pneumatic gripping devices [3, 4]: vacuum [5, 6, 7] (pumpless, piston, ejector, pumping); air-jet [8, 9, 10, 11] (vortex, Bernoulli, combined); combined [12, 13, 14, 15] (pneumatic-pneumatic, pneumatic-other). The complexity of their integration into automated systems is that most of them are built on different physical principles. This does not easily allow for predicting the behavior of the gripper with different objects, especially soft ones.

By considering the most widely used suction cups based on ejector systems, it is obvious that the behavior of the object can be easily predicted by uniform distribution of air pressure by the suction cup over the surface of the object [16, 17]. However, when it comes to air-jet grippers, the interaction between the gripper and the object becomes very complex [10]. This can be seen if we do not consider soft objects but only rigid objects; changing the parameters of the gripper geometry [9, 18], nozzle [19], object geometry [20], supply pressure [21, 22], and object-gripper gap [23, 24, 25] leads to significant changes in both the object deformation and the force characteristics of the gripper. This is due to the fact that the pressure distribution on the surface of the object will not be uniform (Fig. 1(a)), and zones of negative and positive pressure will be formed [26, 27].

Such characteristics of jet grippers have both advantages and disadvantages; for example, they allow grasping an object from a distance [28, 29, 30], but they create additional vibrations [31]. Due to the ability of vortex and Bernoulli grippers to hold objects that are not completely connected to the gripper (like suction cups failing under these conditions), they have gained popularity for grasping fragile [32], porous [11], or electronic parts [33, 34] (Fig. 1(b)). Additionally, the ability to grasp objects from a distance [35] has expanded the scope of applications of jet grippers for deformable [36, 37, 38] and soft [39] objects. They are most widely used for grasping textile objects from a stack [40, 11] and for local control of the position of deformable materials in manufacturing [41, 42]. Many studies have focused on the use of jet grippers for both dexterous manipulation through their integration into the fingers [43, 44] of anthropomorphic hands (Fig. 1(c)) and for dexterously manipulating deformable objects [45] with the robot arm.

However, unlike Bernoulli grippers, vortex grippers have additional characteristics that positively affect the lifting force due to a greater ability to adapt to the surface of the object [46], as well as negatively, which leads to the rotation of the object during grasping. This is because the lifting force is created by the rotation of the airflow, forming a vortex that lifts the object but also creates a torque that rotates the object around the axis of the gripper (Fig. 1(a)). Researchers and developers of vortex grippers usually avoid discussing this negative factor and solve the problem by integrating friction elements, which also works for other jet grippers [47]. Also, if it is not possible to use friction elements, side stops are integrated to prevent the object from rotating. By using wheels as friction elements, we can see the application of vortex technology to mobile robots moving along walls [48].

Despite the torque effect, vortex grippers have many positive effects that allow them to be used for soft tissue grasping in medical applications. In our previous studies [49, 50],
we observed the rotation of bio-inspired tissue during vortex
grasping and mitigated this effect using friction elements
(Fig. 1(d)). However, the influence of compliant-object geometry on vortex-induced torque remains insufficiently characterized, limiting the ability to predict rotational interaction during soft-object grasping. A quantitative understanding of this torque may also enable future manipulation strategies in which the vortex-induced rotational effect is deliberately exploited rather than suppressed. It is also important to understand that knowledge of torque parameters can enable in-hand manipulation without dexterous movements, using only vortex flows. Therefore, in this paper, a detailed study of vortex-induced torque in grasping soft objects was conducted, with 4920 valid trials distributed over 492 experimental conditions. The main contributions of this study are summarized as follows:

Experimental quantification of vortex-induced torque as a function of supply pressure, tangential nozzle diameter, surface geometry, and curvature was conducted.

Identification of geometry-dependent torque amplification for dome-concave surfaces, including a highly repeatable local maximum near a specific object-gripper geometric relationship.

Demonstration that lifting force and vortex-induced torque exhibit different dependencies on the gripper-surface gap, showing that rotational interaction cannot be inferred from lifting force behavior alone.

Introduction of an object-gripper geometric-matching interpretation to describe the observed torque amplification and the differences between dome and cylindrical surfaces.

Development and cross-validated comparison of machine-learning regression models for predicting peak vortex-induced torque from pneumatic and geometric parameters, with Gaussian Process Regression providing the best overall performance.

1. Experimental quantification of vortex-induced torque as a function of supply pressure, tangential nozzle diameter, surface geometry, and curvature was conducted.

2. Identification of geometry-dependent torque amplification for dome-concave surfaces, including a highly repeatable local maximum near a specific object-gripper geometric relationship.

3. Demonstration that lifting force and vortex-induced torque exhibit different dependencies on the gripper-surface gap, showing that rotational interaction cannot be inferred from lifting force behavior alone.

4. Introduction of an object-gripper geometric-matching interpretation to describe the observed torque amplification and the differences between dome and cylindrical surfaces.

5. Development and cross-validated comparison of machine-learning regression models for predicting peak vortex-induced torque from pneumatic and geometric parameters, with Gaussian Process Regression providing the best overall performance.

title: Scale Anchoring via Implicit Semantics and Sequence-Consistent Loop Closure for VGGT-Based SLAM
authors: Ziyi Jin,Kangjin Yu,Beichen Wang,Can Jiang,Zhongpu Xia,Jie Xu
comment: . Submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027
abstract:
Feed-forward geometric foundation models enable dense monocular reconstruction
without requiring camera calibration, but independently reconstructed submaps
can accumulate scale drift, and even a valid revisit can yield an inconsistent
cross-submap measurement. We extend VGGT-SLAM 2.0 with fixed-root scale
anchoring and short-sequence-assisted direct loop connections. SALAD selects
an image pair between the initial submap and each eligible new submap; joint
VGGT inference then uses learned implicit semantic-geometric cues to supply a
scale-only anchor while preserving the original overlap chain. For loop closure,
neighboring image pairs support a consistency
check and translation-scale alignment. Each accepted candidate contributes one
robust Sim(3) factor between existing center-frame nodes, without an auxiliary
loop submap. A 17-sequence comparison lowers mean Sim(3) ATE on nine TUM
sequences from 0.1018 to 0.0451 m relative to the VGGT-SLAM 2.0 baseline.
Anchoring improves all seven no-loop module ablations. On three Clio scenes,
a fixed-loop comparison favors the direct connection pipeline over the tested
auxiliary-submap pipeline.
A separate candidate audit exposes additional rejections of visually
overlapping pairs by the short-sequence check. These comparisons distinguish
the gains from long-range scale anchoring and loop connection choices from
the limitations of candidate verification.
introduction:
Feed-forward visual geometry models simplify dense monocular reconstruction
by predicting cameras and scene geometry directly from images. Their bounded
context, however, requires long streams to be partitioned into independently
reconstructed submaps. VGGT-SLAM 2.0 connects these submaps through a factor
graph [1], extending local reconstruction to longer
trajectories. Two difficulties remain: adjacent-overlap measurements can
accumulate scale drift, and separately reconstructed loop measurements may be
inconsistent with the existing map. The second difficulty is not only a
place-recognition problem: even a true revisit can yield an incompatible
relative scale or local geometry.

Scale drift is particularly relevant when a trajectory traverses new regions
without a verified loop closure. Each overlap provides a local relation, but
the scale of a distant submap depends on a chain of such relations. Small
systematic errors can therefore produce substantial long-range inconsistency
even when neighboring submaps appear well aligned. A loop closure can constrain
this drift only when a suitable revisit is retrieved and accepted. This raises
a complementary question: can learned reconstruction provide useful nonlocal
scale information before a reliable geometric revisit is available?

VGGT offers a potential source of that information. Its DINOv2-initialized
representation and large-scale 3D training support generalization beyond
explicit feature correspondences; the original paper also demonstrates
qualitative reconstruction from non-overlapping views [2].
These observations motivate our working hypothesis that implicit
semantic-geometric priors retain useful relative-scale cues even when little
or no covisibility makes relative pose estimation unreliable. In this view,
learned regularities in scene appearance and structure may inform scale
without establishing the precise spatial relationship between the cameras.
An inaccurate cross-view pose therefore need not make all scale information
unusable. The distinction matters because applying an uncertain full-pose
constraint would impose more information than the scale cue alone supports.
Fig. 1 summarizes this motivation and the
resulting scale-only construction.

We consequently exploit scale separately from pose, without assuming that
arbitrary non-overlapping views yield correct scales. Since VGGT uses
scale-normalized training targets [2], our target is relative
submap scale, not absolute metric scale. Here, semantic awareness refers to learned scene cues used for image selection and potentially supporting scale inference, without explicit semantic labels.

Our fixed-root anchor uses SALAD to select a compatible image pair between
the current submap and submap zero. Joint VGGT inference places the two images
in a shared reconstruction; comparing camera-frame point norms with their
original submap reconstructions then supplies a relative-scale observation.
The descriptor selects the images rather than measuring scale, and the
estimated cross-view rotation and translation are not inserted as constraints.
Connecting eligible submaps to the same initial reference reduces dependence
on sequential overlap-scale propagation. Unlike selecting an arbitrary recent
reference, the fixed root keeps the reference endpoint fixed instead of moving
it along the growing scale chain. It is a common reference, not a guarantee that the first reconstruction
has the correct metric scale. Weak, robust anchor factors accommodate
potentially biased observations while preserving the original overlap chain.
The anchor does not assert a return to the initial location: it seeks scale
consistency without requiring a verified revisit.

Loop closure addresses a different requirement: when a revisit is accepted,
its relative measurement must be compatible with the reconstructed submaps.
We use neighboring image pairs to check cross-submap consistency and align
translation scales. These supporting views inform verification and estimation,
but each accepted center pair adds only one direct Sim(3) factor between
existing poses, without an auxiliary loop submap or extra neighboring-pair
edges. This separates the evidence used to assess a loop from the connections
inserted into the graph. Scale anchors and loop factors are thus complementary:
the former supplies nonlocal scale observations without asserting a revisit,
whereas the latter corrects pose using accepted revisits.
The two modules are detailed in Sec. III.

The contributions are:

Fixed-root scale anchoring guided by learned retrieval, preserving
the original local overlap chain.

Short-sequence-assisted direct loop connections that separate
supporting views from graph edges.

Reference-policy, weight, and module ablations, plus separate
fixed-candidate and fixed-loop comparisons of verification and connection.

We evaluate one configuration on 17 sequences, separating module contributions
on seven sequences and auditing loop acceptance independently of trajectory
accuracy. Per-sequence regressions remain part of the reported evaluation.

1. Fixed-root scale anchoring guided by learned retrieval, preserving
the original local overlap chain.

2. Short-sequence-assisted direct loop connections that separate
supporting views from graph edges.

3. Reference-policy, weight, and module ablations, plus separate
fixed-candidate and fixed-loop comparisons of verification and connection.

title: Corridor-Based Monitoring and Emergency Braking Decision for Automated Vehicle Safety
authors: Junnan Pan,Vladislav Nenchev,Mohak Mansharamani,Prodromos Sotiriadis,Ferdinand Englberger
comment: Submitted to a Springer Nature journal for peer review as an extended version of a paper presented at VEHITS, for consideration in the Special Issue
abstract: This paper addresses emergency-braking decisions for a redundant safety channel in automated vehicles. The channel is responsible for identifiying hazards from sensor data and determining whether braking is necessary, given the constrained computational resources of embedded hardware. We present an emergency-braking approach that uses a predicted motion corridor to filter Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) measurements and then decide whether the ego vehicle must brake. Predictive Motion Corridor Monitoring (PMCM) constructs a curvature-aware boundary from the planned path and vehicle geometry so that the monitored region contains the full swept body on both straight and curved paths. Gated Dual-Evidence Threat Assessment (GDETA) then decides whether the ego vehicle must command an emergency brake for objects inside this boundary, scoring geometric occupancy and temporal urgency independently. Hard gates permit braking when either source is conclusive; soft-OR arbitration combines partial evidence when neither gate is active. Consecutive-scan confirmation reduces sensitivity to transient measurement noise. Corridor coverage is evaluated in controlled collision simulations and recorded campus driving. Braking decisions are evaluated in Monte Carlo simulations of lead-vehicle braking and transverse-crossing encounters.
introduction:
Modern Advanced Driver Assistance System (ADAS) stacks increasingly rely on Artificial Intelligence (AI), especially deep neural networks, to raise nominal perception performance Shivanna and Guo (2023). These models are not easy to inspect and may produce detections that are hard to explain Zablocki et al. (2022), or they may degrade on rare, long-tail traffic situations that are poorly represented in the training data Abrecht et al. (2025); Liu and Feng (2024). A second channel, with its own sensor, decision rules, and authority to stop the vehicle, is an established redundancy when the main autonomy stack misses a hazard or leaves too little time to avoid a collision Hanselaar et al. (2024); Pan et al. (2024).

This paper studies such a second channel that runs on low-cost hardware, such as microcontrollers, and that can support a safety argument. The monitor takes a trajectory planned by the High-Level Autonomy System (HLAS) and raw scans from a single LiDAR, and at each scan decides whether an emergency stop is required within a bounded monitoring region.

For such resource-limited monitoring systems, two questions follow. First, how can the monitoring area be restricted to the traffic participants that may collide with the ego vehicle as it follows the planned path? Second, once those participants occupy that area, how can the available object measurements and the known ego motion be used to decide an emergency brake command?

Last-feasible-brake rules determine when to stop based on objects that have already been tracked Kaempchen et al. (2009); Brännström et al. (2010), but they generally assume that geometric relevance has already been established. Where an explicit monitoring region is used, it is often a coarse keep-out mask Pan et al. (2024); Gutjahr and Werling (2014). On a tight turn, such a mask may be too narrow along the outer edge, so an obstacle enters the monitored region only after the available braking distance has been consumed. The same mask may be too wide beside the path, so curbs or parked vehicles appear relevant.

We use the same predicted motion corridor to retain LiDAR returns within the swept body and to decide whether the ego vehicle must command an emergency brake for the resulting objects. The geometric basis is PMCM, a curvature-aware monitoring boundary. The planned rear-axle path is expressed in a curvilinear frame, the four body corners are propagated along it, and sliding extrema of their tracks form an envelope that contains the swept body at any curvature. GDETA then scores geometric occupancy and temporal urgency independently on this envelope, so either source can command a stop when its evidence is conclusive.

Keeping the two evidence sources separate lets GDETA use the information the tracker already has. Object position is available before velocity is reliable, so the geometric evidence can command braking once the object occupies the emergency envelope for the required number of scans, or immediately if the object is already close and blocks enough of the corridor. After a valid motion estimate exists, the temporal evidence checks whether the object will still overlap the ego width when the ego reaches that longitudinal position, and whether braking has become urgent. The temporal condition must persist over consecutive scans before a command is issued, so a brief predicted overlap or one noisy measurement does not stop the vehicle.

Evaluation starts with corridor coverage and then isolates the brake rule. A controlled collision series places a static obstacle at the outer corridor edge across a range of speeds and turning radii. Among the three masks considered, the PMCM envelope is the only one that both detects the obstacle in every trial and prevents collisions in all tested cases after braking. The parallelogram mask detects the obstacle too late, while the two-point strip often fails to detect it. The GDETA threat assessment decision rule is then evaluated independently in two Monte Carlo campaigns. An established lead-vehicle case tests temporal assessment with the geometric gate suppressed by a confirmed track. A transverse-crossing case tests geometric intervention during the first scans after a sudden corridor entry, before a reliable motion estimate and tracker lock are available.

This article extends our previous conference publication Pan et al. (2026), which introduced the curvature-aware PMCM method and evaluated it in a case study. The present article reformulates PMCM and extends it with:

GDETA, a deterministic threat-assessment rule that scores geometric occupancy and temporal urgency independently, admits a hard gate on either source, and uses soft-OR arbitration when no gate applies.

An evaluation that separates corridor coverage from braking decisions and examines GDETA in established lead-vehicle braking and transverse-crossing encounters.
