title: Riemannian Optimization-based Whole-body Obstacle Avoidance for Mobile Continuum Robots in Cluttered Environments
authors: Duo Tang,Ping Deng,Sophie Armanini,Yajing Shen,Toshio Fukuda,Cosimo Della Santina,Peng Lu
abstract: In nature, snakes, elephant trunks, and octopus arms demonstrate the ability to traverse cluttered and confined environments with remarkable agility, relying on tight coupling between global behavioral intent and local morphological adaptation. This characteristic provides important inspiration for motion planning and control of continuum robots. However, existing approaches for mobile-base continuum robots typically emphasize either high-level path planning or local motion control in isolation, making it difficult to simultaneously ensure dynamic feasibility, kinematic consistency, and operational safety in narrow passages and geometrically complex environments. To address this challenge, we propose a unified planning and control framework for mobile-base continuum robots that enables coordinated long-horizon planning and real-time execution. The framework integrates task-level trajectory reasoning with geometry-aware local motion adaptation, achieving consistent global-to-local decision making under kinematic and environmental constraints. The global layer employs an A*-guided minimum-jerk planning scheme to generate dynamically feasible long-horizon reference trajectories, while the local layer ensures real-time kinematic feasibility and collision avoidance through a geometry-consistent inverse kinematics solver and a Riemannian manifold-based optimization strategy. Extensive validation is conducted in both simulation and real-world systems. In simulation, pipe traversal tasks are designed and evaluated against multiple baseline methods. Real-world experiments include navigation in obstacle-dense environments and manipulation in confined spaces. The results demonstrate that the proposed method improves motion consistency, feasibility, and environmental adaptability for mobile continuum robots operating in constrained environments, providing an effective technical pathway toward real-world deployment.
introduction:
Biological systems with compliant bodies navigate cluttered environments by exploiting their intrinsic kinematic redundancy and distributed sensing. Snakes, octopus arms, and elephant trunks, despite their distinct morphologies, achieve robust locomotion and interaction through continuous body deformation and physical interaction with their surroundings [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Inspired by these biological structures, continuum robots replace discrete rigid-link architectures with bodies that bend and twist continuously [6, 7, 8, 9]. Their inherent compliance and high kinematic redundancy enable access to environments that are difficult for rigid manipulators to reach, including tortuous anatomical pathways in surgical settings [10, 11], collapsed structures in search-and-rescue scenarios [12, 13], and confined spaces for inspection and maintenance [14, 15]. However, translating these morphological advantages into autonomous operation in unstructured environments remains challenging. The continuous deformation of the robot body introduces highly nonlinear kinematics and dynamics, making accurate modeling, inverse kinematics, and collision-aware motion generation considerably more difficult than for rigid-link manipulators [16].

In practical environments, a continuum manipulator cannot always rely on a fixed base to provide a suitable workspace. Mounting the manipulator on a mobile platform can substantially enlarge its reachable workspace and enable navigation and manipulation within large, cluttered, and spatially constrained environments. However, mobility also fundamentally changes the planning problem. The motion of the mobile base and the deformation of the continuum arm are strongly coupled: base motion changes the reachable workspace of the end-effector, while arm configuration determines collision constraints and feasible base poses. Consequently, autonomous operation requires planning over a high-dimensional configuration space while simultaneously maintaining geometric consistency of the deformable arm, avoiding obstacles, and satisfying the computational constraints of real-time execution.

Existing research has made substantial progress in continuum robot actuation, kinematic modeling, and motion planning [17, 18, 19, 20, 6, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25]. However, most studies focus on individual subsystems or operate under restrictive assumptions, with limited consideration of the coupling among mobile-base motion, continuum deformation, and real-time collision avoidance. In particular, coordinated base–arm planning for mobile continuum robots remains relatively underexplored [26].

This gap is particularly important for real-world deployment. Independently planning the mobile base and continuum arm can produce globally inconsistent motions, while jointly optimizing their high-dimensional coupled configuration is computationally expensive. We therefore propose a hierarchical motion planning framework that coordinates long-horizon global planning with real-time local geometric refinement. The local layer incorporates a curvature-based inverse kinematics solver that enforces segment-level geometric consistency and a Riemannian orientation optimizer that generates smooth, singularity-free trajectories. Integrated with a compact mobile continuum robot platform, the proposed system enables coordinated base-arm motion with real-time collision avoidance in cluttered environments.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

An integrated platform for mobile continuum robots is developed, providing a compact and lightweight physical system with integrated mechanical structure, actuation, and onboard electronics for autonomous navigation and manipulation.

An integrated platform for mobile continuum robots is developed, providing a compact and lightweight physical system with integrated mechanical structure, actuation, and onboard electronics for autonomous navigation and manipulation.

A hierarchical motion planning framework is proposed to address the high-dimensional configuration space and coupled base–arm motion of mobile continuum robots. The framework separates global trajectory generation from local geometric refinement while coordinating mobile base motion with continuum arm deformation, enabling real-time planning in cluttered environments.

Two core algorithmic components are developed for local planning. The first is a curvature-based inverse kinematics solver that reformulates FABRIK to enforce segment-level geometric consistency. The second is a Riemannian orientation optimizer that generates smooth and singularity-free orientation trajectories on the orientation manifold.

Comprehensive simulation and real-world experiments validate the proposed system under cluttered and constrained conditions. Comparisons with baseline methods demonstrate improvements in computational efficiency and trajectory quality, while physical experiments further demonstrate robust coordinated navigation and collision avoidance on the mobile continuum robot.

title: Beyond Terminal Constraints: Reliable Robot Control with Learned Safe Sets
authors: Gianni Lunardi,Elias Fontanari,Matteo Saveriano,Andrea Del Prete
abstract: Ensuring safety in advanced robot control methods such as Model Predictive Control (MPC) and Reinforcement Learning remains an open challenge. A common approach relies on control-invariant sets, yet their exact computation for nonlinear systems is generally intractable, and numerical approximations compromise theoretical guarantees. In this work, we show that safety does not need to rely exclusively on control invariance. We introduce novel classes of safe sets, each broader than classical control-invariant sets, and analyze corresponding MPC schemes that guarantee recursive feasibility by constraining different nodes of the prediction horizon rather than only the terminal state. Furthermore, when the safe set is an inner approximation of a suitable control-invariant set, our methods can ensure safety through a safe-abort strategy, even in the absence of recursive feasibility. We validate our approaches in extensive simulations on a 6-joint robot manipulator, showing fewer constraint violations than state-of-the-art methods while maintaining comparable tracking performance and computational efficiency. Hardware experiments further demonstrate the practicality of our schemes for real-world robotic applications.
introduction:
Safety is a fundamental concern in robotics, playing a crucial role in enabling reliable, robust, and trustworthy operations. Safety concerns are multifaceted, including obstacle avoidance, prevention of falls in legged robots, and avoidance of joint and actuator limits, which could otherwise lead to hardware damage or system failure.

Among the many challenges in ensuring robotic safety, two areas stand out due to their importance and relevance: Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) and safe learning control. In HRI [53, 46], robots must operate in proximity to humans, necessitating strict guarantees to avoid collisions and ensure human well-being. This requires advanced perception, planning, and control systems capable of responding rapidly to unpredictable human behavior while adhering to safety standards.

In parallel, the advent of learning-based control methods [23, 40] has revolutionized the field of robotics, enabling robots to adapt to complex and uncertain environments. However, the safety of learning-based control methods remains a critical concern, as they often lack formal guarantees and can exhibit unsafe behaviors during training or deployment. Ensuring safety of learning-based control methods is essential for their widespread adoption in real-world applications.

These challenges motivate the need for advanced control methods that can provide formal safety guarantees while enabling robots to operate in complex and dynamic environments. In the literature, there are three main tools to certify the safety of a controller: Control-Invariant Sets (CISs) [9, 20], Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) [2, 3, 51], and predictive shielding methods based on Back-Up Policies (BUPs) [7]. These tools are typically applied to different control methods, respectively Model Predictive Control (MPC), Quadratic-Programming (QP) based control, and Reinforcement Learning (RL).

Despite the great amount of work devoted to safety in the last decade, ensuring safety for general high-dimensional nonlinear systems is still an open problem.
A key challenge seems to be the computation of so-called CISs (a.k.a. safe sets).

In this paper, we introduce new classes of safe sets that are broader than CISs. Indeed, as shown in Fig. 1, these novel classes contain the class of CISs, and rely on the concept of multi-step safety, which allows the state to leave the set for a limited number of time steps before entering it again. 
These sets generalize the concept of CIS, meaning that they must satisfy weaker requirements than CISs.
We hypothesize that these new sets might therefore be easier to compute and certify with numerical approximation methods. This is confirmed by empirical evaluations on the computed safe sets, even though we do not thoroughly validate this hypothesis in this paper.
Instead, we show that three existing MPC formulations (Receding-Constraint MPC, Hard Terminal-Constraint MPC, and Parallel-Constraint MPC) can ensure RF or safety assuming the safe set belongs to a specific class. Unlike classic approaches that only use the safe set as a terminal constraint, these MPC schemes apply the constraint at different nodes along the prediction horizon.
With respect to our previous work [30, 18], we present the following extensions spanning theory, computational efficiency, and validation:

We present four classes of safe sets that contain the class of CISs, of which only one was discussed in our previous work.

We correct a mistake in the theory of Receding-Constraint MPC [30], clarifying the property of the safe set that it needs to ensure RF.

We prove that Parallel-Constraint MPC can ensure RF under weaker conditions than Receding-Constraint MPC, defining the associated novel class of safe sets (back-and-forth-within-N-step CISs).

We prove that the classic Hard Terminal-Constraint MPC can ensure safety (without RF) even if the terminal constraint set is not a CIS, but it belongs to the larger class of back-and-forth-NN-step CISs.

While in our previous work the safe-abort procedure was too slow for a real-time implementation, this limitation is mitigated through a suitable choice of the safe set and the optimization algorithm.

title: Can Astra Solve RoboMME without Breaking the Bank?
authors: Bingao Chen,Haoquan Fang,C. Karen Liu
comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Memory for Robot Foundation Models and the Workshop on Agentic Robotics, CoRL 2026. Project page:this https URL
abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering information that is no longer visible, such as an object’s location before occlusion or the order of a demonstrated action sequence. A large vision-language planner can read this history, but calling it before every action chunk is slow and costly. We present a three-tier system for the RoboMME benchmark. GPT-6 Astra (System 2) selects a grounded subtask from stored visual history, a π0.5\pi_{0.5} vision-language-action policy (System 1) executes it, and a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-4B monitor (System 1.5) checks after each action chunk whether the subtask is finished. The instruction is kept until the monitor reports completion or a task-specific event occurs, while the policy keeps acting on new observations. On RoboMME, the system succeeds in 79.13% of episodes with an average of 3.63 Astra calls and 80.84 seconds per episode. This is 34.62 points above the best published non-oracle baseline and 4.95 points below GroundSG+Oracle, which gives the low-level policy ground-truth subgoals.
introduction:
Manipulation can depend on information that is no longer visible: an object’s identity before it is covered, the order of a demonstrated sequence, or the number of repetitions already completed. RoboMME [3] tests these dependencies with 16 tasks in four suites: Counting, Permanence, Reference, and Imitation. A common design for such tasks is hierarchical, with a vision-language model (VLM) choosing the next subtask and a vision-language-action (VLA) policy executing it.

In our development runs, small high-level VLMs often misread RoboMME’s video inputs and issued wrong subtasks, so we use GPT-6 Astra [6] as the planner. Calling it before every action chunk, however, is expensive and mostly redundant: a chosen subtask usually remains valid for several chunks, and whether it has finished can be judged from the last few frames.

We therefore place a small learned monitor between the planner and the policy. Astra is called at the start of an episode and again only when the monitor reports completion or a task-specific event occurs. In between, the VLA keeps executing the same instruction from fresh observations. We evaluate the full system on RoboMME and report success rates, planner usage, and failure cases.

RoboMME compares symbolic and perceptual memory interfaces [3]. SAM2Act adds a visual memory bank [4], MemER retrieves keyframes [8], and MEM combines short-horizon video with long-horizon text memory [9]. Hierarchical systems such as τ0\tau_{0}-VLA use execution memory and test-time reasoning to select subtasks [2]. Our system instead sends task-dependent history to an external planner at each call and lets a local monitor decide when to call it.

title: 3D Pose Estimation in Projection Space via Pixel-level Visible Light Communication
authors: Michikuni Eguchi,Takefumi Hiraki
comment: submitted to IEEE Access
abstract:
Projector-based augmented reality enables natural interaction between users and devices by overlaying digital information onto the physical world through projected imagery.
A key technical requirement of such systems is accurate positional alignment between the projector and the devices.
Pixel-level Visible Light Communication (PVLC) achieves this alignment without external sensing infrastructure by embedding invisible spatial codes into each projected pixel through high-speed brightness modulation that preserves image quality.
However, the information that PVLC transmits is inherently planar.
PVLC has therefore been limited to devices moving on a flat surface and cannot estimate the 3D pose of devices in three-dimensional space, such as aerial robots.
To extend PVLC-based pose estimation to three dimensions, we formulate it as a Perspective-n-Point (PnP) problem.
The 2D pixel positions that four coplanar photosensors on the device receive via PVLC serve as the image points, and their known 3D layout provides the object points.
Experiments show that the proposed system estimates 3D pose with a latency of approximately 8 ms and a 3D position RMSE of 19.2 mm after Kalman filtering.
These results confirm the first realization of real-time 3D pose estimation coordinated with high-quality projected image content without external sensing infrastructure.
introduction:
Interaction systems based on augmented reality (AR) enable natural collaboration between users and devices by superimposing digital information onto the real world.
Among them, projector-based AR, also known as Spatial Augmented Reality (SAR) [1], overlays information directly onto real space with projected images.
Because users do not need to wear special devices such as head-mounted displays, SAR enables more natural interaction.
This technology has already produced many promising applications, including efficient teaching operations for industrial robots [2, 3], tabletop interfaces using mobile robots [4, 5, 6], and interactive art [7].

To seamlessly coordinate device behavior with projected image content, the system must obtain the position of the device relative to the projector with high accuracy.
Achieving such accuracy typically requires external sensing equipment such as cameras [8] or motion capture systems [9], as well as geometric calibration between the projector and these sensors [10].
This requirement increases setup complexity and limits practical deployment.

Pixel-level Visible Light Communication (PVLC) [11], a projector-based visible light communication technique, has been proposed to address these challenges.
PVLC embeds invisible position codes into each pixel of the projected image through high-speed brightness modulation.
A photosensor on the device decodes the pixel coordinate at its location to obtain its own position within the image.
Because no external sensors or projector-sensor calibration is required, and because the embedded information is invisible to the human eye, PVLC enables device localization alongside high-quality projected content.
However, the projected image is inherently planar, and the position that a device obtains from it is limited to two dimensions.
PVLC has therefore been applied only to devices moving on a plane, such as ground robots [12], and cannot support devices that operate in three-dimensional space, such as aerial robots.

t!](topskip=0pt, botskip=0pt, midskip=0pt)[width=0.99]figures/concept.png
Conceptual overview of the proposed 3D pose estimation system using Pixel-level Visible Light Communication (PVLC). The projector embeds invisible position codes into each pixel. Multiple photosensors on the device decode their 2D pixel coordinates, which are combined with the projector’s intrinsic parameters and the known 3D sensor geometry, and fed into a PnP solver to estimate the device’s 3D pose.

To overcome this limitation, we extend PVLC-based localization from two dimensions to three by formulating it as a Perspective-n-Point (PnP) problem [13].
Fig. I shows an overview of the proposed method.
The PnP problem is widely used for camera-based pose estimation.
In our formulation, the 2D pixel coordinates that multiple photosensors on the device decode via PVLC serve as the image points, and their known 3D layout provides the object points.
Solving this problem gives the 3D pose of the device with respect to the projector.
This approach enables 3D device control in coordination with high-quality projected images without projector-sensor calibration and opens up applications such as aerial robot navigation.

We conduct three experiments to validate the proposed method:
(1) evaluation of pose estimation accuracy under different movement speeds and photosensor layout sizes, with a camera-based AR marker method as a baseline,
(2) comparison of multiple PnP solvers to identify the most suitable one for the system, and
(3) investigation of the effectiveness of Kalman filter-based smoothing on estimation accuracy.
The results demonstrate that the system achieves centimeter-order position estimation accuracy with a latency of approximately 8 ms.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

The first application of PnP-based 3D pose estimation to PVLC. By solving the PnP problem with the 2D pixel coordinates decoded by multiple photosensors, the method extends PVLC-based localization from 2D to 3D.

A content display region and a 3D pose tracking region that both cover the entire projection area at the same time. Because PVLC embeds the position codes into every pixel of the displayed content, the tracking region coincides with the content display region. Neither a dedicated tracking region nor an external sensor is required.

Evaluation on a device moving at speeds from 50 to 400 mm/s. By combining the pose estimation with a Kalman filter, the method achieved a 3D position RMSE of 19.2 mm over all trajectories and movement speeds with the 80 mm photosensor layout.

1. The first application of PnP-based 3D pose estimation to PVLC. By solving the PnP problem with the 2D pixel coordinates decoded by multiple photosensors, the method extends PVLC-based localization from 2D to 3D.

2. A content display region and a 3D pose tracking region that both cover the entire projection area at the same time. Because PVLC embeds the position codes into every pixel of the displayed content, the tracking region coincides with the content display region. Neither a dedicated tracking region nor an external sensor is required.

3. Evaluation on a device moving at speeds from 50 to 400 mm/s. By combining the pose estimation with a Kalman filter, the method achieved a 3D position RMSE of 19.2 mm over all trajectories and movement speeds with the 80 mm photosensor layout.

title: Online Adaptation to Latent Physical Properties for Learning from Demonstration
authors: Kotaro Kajitsuka,Masaki Murooka,Fumio Kanehiro
comment: Accepted for the 2027 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration (SII 2027)
abstract:
Manipulating visually identical objects with different physical properties requires adapting actions based on information acquired through interaction.
We address the problem of learning from demonstrations how to adapt manipulation actions, such as regrasping and changing contact locations, based on physical-property information acquired during interaction.
To this end, we propose a learning-from-demonstration method that learns latent representations of physical properties needed to predict object responses and conditions a policy on online estimates of these representations.
A dynamics model and object-specific latent representations are jointly learned from demonstrations that include behaviors adapting to the objects’ physical properties, and the learned representations are then used to condition an imitation policy.
During execution, the dynamics model and policy weights remain fixed, while the latent representation is updated based on the discrepancy between predicted and actual observations, allowing interaction with the object to inform action generation.
Real-world and simulation experiments with objects whose centers of mass differ suggest that online adaptation through latent representations of physical properties can improve task success rates.
However, in simulation, success rates on center-of-mass locations absent from the demonstrations remained around 30%, indicating limited adaptation to unseen physical properties.
Project page: https://isri-aist.github.io/latent-dynamics-project-page/
introduction:
Learning from demonstration (LfD) has been applied to a wide range of robotic manipulation tasks, including manipulation of deformable objects and long-horizon tasks.
These methods have shown strong performance in settings where visual observations provide sufficient information for action selection [1], while adding force measurements supports delicate tasks such as wiping [2, 3].
Humans infer physical properties such as mass and friction through interaction and use this information to guide subsequent actions, for example, adjusting their grasp and posture when lifting a heavy object.

Regrasping or changing contact locations based on inferred properties requires retaining information from earlier contacts and using it to select subsequent actions.
Policies conditioned on a short observation window may struggle when action selection requires information outside that window [4].
In this work, we focus specifically on physical properties inferred from earlier interactions.

Beyond LfD, online system identification has been extensively studied through analytical approaches, dynamics-based property estimation [5], and adaptation using simulation-trained dynamics models [6].
Connecting this body of work with LfD could substantially broaden the range of manipulation problems that can be learned from demonstrations.

In this work, we collect demonstrations of property-dependent manipulation using visually identical objects with different centers of mass (CoM) or centers of friction (CoF).
The demonstrations include corrective actions in response to unexpected object motion, such as regrasping or changing contact locations.
Within this setting, we propose and evaluate an imitation learning method that adapts online to differences in object physical properties.

Fig. 1 provides an overview of the proposed approach.

To adapt to these latent physical properties, we introduce an implicit dynamics parameter 𝐝i\mathbf{d}_{i} as a latent representation of object ii.
We first learn the dynamics model and 𝐝i\mathbf{d}_{i} from demonstrations, then train a policy conditioned on the learned representation.
During execution, we update the estimate 𝐝^\hat{\mathbf{d}} online using discrepancies between model predictions and actual observations, and generate actions conditioned on the inferred properties.

The method has two advantages.
First, it initially learns a dynamics model and implicit physical representations solely from demonstrations, without prior measurements of the objects’ physical properties.
Second, its continuous representation, rather than a discrete object category, is intended to support adaptation to unseen objects.

Our contributions are as follows:

We show that interaction data in manipulation demonstrations can be used to learn implicit representations of differences in object physical properties.

We demonstrate that combining LfD with dynamics-based property estimation improves performance on tasks involving visually identical objects with different physical properties, including deformable objects.

1. We show that interaction data in manipulation demonstrations can be used to learn implicit representations of differences in object physical properties.

2. We demonstrate that combining LfD with dynamics-based property estimation improves performance on tasks involving visually identical objects with different physical properties, including deformable objects.

title: The Effectiveness of Sliding Mode Control for Robust Vision Stabilization under the Plant-Binding Condition
authors: Sooyeun Yang,Jongseong Brad Choi,Seung Bok choi
abstract:
Boundary-layer Sliding Mode Control (SMC) has been applied to vision-based
stabilization, but identifying its activation condition against
simpler causal baselines (LPF, PID) has been elusive. The operational
condition is plant binding: the disturbance velocity approaches
or exceeds the actuator slew limit, so the bounded per-step actuation
budget binds. We validate this
in two independent vision domains: handheld translation stabilization
(1212 10801080p clips; LPF, PID, SMC, L1L^{1}) and angular re-framing
against a virtual slew-rate-limited pan–tilt–zoom (PTZ) plant. Outside binding,
leave-one-out cross-validation makes SMC and LPF on translation
statistically indistinguishable, and PID beats SMC on the angular
9999th-percentile pointing offset by 5.85∘5.85^{\circ}
(95% CI clear of zero); inside binding — reached only by sweeping the
simulated slew limit, as both captured datasets land outside it — the
translation gap stays a tie
and SMC beats PID on the angular worst case (Cohen’s dd up to +0.83+0.83).
The PTZ plant’s 100∘/100^{\circ}/s default sits on the cross-over,
which explains a small-margin PID result previously reported
in the angular setting. A complementary ablation shows raising the SMC reaching gain
kk costs mean tracking outside a narrow window.
introduction:
Boundary-layer Sliding Mode Control
(SMC) [1, 2] is a natural candidate for
vision-based stabilization: the per-frame stabilizing warp can be cast
as a virtual unit-mass plant disturbed by an unknown but bounded shake
signal, and the boundary-layer reaching law of Slotine and
Li [2, 3] drives the sliding variable
into a tunable layer
in finite time. Yet across recent practical work, SMC variants have
produced mixed and often negative comparisons against simpler causal
baselines such as causal low-pass filtering (LPF) and PID. Our own
prior single-domain experiments are no exception: handheld translation
stabilization placed SMC behind LPF by 2.672.67 px above-cutoff residual
on 1111 test clips, and active angular re-framing placed SMC behind PID
by 5.85∘5.85^{\circ} at the 9999th-percentile pointing
offset on a virtual PTZ plant. Both first-draft conclusions read as
“SMC under-performs” without identifying the regime in which the
bounded-disturbance robustness actually becomes load-bearing.

An explanation draws on three separate literatures. SMC’s
robustness to bounded matched disturbances is
classical [1, 4], and practical deployment
guides caution that the discontinuous machinery pays for
itself only against a genuinely binding
uncertainty [5]. Software video stabilization spans
causal filtering through offline optimal-path
methods [10, 11, 12], but comparisons
run on an unconstrained (software-warp) actuator. PTZ platforms
carry an explicit mechanical pan–tilt rate
limit [14], and the saturation literature treats
bounded actuation as the central design
obstacle [15, 16]. To our knowledge, the
point at which that constraint activates SMC’s advantage over
simpler laws in a vision loop has not been isolated experimentally.

This paper resolves both negatives with a single observation. The
boundary-layer machinery activates only when the disturbance velocity
approaches or exceeds the actuator’s slew limit — i.e. when a
bounded per-step actuation budget binds against a near-binding
disturbance. We call this the plant-binding regime and show
across two independent vision-control domains that it is the
operational activation condition for boundary-layer SMC.
Fig. 1 (Sec. 2) summarizes the unified
per-axis control loop in which the claim is tested.

Primary contributions.
(1) An operational binding condition for boundary-layer SMC on
vision-control tasks.
We identify and empirically validate the binding regime: it is
stated as a normalised binding ratio (Sec. 2) and
verified directly by sweeping the plant slew limit through the
crossing in both domains (Sec. 3.5); the sweep
is simulated, and Sec. 4.3 scopes the claim
accordingly.
(2) Robust vision stabilization inside binding.
Once the plant binds, boundary-layer SMC uses its
provable insensitivity to the matched shake disturbance and to plant
uncertainty to improve worst-case stabilization over
PID (Cohen’s dd up to +0.83+0.83) while staying at least as good on the
mean. On the present simulation evidence, SMC is therefore the
stronger controller inside this actuation-constrained regime; the
hardware demonstration is future work.
(3) A two-domain unification.
The same binding condition governs SMC activation in translation
stabilization and in angular re-framing against a slew-limited plant.
The 100∘/100^{\circ}/s default of the angular PTZ plant sits
on the cross-over, so earlier draft comparisons that read SMC as
“no better than PID” were taken at an unbinding
operating point, not a structural SMC deficiency.

Supporting contributions.
(4) A disclosed bandwidth Pareto for the translation
σt​y\sigma_{ty} metric.
SMC and LPF tie under leave-one-out cross-validation (+0.050+0.050 px,
CI crosses zero); the residual gap at the conservative operating
point c=25c{=}25 is a bandwidth choice
(Sec. 3.4), not an SMC deficiency.
(5) A “higher gain is not free” ablation.
We confirm the binding gap is closed by the plant, not by gain
inflation: pushing the SMC reaching gain kk from 5050 to 400400
over-actuates and gives no broad improvement, so the tuned
boundary-layer SMC is already the right robust design.

Sec. 2 unifies the two-domain model and the
boundary-layer design; Sec. 3 presents the harness,
the disclosed Pareto trade-off, and the binding cross-over;
Sec. 4 gives the ablations and limitations;
Sec. 5 concludes.

title: Learning Object-Centric Motion Priors from Human for Robotic Dexterous Manipulation
authors: Zhengdong Hong,Guofeng Zhang
comment: Accepted as an oral paper at AAAI 2026 (Website:this https URL)
abstract: Manipulating diverse objects with multi-fingered dexterous hands is challenging due to the high dimensionality and complex dynamics. Human-Object Interaction (HOI) datasets provide rich knowledge about task information and embodied interactions. Instead of solely imitating the human demonstrations, our method learns to holistically predict future hand-object states by leveraging these datasets. The predicted future states of the object can serve as a general-purpose reward term for reinforcement learning, reducing reliance on task-specific reward engineering and enhancing generalization across tasks. We conduct extensive experiments on three manipulation tasks in simulation and the real world. Our approach outperforms existing SOTA methods in both success rate and generalizability on novel objects. Furthermore, we validate the cross-embodiment compatibility of our methods by successfully deploying the skills on different robot hands.

title: Reflection-Robust Stereo Visual-Inertial Odometry via Kalman-Filtered Ground-Height Estimation
authors: Uihyun Hwang,Sungjae Shin,Dongjae Kim,Hyun Myung
comment: . Presented at the 26th International Conference on Control, Automation, and Systems (ICCAS 2026), Sapporo, Japan. Included in the conference proceedings
abstract: Visual-inertial odometry relies on visual features that correspond to 3D points with consistent projections across sequential frames. In reflective indoor-floor environments, however, specular floor patterns can be detected and triangulated as virtual features below the physical ground plane, producing unreliable feature associations and inconsistent visual residuals. This paper proposes a lightweight reflection-aware front-end for feature-based stereo VIO. Rather than suppressing all floor-region features, the proposed method estimates the ground height in real time and rejects only feature candidates whose inferred 3D positions are below the estimated ground height. A floor-region mask restricts the validation process to reflection-prone regions, while stereo height uncertainty and pose uncertainty are used to construct frame-level ground-height measurements. A scalar Kalman filter with Normalized Innovation Squared (NIS) gating then provides a stable ground-height estimate, and an uncertainty-aware safety margin is used for selective below-ground virtual feature rejection. Experiments on real reflective-floor indoor sequences show that the proposed front-end generally improves trajectory accuracy in reflection-dominant environments while maintaining accurate ground-height estimates and recovering from actual ground-height changes.
introduction:
Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) estimates camera motion by combining inertial measurements with visual feature observations. In feature-based stereo-inertial systems, feature detection, tracking, stereo matching, and triangulation precede the formation of visual constraints [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. The reliability of these front-end features is therefore critical, as erroneous feature geometry degrades residual consistency and odometry stability.

Indoor mobile robots frequently operate on reflective floors such as polished tiles or coated concrete, where ceiling lights, window illumination, and surrounding structures are reflected and produce high-contrast image patterns. Standard feature extractors [7, 8] treat these reflected patterns as valid features, even though they do not correspond to stable 3D structures. The severity of this effect depends on the geometry of the surface. Herbert et al. [9] showed that geometrically consistent virtual features from smooth mirrors can occasionally provide useful odometry constraints, whereas Pyykola et al. [10] demonstrated that non-Lambertian surfaces such as tiles or windows yield view-dependent appearances that cause false matches, erroneous depth, and trajectory drift. Indoor reflective floors fall into the latter case, producing view-dependent specular patterns that violate multi-view consistency and degrade feature-based VIO.

As illustrated in Fig. 1, the original VIO front-end extracts many features from the floor region, including reflection-induced virtual features. A naive floor rejection strategy that simply discards all features in the floor region could suppress these reflections. However, it also removes physically valid on-floor features, such as tile edges or surface texture, which can still provide meaningful visual information for VIO. This naive rejection strategy is overly conservative and may degrade the front-end, especially when background features are sparse.

A natural way to realize such a geometry-based criterion is to estimate the ground plane explicitly and reject features that lie far from it. Zhou et al. [11] followed this idea in an RGB-D SLAM system, fitting the ground plane from dense depth via RANSAC and discarding features distant from the fitted floor. However, per-pixel depth processing with iterative RANSAC is computationally expensive for a lightweight stereo VIO front-end. Moreover, when virtual features dominate the floor observations, the RANSAC inliers become contaminated and the fitted plane is biased below the true ground, which undermines the very geometric reference used for rejection.

This paper proposes a reflection-robust stereo VIO front-end for selective below-ground virtual feature rejection. Instead of fitting a dense ground plane, the proposed method maintains an adaptive scalar ground-height estimate from sparse stereo features and Kalman filtering [12], and rejects features whose triangulated positions fall below the estimated ground height by more than an uncertainty-aware margin. This keeps the rejection criterion robust to reflection-induced contamination while retaining real-time operation. The contributions of this paper are summarized below.

1) We propose a lightweight Kalman filter-based ground-height estimation method that adapts to robot pose variation and physical ground-height changes.

2) We present a selective below-ground virtual feature rejection strategy for VIO front-end reliability, which is applicable to feature-based stereo VIO pipelines.

title: LumiTac: Compact, High-Rate Six-Axis Optical Tactile Sensing for Human-Robot Interaction
authors: Hao Wu,Haotian Guo,Yu Feng,Yutong Wang,Jianshu Zhou
abstract: Integrating six-axis tactile feedback into robotic interfaces requires compact sensors with accurate load measurement and rapid online reconstruction. This paper presents LumiTac, a low-profile, camera-free optoelectronic tactile sensor combining spatially distributed illumination with spectral encoding. Five photoemitters and five RGBW photoreceivers are mounted on opposing circuit boards coupled through translucent silicone. Load-induced interlayer motion modulates the internal light field under compression, shear, bending, and torsion. The sensing head measures 12 mm in diameter and 4.75 mm in thickness, weighs less than 2 g, and has a component cost of approximately USD 7. A compact multilayer perceptron reconstructs three force and three moment components from 20 optical channels. Independent testing yielded coefficients of determination (R2R^{2}) of 0.9657–0.9941, with mean absolute errors of 0.054–0.190 N for forces and 0.304–1.419 mN⋅\cdotm for moments. Online prediction achieved an average update rate of 303.57 Hz and a median software processing latency of 0.722 ms. Experiments involving combined loading, light weights, and rapid tapping evaluated load tracking, sensitivity to small forces, and transient response, respectively. Robotic demonstrations further validated its applicability to tactile-guided manipulation and physical human–robot interaction. This study paves the way for compact, high-rate optical tactile sensing in robotic manipulation and human–robot interaction.
introduction:
Robotic manipulation requires continuous adjustment to contact forces during grasping, alignment, and physical interaction. To enable responsive and adaptive manipulation, embedded sensing [1] and intuitive control interfaces [2, 3] have been explored to enhance robotic perception and interaction. In particular, tactile sensing provides local contact feedback that external vision alone cannot readily supply [4, 5]. Beyond normal and tangential forces, bending and torsional moments characterize rotational loading relevant to contact alignment and orientation control. Measuring the complete six-axis contact wrench therefore supports multidimensional interaction feedback. Integrating this capability into space-constrained robotic interfaces, such as fingertips [6], grippers [7], and wearable devices [8], requires sensing structures with a small footprint, limited thickness, and low mass. Rapid load reconstruction is equally important for timely feedback in contact-rich tasks.

Multi-axis force/torque (F/T) measurement has been implemented using various transduction mechanisms, including capacitive [13, 11], magnetic [14], thermal [6], piezoelectric [15], and optical [16, 9] sensing. Capacitive designs organize deformation-dependent responses through electrode geometry and spacing [13]. Lee et al. improved directional sensitivity through isotropic optimization and redundant measurements [17]. CoinFT achieves a thin, low-cost structure using silicone pillars and configurable electrode readout [11], while HexaTouch reconstructs six-axis loads and contact position from capacitive images [12]. These studies demonstrate the potential of capacitive sensing for compact six-axis measurement. However, parasitic capacitance and electrode misalignment can introduce measurement errors, while cross-axis coupling complicates calibration and the reconstruction of individual force and moment components.

Magnetic tactile sensors infer contact loads from deformation-induced field changes detected by Hall elements [14]. MagCilia combines flexible magnetic cilia with a Hall sensor to reconstruct normal and tangential forces from field changes induced by compression and bending [18]. Veliky et al. use distributed Hall-sensor and magnet pairs to capture translations and rotations of a silicone-supported structure for six-axis load reconstruction [19]. Although magnetic sensing enables compliant multiaxis measurement, external magnetic fields and nearby ferromagnetic objects can distort the measured field, introducing errors that require shielding or compensation.

Thermal and piezoelectric transduction offer further approaches to six-axis sensing. Mao et al. used thin-film thermistors to detect deformation-induced changes in the thermal conductance of a compliant medium, enabling an ultralight design but requiring active heating and temperature compensation [6]. Gong et al. combined an ultrathin piezoceramic shell with patterned electrodes to distinguish load-induced charge distributions. This monolithic architecture supports sensitive dynamic measurements, although its AC-coupled readout limits absolute quasi-static load measurement [15].

Vision-based tactile sensors encode contact-induced deformation in camera images and infer forces from surface appearance or marker displacement, as demonstrated by GelSight, TacTip, and DIGIT Pinki [20, 21, 22]. Camera-based pose tracking enables six-axis force and moment reconstruction in fiducial-based sensors [23]. Optical feedback has been integrated into compliant grippers for manipulation and force regulation [24, 16, 25]. Despite their high spatial resolution, camera acquisition and image processing can limit update rates. Camera size, optical working distance, and computational demands also complicate integration into thin, compact robotic interfaces.

Camera-free optical sensors recover loads from wavelength shifts or discrete light measurements. Fiber Bragg grating-based designs distribute strain measurements along an optical fiber to achieve low-coupling six-axis sensing, although they require fiber attachment and wavelength interrogation [26]. Discrete optoelectronic designs instead measure deformation-dependent light signals using distributed emitters and receivers [27, 28]. LiVec combines local optical measurements to recover forces, displacements, and resultant moments [7], whereas El-Azizi et al. use LEDs as both emitters and receivers to measure motion between elastomer-connected plates [9]. By avoiding image formation, discrete optical readout supports compact layouts, low-dimensional signal processing, and high-rate acquisition. Ambient light, optical alignment, and elastomer nonlinearity nevertheless remain design and calibration considerations.

A central challenge in compact six-axis optical sensing is to distinguish coupled translations and rotations, since different deformation modes may produce similar changes in received light intensity. Previous studies have explored overlapping light signals and patterned color encoding to introduce spatial and spectral information into deformation measurements [29, 30]. The comparison in Table I further motivates combining informative optical measurements with a low-profile structure and rapid online reconstruction. To address these requirements, we present LumiTac, a camera-free optoelectronic tactile sensor shown in Fig. 1. Five photoemitters and five RGBW photoreceivers are mounted on opposing PCBs coupled through translucent silicone. The spatially offset emitter–receiver layout and multiple LED colors provide spatial and spectral cues associated with load-induced interlayer motion. A compact multilayer perceptron (MLP) jointly processes the resulting 20 optical channels to estimate three force and three moment components, enabling frame-wise online load reconstruction. The main contributions are as follows:

A miniaturized hardware design that integrates six-axis tactile sensing into a head measuring 12 mm in diameter and 4.75 mm in thickness, with a mass below 2 g and an estimated component cost of approximately USD 7.

Its online implementation delivers an average prediction update rate of 303.57 Hz with a median software processing latency of 0.722 ms.

Experimental validation of load tracking, sensitivity to small forces, and transient response, together with demonstrations of simulated manipulator guidance and physical robot admittance control, establishing a single tactile interface for robot motion and gripper operation.

title: Diversity-Aware Experience Replay via Statistical Leverage Scores
authors: Shaifalee Saxena,Alexander Scheinker
abstract: Off-policy deep reinforcement learning trains on random samples from a replay buffer of past experience. In physical robot settings, that buffer is dominated by routine: thousands of near-identical transitions from normal operation, while the rare events that define the edges of the task are rarely sampled. We propose scoring every stored transition by its statistical leverage, which measures how unusual it is relative to the buffer’s own data, computed from the stored numbers alone, with no labels, rewards, or value network. We draw each mini-batch from a mixture of this score and uniform sampling. First, the natural way to build the score along the directions where the data varies most turns out to be blind when actions are stored as one-hot indicators, because indicator columns always win the variance ranking; we instead select the feature columns with the heaviest tails (largest kurtosis) where small far-away populations are revealed. Second, the importance weights that prioritized replay uses to keep gradients unbiased cancel the method exactly: with full correction, training matches uniform sampling, so we drop the correction and deliberately optimize the rebalanced objective. Third, when the rare situations of a log are relational, visible only in how a stretch of behavior relates to its goal, not in any single stored coordinate—per-transition scores are blind; applying the same tail rule to short trajectory windows described relative to their goal restores the signal, and on a three-joint arm that must push an object around an obstacle it raises the rare-task success from 0.49 to 0.69 against a labeled-oracle ceiling of 0.74.
introduction:
Deep reinforcement learning (RL) [1] has become a practical tool for synthesizing feedback controllers directly from interaction data. The modern off-policy template descends from the Deep Q-Network (DQN) [2], which revived the classical idea of experience replay [3]: transitions (s,a,r,s′)(s,a,r,s^{\prime}) are stored in a large ring buffer, and mini-batches drawn from the buffer decorrelate consecutive updates and allow each interaction to be reused many times. Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) [4], followed by Twin Delayed DDPG (TD3) [5] and Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) [6] carried this template to continuous control, where they remain the workhorse algorithms of robot learning [7]. Sample efficiency has been improved mainly by extracting more gradient signal from the same stored data: ensembling and high update-to-data ratios [8], normalization and network scaling [9], and learned state–action representations with prioritized replay [10]. These advances support real-robot manipulation pipelines that train in minutes to hours [11, 12] and autonomous control of large scientific instruments, including the tuning of particle accelerators [13, 14]. Despite this progress, uniform sampling remains the default replay rule in standard off-policy RL.

Uniform sampling implicitly assumes that every stored transition is equally worth revisiting, and this assumption degrades precisely as learning succeeds. A partially converged policy fills the buffer with thousands of near-identical transitions, such as the gripper hovering over the object in almost the same pose, or the beam sitting at a near-optimal setpoint with very low beam loss. At the same time, rare transitions that delineate the boundaries of the task (unusual contacts, failed grasps, off-nominal beam excursions) are sampled with vanishing frequency and eventually overwritten. In this work, we make the buffer’s own geometry the sampling signal. We view the buffer as a tall data matrix, one standardized transition per row, and score each transition by its statistical leverage [15]: the squared, whitened length of its projection onto a chosen score subspace, equivalently a (truncated) Mahalanobis distance from the buffer’s own empirical distribution. Mini-batches are drawn from a mixture placing weight β\beta on the normalized leverage scores and 1−β1-\beta on the uniform distribution. Because N≫dN\gg d, the scores can be refreshed efficiently with buffer-wide statistics and a vectorized pass over the stored transitions.

Our contributions are: (1) a leverage-mixture replay rule using excess-kurtosis column selection to avoid variance-subspace blindness under one-hot actions, and omitting importance-sampling correction, which we show cancels the rebalancing exactly; (2) exact, numerically verified sampling-share laws on Gaussian-mixture buffers, including a rarity-independent amplification ceiling and a multi-cluster mass law; (3) offline Q-learning experiments against exact Q∗Q^{*}, demonstrating improved learning in an underrepresented region; and (4) a window-level extension for relational rare behaviors, where goal-relative trajectory scoring on a three-joint arm trained with TD3+BC improves over transition-level replay and approaches a labeled oracle.

title: FWIK: Multi-Waypoint IK Selection via Lookahead Graph Search
authors: Jinglan Cao,Guohui Zhong,Chengwei Zhang
abstract: An ordered sequence of end-effector poses can give a redundant robot arm multiple valid joint configurations at each waypoint. Inverse kinematics (IK) computes these configurations. Choosing a configuration only for the next waypoint can leave the arm poorly placed for later waypoints. This may increase planned motion time or cause a later planning failure. This paper presents Future-Window Inverse Kinematics (FWIK), an online method that selects IK solutions by considering a small window of future waypoints. FWIK generates several IK candidates, connects them in a layered joint-space graph, and ranks candidate paths with a simple motion-time estimate. A learned model removes paths whose transitions are likely to cause self-collision. A standard MoveIt 2 planner then checks the next-waypoint IK goals from the remaining paths in ranked order, and the first goal that yields a valid trajectory is selected for execution. We evaluate FWIK in simulation on two 7-DoF manipulators, the Franka Emika Panda and the KUKA LBR iiwa. Each method-planner setting contains five repetitions of 100 sequences with 50 waypoints. Across Pilz, RRT-Connect, CHOMP, and STOMP, FWIK completes 96.8–100% of sequences and gives the shortest planned trajectory duration in all eight robot-planner settings. Its mean duration is 12.8–13.1% lower than STAMPEDE, 22.5–25.6% lower than IKLink, and 27.5–37.2% lower than retry-based TRAC-IK. The results show that a small future window can improve sequence completion and reduce planned motion time while leaving final trajectory validation to the motion planner.
introduction:
Many robot tasks require an ordered sequence of end-effector poses rather than a single isolated goal. Welding, surface inspection, and multi-stage pick-and-place are common examples. For a redundant manipulator, the same end-effector pose may admit multiple valid joint configurations because the robot has more degrees of freedom (DoF) than are required to specify the end-effector pose [1]. Inverse kinematics (IK) determines such configurations for a desired end-effector pose.

The choice of IK solution affects more than the current motion. The selected configuration becomes the start state for the next planning request, so locally equivalent IK solutions can have very different consequences for the remaining waypoint sequence. One configuration may preserve joint range and maintain connectivity to future IK branches, whereas another may require a large posture change or make a later waypoint difficult to reach. Repeated local choices can therefore increase planned trajectory duration, introduce discontinuous motion, or cause the sequence to terminate when a later waypoint cannot be planned [2, 3, 4].

Standard online IK interfaces are typically pointwise: given a target pose, they return a feasible configuration for that pose without explicitly reasoning about downstream waypoints. A solver such as TRAC-IK can quickly provide a valid configuration under joint limits [5], after which a motion planner generates a trajectory toward that goal. This separation is simple and efficient, but it discards useful future information when several upcoming waypoints are already known.
Methods that generate diverse IK solutions or optimize configurations over an entire path address related aspects of this problem [2, 6, 7, 8, 9]. However, full-path methods exploit the complete known sequence before execution, whereas an online system may instead benefit from bounded lookahead: using only a short future window, executing one decision, and updating that decision as the task progresses or new information becomes available.

Self-collision introduces a second source of inefficiency. Geometric collision checkers such as the Flexible Collision Library (FCL) provide accurate collision tests and remain essential for final validation [10]. However, if the IK selection layer proposes a goal whose transition from the current configuration is likely to self-collide, the downstream planner may spend substantial effort on an unfavorable target before failing and retrying another IK solution. Learning-based collision models have shown that approximate configuration-space representations can reduce the cost of repeated collision queries [11, 12, 13]. For multi-waypoint execution, however, configuration validity alone is insufficient: the relevant question is also whether the transition from the current state to a candidate IK solution is likely to be collision-prone.

These observations motivate the central question of this paper: Can finite-horizon IK selection with edge-level self-collision screening improve the success–time trade-off of online multi-waypoint manipulation compared with pathwise or retry-based IK selection?

We answer this question with Future-Window Inverse Kinematics (FWIK), an online IK decision layer that operates upstream of a standard motion planner. At each execution step, FWIK constructs a layered graph over a finite window of upcoming waypoints. Each node represents an IK candidate, and each edge represents a possible transition between two candidates with an associated synchronized joint-motion time estimate. Rather than selecting the next IK target independently, FWIK ranks candidate paths according to their connectivity and estimated motion cost across the visible window. The leading transitions of promising paths are then screened using a learned edge-level self-collision model before distinct first-goal candidates are submitted to a MoveIt 2 planner for geometric validation. Only the first validated IK target is executed; the window then advances by one waypoint and the decision process is repeated. In this way, FWIK uses future information without replacing the downstream motion planner or committing to a complete trajectory in advance.

The main contributions of this paper are:

A finite-window formulation of online IK selection that chooses the next IK target according to its connectivity with near-future waypoint solutions, rather than considering the next pose in isolation.

An edge-level self-collision screening module that rejects risky leading transitions before costly planner retries while retaining geometric collision checking in the downstream planning pipeline.

A repeated evaluation on two manipulators and four motion planners, comparing FWIK against IKLink, STAMPEDE, and TRAC-IK in terms of sequence success, waypoint completion, IK decision time, and planned trajectory duration.

1. A finite-window formulation of online IK selection that chooses the next IK target according to its connectivity with near-future waypoint solutions, rather than considering the next pose in isolation.

2. An edge-level self-collision screening module that rejects risky leading transitions before costly planner retries while retaining geometric collision checking in the downstream planning pipeline.

3. A repeated evaluation on two manipulators and four motion planners, comparing FWIK against IKLink, STAMPEDE, and TRAC-IK in terms of sequence success, waypoint completion, IK decision time, and planned trajectory duration.

title: Does RRT* Work on Uneven Terrain Meshes?
authors: Otobong Jerome,Tiago Nascimento
comment: . Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters
abstract: The optimal rapidly exploring random tree (RRT∗) is proven asymptotically optimal on open subsets of Euclidean space with straight-line local planning. We ask whether it works on a triangle-mesh terrain, a two-dimensional surface in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}. First, the original RRT∗ cannot run on a mesh: the surface has zero volume, so uniform sampling never hits it, no clearance ball fits in it, and chords across a fold leave it. Second, the surface reformulation we call Mesh RRT∗, with its naive edge, the chord costed by its length, solved every run on heightfields with slopes up to 75∘75^{\circ} but minimises the wrong objective: its cost, the straight-line length of a polyline whose vertices lie on the surface while its segments may leave it by a tolerance τ\tau, is the length of no route on the surface and lies strictly below the geodesic length on any curved mesh. In numeric simulation and after 30 000 iterations the reported cost is on average up to 2.7% below the exact geodesic, a cost no path attains, and the returned route on average 0.1–0.5% longer than it. Rewiring keeps the biased edges, the bias decays only linearly with the step on polyhedral surfaces, and shrinking τ\tau trades bias for connectivity. Third, replacing each chord by a path on the surface above it, built from projected points joined across the mesh edges they straddle and costed by its own length, makes every edge cost the exact length of a feasible path; with no other change the exact length of the returned routes is on average within 0.07–0.16% of the geodesic at every roughness tested, two to 3.4 times closer than with chords on the rougher terrains. The planner is in MeshNav3D 0.2.0 (release pending).
introduction:
Ground robots on rough terrain and surface-bound aerial vehicles plan on a surface, usually a triangle mesh, and the natural cost is geodesic length. The established tools are graph planners on the mesh (Dijkstra, A∗, Theta∗) and geodesic solvers such as the exact Mitchell–Mount–Papadimitriou (MMP) algorithm [1], fast marching [2] and the heat method [3]. Sampling-based optimal planners, led by the optimal rapidly exploring random tree (RRT∗) of Karaman and Frazzoli [4], are rarely applied here, and their guarantees are stated for Euclidean free space. This paper is about one of their primitives, Line, the routine that connects two tree nodes and prices the connection.

Jaillet and Porta extended RRT∗ to implicitly defined configuration manifolds such as closed kinematic chains, with local charts built by higher-dimensional continuation, and argued asymptotic optimality on the manifold [5, 6]; here the manifold is an explicit triangle mesh whose faces are the charts and whose geodesics can be computed exactly. Mesh geodesics are a mature field [1, 7, 3]; exact MMP is our ground truth. Sampling-based mesh planning has been used for ground robots with the basic rapidly exploring random tree (RRT), where the geodesic computations between tree nodes are a heavy load that the method reduces [8]; surface-bound aerial vehicles have instead been steered along the mesh by Riemannian motion policies on a planar parametrisation of it [9]. A∗ on the mesh graph and Theta∗ [10] serve as graph-planner reference points. We know of no prior work measuring sampling-based mesh planners against exact geodesics or identifying the cost inconsistency studied here.

This paper keeps two quantities apart. The length of a route is geometry: how far it runs along the mesh surface, measured here exactly with a geodesic solver. The cost of a route is what the planner computes, optimises and reports: the number its Line primitive assigns to each edge, summed along the route. In Karaman and Frazzoli’s setting the two coincide, because an edge is a straight segment inside the free space and its cost is its length. On a mesh they coincide only if the primitive makes them: a straight chord between two surface points is not a path on the surface, so its length is the length of no route, and a planner that charges it optimises and reports a cost below the surface length of the route it returns. Whether that happens on terrain meshes, by how much, and with what effect on the returned route is what we measure.

We test the hypothesis that RRT∗ does not work on uneven terrain meshes in its literal and in its practical form. Literally, RRT∗ is the algorithm and guarantees of [4], defined on an open subset of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, d≥2d\geq 2, with volume, uniform sampling and straight-line local planning. Practically, it is the reformulation an implementation on a mesh could make once the literal algorithm is found not to run there (Section III): sample the surface, steer along it and, in the naive form, connect nodes by straight chords costed by Euclidean length.

Our contributions are:

A structural argument that literal RRT∗ cannot run on a mesh, because a surface has zero volume in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} (Section III).

Mesh RRT∗, which follows Algorithm 6 of [4] primitive by primitive, with two implementations of Line, naive (chords costed by their length) and consistent (surface paths costed by their own length), all else identical (Section IV).

The chord-polyline cost Jη,τJ_{\eta,\tau} (Definition 1) that the chord variant optimises, with proofs that it never exceeds the surface length of the same route (Proposition 1) and that its optimum lies strictly below the geodesic length whenever the geodesic bends (Proposition 2), and why rewiring keeps the biased edges (Section V).

Experiments against exact geodesics on terrains of controlled roughness: a dense-graph estimate of the chord optimum Jη,τ,k∗J^{*}_{\eta,\tau,k}, the dependence of the bias on the step η\eta and the tolerance τ\tau, and the convergence of both variants (Sections VI–VII).

An implementation in MeshNav3D 0.2.0 [11] (release pending).

title: Time-to-Goal: Learned Temporal Metrics for Long-Horizon Planning with JEPA World Models
authors: Ruilong Yu,Fei Ye
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) support planning by comparing predicted latent states with an encoded goal. For this comparison to guide temporal progress, states closer in time to the goal should receive lower costs. However, training representations for prediction and distribution regularization does not directly enforce this ordering. We examine this mismatch in flat LeWorldModel (LeWM) by analyzing how its Euclidean goal cost changes with temporal separation. Our analysis identifies conditions under which states at different long offsets receive similar average costs, weakening their temporal distinction. To learn the missing ordering explicitly, we introduce Time-to-Goal (T2G), a lightweight metric trained on latent triples from offline trajectories. A margin ranking loss encourages smaller distances for temporally nearer states, requiring no rewards or policy labels. The learned metric then replaces the Euclidean planning cost while the JEPA encoder and predictor remain frozen. Diagnostics on AntMaze and FourRoom show that T2G preserves stronger temporal contrast and improves near–far ranking at long offsets. Across four navigation and manipulation benchmarks, T2G improves the average planning success rate from 32.7% (flat LeWM) to 63.0% and approaches or even surpasses the performance of the hierarchical H-JEPA baselines. These results show that learning temporal ordering for the goal cost can substantially improve latent planning even with a flat world model. Code is available at https://github.com/yrluestc/T2G-JEPA.
introduction:
Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) [1, 2, 3] learn world models by predicting future observations in a latent space. An encoder maps observations to representations, and an action-conditioned predictor models how these representations evolve under actions. This avoids pixel reconstruction and allows planning by comparing predicted future states with an encoded goal. LeWorldModel (LeWM) [4] implements this with a next-embedding prediction loss and a sketched isotropic Gaussian regularizer (SIGReg), which discourages representation collapse. Its planner optimizes actions using the Euclidean distance between predicted states and the goal. However, as shown in Fig. 1, this flat planner may provide an unreliable progress signal over long horizons, where reliable predictions and a cost that reflects distance to or progress toward a distant goal are both required. A flat model must roll out many prediction steps, leading to error accumulation. Moreover, matching a distant goal in a representation space that also carries low-level details can be difficult. H-JEPA [5] addresses these challenges with a hierarchy of JEPAs operating at increasing temporal strides in which subgoals divide a long task into shorter planning problems, and higher levels provide more abstract spaces for goal matching. Because this hierarchy changes both how futures are predicted and how they are evaluated, its gains conflate architectural and cost-related effects. This motivates isolating the goal cost and examining whether a better cost estimate alone can improve flat planning in long-horizon settings.

We ask whether the goal-matching cost of a flat model can guide planning without introducing a hierarchy. Intuitively, a useful cost should assign lower values to states that are closer to reaching the goal. However, LeWM’s Euclidean cost is applied to representations trained for next-state prediction and distribution regularization. Its training objective does not explicit impose supervision of progress toward a goal. We therefore examine the Euclidean costs of states along a saved planning trajectory. Specifically, we compare pairs of states separated by an interval of several model steps. Our analysis shows that, as this interval increases, the difference in their Euclidean costs becomes progressively smaller. This weakens the cost signal for ranking candidate futures when the states are far from the goal.

To provide this temporal signal, we propose Time-to-Goal (T2G), a lightweight learned temporal metric for long-horizon planning. T2G learns a small embedding network on flat LeWM latents and uses Euclidean distance in this embedding as a temporal-distance score. It is trained on latent triples sampled from offline trajectories, where a ranking objective encourages a temporally nearer future state to be closer to the anchor state than a farther future state. The LeWM encoder and predictor remain frozen, and no rewards or policy labels are required during this process. During planning, the same predictor rolls out candidate action sequences, and T2G scores their predicted states by their learned distance to the goal.

Our contributions are summarized as follows.

We analyze the case where Euclidean latent distances provide little distinction across temporal separations when states are far from the goal.

We introduce Time-to-Goal, a lightweight learned temporal metric with only 0.182M parameters (1.6% of the flat LeWM), which substantially improves flat LeWM on long-horizon tasks without changing the latent world model.

Comprehensive experimental results demonstrate that T2G enables flat LeWM to approach or even surpass multi-level H-JEPA in our long-horizon evaluations.

1. We analyze the case where Euclidean latent distances provide little distinction across temporal separations when states are far from the goal.

2. We introduce Time-to-Goal, a lightweight learned temporal metric with only 0.182M parameters (1.6% of the flat LeWM), which substantially improves flat LeWM on long-horizon tasks without changing the latent world model.

3. Comprehensive experimental results demonstrate that T2G enables flat LeWM to approach or even surpass multi-level H-JEPA in our long-horizon evaluations.
