title: Ctrl-F: Force as an Interface for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Mengjie Zhao,Yuxin Chen,Yiyang Shao,Chuye Hong,Jiakang Chen,Koushil Sreenath,Masayoshi Tomizuka
comment: Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Humanoid motion tracking has scaled to general policies that reproduce
diverse human motion, but the resulting behavior is in free-space: the tracker
knows where the body should be, not how it should interact with the
environment. Other work makes the object part of the objective, yet abstracts
that interaction to contact or geometry, which leaves the demanding cases
under-explored. We argue that force is a natural command channel between motion imitation
and object interaction, one that specifies not just where to make contact but
how hard.
We present Ctrl-F, a hierarchical motion–force framework that
augments motion tracking with an explicit force command, a 3-D force at each
designated contact body such as a hand or a foot. The hierarchical framework comprises:
(1) A unified motion–force controller tracks the reference motion
while applying the commanded force to the world.
(2) A high-level force planner that issues a force command online based on
object state and proprioception observations.
In simulation and on hardware, Ctrl-F completes loco-manipulation that demands
large, sustained interaction force and adjusts its command online as the load
changes, both out of reach of a force-blind tracker.
On hardware, Ctrl-F demonstrates hand-based dragging, pushing, and lifting, as well as foot-based kicking, successfully manipulating boxes weighing up to 2020 kg in pushing and kicking tasks where the force-blind baseline fails, while adapting online to additional loads introduced mid-task.
introduction:
Many everyday whole-body tasks require sustained physical interaction with the environment, such as carrying a heavy box, dragging a crate, or pushing against a resistant door. These tasks demand coordinated whole-body motion and continuous force regulation as the environment responds. A heavier box requires a stronger grip, while a stuck crate demands greater pulling force.

Humanoid robots have made remarkable progress in reproducing human motion.
Policies have evolved from tracking individual clips [1] to general trackers capable of reproducing hours of motion capture with a single model [2, 3, 4, 5], leveraging the scalability of motion data. However, reference motions specify only where the body should move, without accounting for physical interaction. Even a strong motion tracker can fail when manipulating objects: in our experiments, a force-blind tracker fails to lift boxes weighing 1.51.5–66 kg, as the boxes slide off the robot’s palms, resulting in zero successful episodes. The motion is reproduced, but the intended interaction is not.

Recent work has incorporated object interaction into the tracking objective through representations such as object motion, contact labels, and distance fields [6, 7, 8]. While these abstractions enable scalable learning, they primarily describe when and where contact occurs, rather than how much force should be exerted. Consequently, the policy cannot be explicitly commanded to apply greater force or adapt to heavier loads under the same reference motion. Force provides a natural and unified representation of physical interaction, directly capturing what the object experiences. Unlike discrete contact labels, force encodes both magnitude and direction, making it a continuous and expressive command signal for controlling physical interactions.

Force has been incorporated into humanoid control in several ways, though not as a general interaction command: as an external
disturbance resisted through force curriculum training [9], as end-effector stiffness modulated through hindsight goal perturbation [10], as a commandable position-force target at a single interaction point [11].
While each addresses aspects of force control, none of them combines general motion imitation with explicit force commands and online force adaptation based on object feedback during interaction.

To bridge this gap, we introduce Ctrl-F, a hierarchical humanoid loco-manipulation framework that explicitly commands the forces exerted on the environment. At the low level, a general motion–force controller jointly tracks a reference motion and executes a 3-D force command for each designated contact body. Trained without objects through inverse-force training, the controller preserves the scalability of general motion tracking without requiring object models or paired interaction data, while exposing force as an independently controllable input. Building on this frozen controller, a high-level force planner generates force commands from object states and proprioceptive observations. The planner is initialized through on-policy learning from an analytical force model and further refined via reinforcement learning, enabling it to adapt to contact dynamics beyond those captured by the analytical model.

Our contributions are:

We define a general force interface for humanoid interaction and train it without objects. Interaction is specified as a 3-D force at each designated contact body. The motion–force tracker is trained via inverse-force training without paired object assets or interaction data, enabling generalization across objects and interaction patterns without task-specific representations.

We train a high-level force planner to generate force commands from object and robot states. At deployment, the policy requires neither force measurements nor object mass, yet continuously adapts its commands to changes in object state and load.

We demonstrate sim-to-real deployment of our framework on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot across multiple physical interaction tasks and loading scenarios, including online adaptation to load changes during execution.

1. We define a general force interface for humanoid interaction and train it without objects. Interaction is specified as a 3-D force at each designated contact body. The motion–force tracker is trained via inverse-force training without paired object assets or interaction data, enabling generalization across objects and interaction patterns without task-specific representations.

2. We train a high-level force planner to generate force commands from object and robot states. At deployment, the policy requires neither force measurements nor object mass, yet continuously adapts its commands to changes in object state and load.

3. We demonstrate sim-to-real deployment of our framework on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot across multiple physical interaction tasks and loading scenarios, including online adaptation to load changes during execution.

title: Jev with Foresight: Safe Language-Guided Autonomous Driving via a Language World Model
authors: Yansong Qu,Jiancong Chen,Samuel Labi
abstract: Large language models understand passengers’ driving commands, but as driving agents they reason in generated text for seconds and must infer each action’s consequences implicitly from the scene. We present Jev-AD, which pairs Jev, a typed decision model that answers predefined questions with probabilities, not generated text, with a language world model that predicts for every candidate action how nearby vehicles move over the next two seconds. Code turns these predictions into foreseen consequences, which Jev compares instead of inferring them from coordinates. In simulated highway merging (500 car-episodes), this foresight lowers the same decision model’s collision rate from 26.0% to 2.4% at 0.25 seconds per decision, and Jev-AD achieves the passenger’s intent in 93% of free-form command trials. In 500 replayed real-world NGSIM episodes, foresight lowers the collision rate from 48.2% to 2.8%, and the world model, learned from this traffic, foresees 93% of dangerous actions. Project page: https://ys-qu.github.io/jev-ad-website.
introduction:
As autonomous vehicles (AVs) move from test tracks to public roads [1], passengers will expect to tell them how to drive in their own words rather than through a menu of driving modes [2, 3]: “I’m late for a meeting, please get me there quickly”, “Please drive gently, I get carsick easily”, or “Let the car on the ramp merge in front of us”. Such an interface has to understand free-form commands, turn them into measurably different driving, refuse requests that would endanger anyone, and respond within the decision period of the vehicle.

Large language models (LLMs) have made this kind of interaction plausible. Beyond understanding language, they bring commonsense knowledge about traffic, and a growing line of work uses them as driving agents that describe the scene in text, reason about it, and decide how to drive [4, 5, 6, 7]. Two problems stand in the way of using them for every decision. First, an LLM agent typically writes a chain of thought before it answers, which is slow and costly when a decision is due every fraction of a second. Second, the agent decides from what it has observed so far and must anticipate implicitly, from positions and speeds in text, what each action will lead to; in dense interactions such as merging, this can fail.

For the first problem, dual-process designs keep the large model out of the fast loop: DriveVLM runs a vision-language model alongside a conventional planner [8], and LeapAD transfers the experience of its slow analytic process to a small fast model [9]. Typed decision models instead make the decision itself fast: they read the state as text and return probabilities over predefined answers, computed in parallel rather than generated one token (word piece) at a time [10], and have served as fast decision layers that call a strong LLM only when unsure [11] or control an agent’s memory [12]. They are called typed because each question fixes the type of its answer (a choice among named options, a score on a scale, or yes/no), and the model returns a probability for every possible answer. Jev, released by TypeSafe AI in limited early access in September 2026, is one such model: it answers typed questions (choices, scores, and yes/no questions) with probabilities and confidence scores [10]. Its developer calls this class System One models, and several other such models now exist [13]; we use the descriptive name typed decision models.

For the second problem, world models predict how the environment evolves under an action [14, 15], and agents can learn their behavior by imagining the future with them [14, 16]. An LLM can act as a world model that simulates the outcome of each reasoning step [17], and driving world models evaluate candidate trajectories by generating their future views [18], condition actions on imagined future scenes [19], or predict the future scene together with the ego motion [20]. Foreseeing consequences helps to decide safely, but most of these models generate images or long token sequences, which is costly to repeat for every candidate action at every decision.

In this paper, we explore a lightweight way to address both problems in language-guided driving, which combines the two paradigms (Fig. 1). We pair Jev [10], a typed decision model that answers in about 0.13 s, with a small language world model that predicts, for each candidate action, how the nearby vehicles move over the next 2 s. Code turns these predictions into short foreseen consequences, and Jev chooses the action that is foreseen as safe and best matches the passenger’s request (Fig. 2). By foresight we mean these consequences: for each candidate action, whether and when the AV would collide, the minimum time to collision, and its final lane and speed, stated in words. We call the resulting agent Jev-AD (Jev for autonomous driving). We address five research questions (RQs):

How accurately does Jev ground free-form commands, including unsafe ones (Sec. IV-B)?

How well does the language world model foresee dangerous actions (Sec. IV-C)?

How much does foresight reduce collisions, and at what cost in time (Sec. IV-D)?

How often does Jev-AD achieve the passenger’s intent (Sec. IV-E)?

How accurate is the foresight, and how much does it reduce collisions, with altered simulated drivers and in replayed real-world traffic (Secs. IV-F and IV-G)?

Typed decisions for language-guided driving. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first evaluated language-guided driving architecture that uses a typed decision model, as defined in this paper, for recurring closed-loop action selection: Jev grounds each free-form command once and makes every driving decision with one typed call, which is fast and cheap and leaves nothing to parse. A concurrent benchmark runs such models in simulated driving, without commands or foresight [13].

Foresight for safer decisions. The decision model sees, for every candidate action, its foreseen consequences instead of coordinates, and we show that this foresight, more than the way it is predicted, is what lowers its collision rate: even with constant-velocity prediction, the rate of the same decision model falls from 26.0% to 2.8%. Our language world model, which reads the recent history as text and predicts how the nearby vehicles move over the next 2 s, including how they react to the AV, makes the foresight more accurate and lets the car also stop promptly when asked.

Closed-loop evaluation. On KoMA’s merge scenario [5] in highway-env [21], foresight lowers the collision rate of the same decision model from 26.0% to 2.4%, Jev-AD achieves the passenger’s intent in 93% of trials with 24 scored free-form commands, including negated requests and requests in Chinese, and a decision takes about 0.25 s; on real traffic replayed from NGSIM, foresight lowers the collision rate from 48.2% to 2.8%.

1. How accurately does Jev ground free-form commands, including unsafe ones (Sec. IV-B)?

2. How well does the language world model foresee dangerous actions (Sec. IV-C)?

3. How much does foresight reduce collisions, and at what cost in time (Sec. IV-D)?

4. How often does Jev-AD achieve the passenger’s intent (Sec. IV-E)?

5. How accurate is the foresight, and how much does it reduce collisions, with altered simulated drivers and in replayed real-world traffic (Secs. IV-F and IV-G)?

Schoellig,Andreas Krause,Max Simchowitz,Andrew Wagenmaker
abstract:
The introduction of generalist robot policies has enabled a single, large model to learn to perform a variety of tasks from a vast pre-training corpus.
While these models often exhibit powerful zero-shot generalization capabilities, they typically require an adaptation phase to achieve sufficient performance in deployment.
Iterated self-improvement via reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated promise in enabling this adaptation, yet such approaches have been largely explored in single-task settings – where the goal is to simply improve on a narrow deployment task – which lies in stark contrast to the multi-task capabilities of the base policy.
In this work we ask whether generalist robot policies are capable of multi-task, generalist improvement in deployment – targeting many diverse tasks simultaneously – and what algorithmic recipe enables this.
To answer this question, we first develop a set of structured evaluations to test generalist improvement capabilities, and systematically evaluate algorithmic and practical design choices regarding value estimation, policy extraction and resource allocation.
We show that not only can generalist policies be improved online across diverse tasks, but that the right recipe can enable generalization and increase performance on tasks not considered during online training.
We characterize when this generalization occurs and show that both the training task distribution and the use of value-based RL are critical.
To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first evidence for online generalist improvement for robot foundation models.
introduction:
Generalist robot policies, particularly Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs), have shown promise in enabling general-purpose robotic capabilities, allowing a single policy to be deployed across diverse tasks (Brohan et al., 2023; Octo Model Team et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025).
However, despite encoding diverse task-solving behaviors, such policies often lack sufficient reliability for robust deployment, and a degree of adaptation is typically necessary for effective performance (Kim et al., 2025; Intelligence et al., 2025b; Reuss et al., 2025). While enabling this adaptation through human supervision is often prohibitively expensive, autonomous adaptation through reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising approach to scale policy improvement, enabling robots to learn from their own experience in deployment (Intelligence et al., 2025a).
Yet, such autonomous improvement is typically limited to narrow single-task settings. As such, while these approaches enable generalist policies to improve, they may also specialize this improvement to the particular deployment task considered, and achieving improved performance on additional tasks of interest generally requires further online interaction and fine-tuning.

A generalist policy, however, can produce a wide range of behaviors across diverse tasks, even if these behaviors may be far from optimal. Ideally we might hope that, by deploying on a diverse range of tasks, we could improve the performance of the policy across all tasks simultaneously – boosting its performance not just on a single deployment task, but on the entire distribution of tasks of interest.
In particular, we might hope to enable truly generalist improvement: improvement on both the diverse set of tasks we deploy on, as well as generalization beyond these deployment tasks and improved performance on future novel deployment settings.
This motivates the central question we consider in this work: how can we leverage interaction across a diverse set of tasks to enable online generalist improvement of generalist policies?
That is, can a careful adaptation phase over multiple tasks enable both (i) improvement across these tasks simultaneously, and (ii) generalization beyond them, improving performance on tasks not encountered during post-training?

In this paper, we undertake a systematic study to quantify generalist policy improvement across different axes of generalization. We show that appropriate recipes, when instantiated carefully, can enable not only generalist policy improvement across a diverse set of training tasks, but also task-generalization – improvement on tasks not seen during training.
Further, we show that this improvement scales with the number and diversity of tasks trained on, as we showcase in Figure 1.
Our results suggest that moving beyond the single-task paradigm is not only possible but also crucial for achieving broader, generalist improvement.

We isolate the essential algorithmic ingredients that enable multi-task learning and generalization.
Specifically, we compare three families of learning approaches:

Direct Policy Adaptation, which directly improves the policy via filtered supervised fine-tuning on successful trajectories (Peters and Schaal, 2007; Zhou et al., 2024; Qin and Springenberg, 2025, FSFT,).

Critic-Guided Test-Time Refinement, which uses test-time optimization against a learned state-action critic to improve actions. Here, we focus on Best-of-N sampling  (Nakamoto et al., 2024; Giridhar et al., 2026, BoN,) with respect to that critic’s induced action ranking as a representative recipe.

Critic-Guided Policy Extraction, which updates a policy so as to maximize the value the critic assigns to the actions produced. Here, we adopt off-policy generative policy optimization (Patil et al., 2026, OGPO,) as a representative recipe, while also ablating alternative approaches such as combining FSFT and BoN sampling, or using AWR-inspired policy updates (Peng et al., 2019).

In addition to investigating algorithmic choices, we also systematically evaluate the training task distribution necessary for achieving such generalist improvement. We show that both the number of distinct training tasks, as well as the type of diversity exhibited in these training tasks, is critical to achieving generalist improvement. In particular, we find that a high degree of diversity in the required solution strategies within the training task distribution is crucial to learning generalizable task-solving behaviors.

We believe these results illustrate a path forward for efficient online improvement of generalist robot policies. Rather than expensive single-task improvement on each deployment task of interest, our results show that, by amortizing this cost across a diverse set of tasks, one can enable generalist improvement, achieving improved performance on future deployment tasks of interest without paying the cost of additional online fine-tuning.

1. Direct Policy Adaptation, which directly improves the policy via filtered supervised fine-tuning on successful trajectories (Peters and Schaal, 2007; Zhou et al., 2024; Qin and Springenberg, 2025, FSFT,).

2. Critic-Guided Test-Time Refinement, which uses test-time optimization against a learned state-action critic to improve actions. Here, we focus on Best-of-N sampling  (Nakamoto et al., 2024; Giridhar et al., 2026, BoN,) with respect to that critic’s induced action ranking as a representative recipe.

3. Critic-Guided Policy Extraction, which updates a policy so as to maximize the value the critic assigns to the actions produced. Here, we adopt off-policy generative policy optimization (Patil et al., 2026, OGPO,) as a representative recipe, while also ablating alternative approaches such as combining FSFT and BoN sampling, or using AWR-inspired policy updates (Peng et al., 2019).

title: CoSafe: Cooperative Runtime Safety Assurance for Mixed-Traffic Autonomous Driving
authors: Dingji Wang,You Lu,Haowen Jiang,Yanggang Chen,Yuyang Bi,Bihuan Chen,Shenglin Bao,Xin Peng
comment: Accepted by the 49th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE 2027).
abstract:
With the rapid development of autonomous driving systems (ADSes), real-world roads are evolving into mixed-traffic environments where autonomous vehicles (AVs) and other traffic participants (e.g., human-driven vehicles (HDVs), cyclists, and pedestrians) coexist and interact with each other. However, current ADSes still incur various safety violations in mixed traffic scenarios, raising a strong demand for runtime safety assurance frameworks that can continuously monitor hazards and prevent potential violations.
Existing ego-centric assurance approaches are insufficient for mixed traffic, where violations
often arise from locally reasonable yet jointly incompatible decisions among multiple vehicles and cannot be reliably resolved through independent takeover.
introduction:
With the rapid development of ADSes, real-world roads are increasingly evolving into mixed-traffic environments where AVs (i.e., vehicles equipped with ADSes) and other traffic participants (e.g., HDVs, cyclists, and pedestrians) coexist and interact [54]. However, the performance of AVs in open-road mixed traffic remains far from satisfactory. Scenario-based testing approaches [12, 66, 43] have indicated that even advanced ADSes may still incur safety violations in mixed-traffic environments. Besides, a 2024 U.S. Department of Transportation analysis of California ADS disengagement reports [31] found that 69% of disengagements were caused by ADS insufficiency. These limitations underscore the need for runtime safety assurance frameworks to prevent safety violations in mixed-traffic environments.

Runtime safety assurance [53] for ADSes aims to continuously monitor driving hazards, intervene before potential safety violations occur, and maintain safe operation at runtime. To prevent safety violations, several approaches monitor basic safety properties and trigger emergency braking [33, 65] or conservative fallback maneuvers [10, 44] before these properties are violated. However, these approaches rely on predetermined emergency interventions rather than adapting to the specific hazardous scenarios encountered. To intervene more adaptively, REDriver [52] intervenes in the planning process by refining ADS-generated planned trajectories to enforce specification compliance, but it requires intrusive modifications to the original ADS stack, and is tied to Apollo [3]. Without modifying the underlying ADSes, Argus [53] formulates runtime assurance as a hazard-aware takeover-and-recovery process for the trajectory of one single AV.

However, these ego-centric approaches assess and mitigate hazards on a per-vehicle basis, treating each AV as an independent takeover target rather than viewing mixed traffic as a software-intensive cyber-physical system of interacting AVs, other traffic participants, and RSUs [46]. As shown in Fig. 1a, two ADS-controlled AVs may generate trajectories that conflict at an unsignalized intersection. Although independently taking over each AV can avoid an immediate collision, the two AVs may enter a circular wait-for chain because neither vehicle has a scene-level view to determine yield priority, causing a deadlock in Fig. 1b. Mixed-traffic safety violations often arise from locally reasonable yet jointly incompatible decisions among multiple vehicles, which cannot be reliably resolved via ego-centric takeover. As shown in Fig. 1c, resolving this interaction-induced safety violation requires scene-level intervention, where one AV is assigned to proceed while the other slows down and yields.

Such intervention, which no single AV can reliably produce on its own, requires a scene-level view across multiple vehicles. V2X communication provides a practical foundation for this view, allowing AVs to exchange state, intent, and agreement-seeking information with RSUs.
However, most existing V2X-enabled cooperative driving approaches still leave the driving decisions to individual vehicles, which may incur safety violations in mixed traffic. Representative work includes shared perception [42, 55, 37, 62, 15], decentralized multi-vehicle planning [68, 8, 69], and LLM-mediated negotiation [18, 36, 20].
In contrast, centralized multi-vehicle planning approaches [39, 25, 26] coordinate traffic behavior at the scene level, but they typically assume an AV-dominated fleet with homogeneous ADSes under direct centralized control, a setting at odds with real-world mixed traffic, where AVs run heterogeneous, vendor-specific ADSes. Migrating such coordination into a safety assurance layer is non-trivial, as ADSes are black boxes and mixed traffic is only partially controllable (i.e., HDVs and pedestrians cannot be overridden, and safe AVs should not be).
In summary, existing work lacks V2X-enabled scene-level safety assurance for mixed traffic with heterogeneous AVs. To the best of our knowledge, no existing work monitors scene-level hazards and jointly intervenes on unsafe AVs without modifying their underlying planning logic.

To bridge this gap, we present CoSafe, a modular and ADS-agnostic cooperative runtime safety assurance framework for mixed-traffic autonomous driving that extends runtime safety assurance from ego-centric takeover to scene-level cooperative intervention.
Specifically, CoSafe consists of three RSU-side modules, namely cooperative perception, hazard assessment, and joint hazard mitigation, together with an AV-side control switch module. Within the coverage area of an RSU, the cooperative perception aggregates V2X information from participating AVs with RSU-side observations to construct the scene-level traffic information. Based on this information, the hazard assessment detects potential driving hazards, and identifies corresponding unsafe AVs; and the joint hazard mitigation jointly generates safe reference trajectories for unsafe AVs. For each participating AV, the control switch either passes through the original ADS-generated planned trajectory if no intervention is needed, or executes the generated safe reference trajectory.

We conduct large-scale experiments to evaluate the effectiveness and efficiency of CoSafe in mixed-traffic environments. We integrate CoSafe with seven state-of-the-art ADSes spanning five families,
and evaluate them on the InterDrive benchmark [36]. Our experiments demonstrate that CoSafe effectively improves the driving score of AVs by 70.03%, while reducing safety violations by 87.80% on average, with runtime latency satisfying real-time constraints. In addition, CoSafe accurately identifies unsafe AVs with an F3\text{F}_{3} score of 0.930; and our ablation and mixed-deployment results demonstrate that each module contributes distinctly and that CoSafe remains effective when coexisting AVs run heterogeneous ADSes.

The main contributions of our work are as follows.

We formulate cooperative runtime safety assurance as a scene-level pass-through-or-override safety layer over multiple ADSes, shifting the safety assurance paradigm from ego-centric takeover to scene-level cooperative intervention.

We design CoSafe, a modular cooperative runtime safety assurance framework, which can be integrated with heterogeneous AVs without modifying their underlying ADSes.

We develop a scene-level hazard assessment and joint mitigation mechanism that identifies unsafe AVs and generates coordinated safe reference trajectories to resolve hazards.

We integrate CoSafe with seven state-of-the-art ADSes, and conduct experiments on the InterDrive benchmark to demonstrate its effectiveness, efficiency, and generality.

1. We formulate cooperative runtime safety assurance as a scene-level pass-through-or-override safety layer over multiple ADSes, shifting the safety assurance paradigm from ego-centric takeover to scene-level cooperative intervention.

2. We design CoSafe, a modular cooperative runtime safety assurance framework, which can be integrated with heterogeneous AVs without modifying their underlying ADSes.

3. We develop a scene-level hazard assessment and joint mitigation mechanism that identifies unsafe AVs and generates coordinated safe reference trajectories to resolve hazards.

4. We integrate CoSafe with seven state-of-the-art ADSes, and conduct experiments on the InterDrive benchmark to demonstrate its effectiveness, efficiency, and generality.

title: ReactWorld: Structuring Interaction Responses for Embodied Video Generation
authors: Hanwei Liu,Huijia Zhang,Hanzhang Wang,Guangyu Liu,Hanbei Zhan,Linjie Hu,Bin Xiao,Xuan Zhou,Dong Zhang
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: . Project page:this https URL
abstract: Embodied video world models predict scene changes caused by robot actions, yet generated object responses may remain inconsistent with task intent and contact dynamics. Critical responses in embodied scenes often concentrate in local regions and specific time intervals. Inspired by chain-of-thought reasoning, we introduce ReactWorld, an embodied video generation model guided by structured interaction anticipation. In the generation backbone’s feature space, an interaction response field predictor anticipates how the interaction will unfold, explicitly describing participant roles, future motion response intensity, and local motion changes. A response feedback adapter forms increments to object features from the difference between the object branch’s outputs with predicted and zeroed local dynamics inputs. It also converts predicted displacements into positional biases for temporal attention. These two mechanisms guide object feature updates and information retrieval across frames, respectively. Through interaction anticipation and generative feedback, ReactWorld achieves an average score of 77.51 on RBench, outperforming PhysisForcing by 3.29 points with improvements in all nine categories. On EZS-Bench, it achieves a Domain score of 86.98 and an average score of 81.87.
introduction:
Embodied video world models represent the consequences of robot actions as future visual sequences, allowing interactions to be previewed [34, 35]. Unlike general video generation, embodied interactions require object changes to agree with task intent, contact relations, and motion dynamics [31, 21]. Image-to-video models can generate realistic appearance and coherent motion, and exhibit the ability to capture some physical regularities. However, visually plausible motion does not ensure that objects respond reliably to interaction conditions [24, 8]. A target may move before contact, a grasped object may detach from the gripper, or nearby objects may respond unnecessarily. Even when the overall video is smooth, such local errors can alter the outcome of grasping, placement, or tool use.

The dynamics that determine an interaction’s success often occur at a few locations and critical moments; their importance is not proportional to their visual extent [31, 21]. When folding a garment, for example, the entire garment is the target, but the initial response may be confined to the corner being lifted. VideoJAM [7] identifies an imbalance between appearance fitting and motion learning, while IMPACT [21] shows that globally averaged denoising supervision can underweight sparse regions containing dynamic objects. These findings suggest that embodied video generation must learn not only motion, but also which objects participate, where local responses occur, and when they unfold.

Existing methods strengthen dynamics modeling at different stages. PhysisForcing [31] aligns intermediate features with trajectories and relations between regions; Motion-I2V [20] and VideoJAM [7] use predicted motion for temporal feature propagation or generation guidance. VPT [23] introduces entity roles and uses modality-decoupled denoising and auxiliary loss annealing to reduce optimization conflicts and error propagation in joint modeling. Meanwhile, RecCAR [18] finds that bidirectional connections do not guarantee that auxiliary modalities constrain video generation equally effectively when jointly generating video with human motion and audio. These advances provide a foundation for motion modeling and generation guidance, but coherent motion alone does not ensure that object responses follow task intent and contact dynamics. For embodied interactions, the key is to specify where, when, and how objects should respond, and to make these task-relevant local dynamics effective conditions for generation.

Inspired by chain-of-thought’s use of explicit intermediate steps to structure complex reasoning [26], we propose ReactWorld, an embodied video generation model guided by structured interaction anticipation. Response prediction and generative feedback are performed within the same denoising forward pass, as shown in Fig. 2.

Given an initial image and a task instruction, the interaction response field predictor uses intermediate backbone features to anticipate how the interaction will unfold: which roles objects play, which local regions will respond and how strongly, and how those regions will subsequently move.

The response feedback adapter pools interaction context using roles and future motion response intensity. Holding the features and context fixed, it takes the difference between the object branch’s outputs with predicted and zeroed local dynamics inputs to form an increment to object features. It then converts predicted displacement into a temporal attention bias within a fixed local window in the next state. The former guides object feature updates; the latter guides where information is retrieved across frames. Inference requires only a task instruction and an initial image, without external role maps or trajectories.

ReactWorld achieves an average RBench score of 77.51, compared with 71.94 for Video-FT trained on the same data, and improves on PhysisForcing by 3.29 points. On EZS-Bench, its Domain and average scores reach 86.98 and 81.87. These results indicate that ReactWorld better captures the relationship between task requirements and object dynamics in embodied scenes, improving task completion and physical plausibility.

Our main contributions are:

We propose ReactWorld, an embodied video generation model guided by structured interaction anticipation, explicitly predicting participant roles, future motion response intensity, and interval dynamics in the backbone feature space.

We develop an interaction response field predictor and a response feedback adapter, using output differences relative to a zero-dynamics reference to update object features and displacement-based attention biases to guide cross-frame aggregation.

Improved overall scores on RBench and EZS-Bench, with more reliable interaction generation in terms of task completion, participant stability, and physical plausibility.

1. We propose ReactWorld, an embodied video generation model guided by structured interaction anticipation, explicitly predicting participant roles, future motion response intensity, and interval dynamics in the backbone feature space.

2. We develop an interaction response field predictor and a response feedback adapter, using output differences relative to a zero-dynamics reference to update object features and displacement-based attention biases to guide cross-frame aggregation.

3. Improved overall scores on RBench and EZS-Bench, with more reliable interaction generation in terms of task completion, participant stability, and physical plausibility.

title: Fluidic Body: Swarm Robots as a Fluid Extension of the Hand
authors: Michikuni Eguchi,Shigeo Yoshida,Mai Nishimura,Takefumi Hiraki
comment: accepted to ACM ISS 2026 (ISS track of PACMHCI)
abstract:
Swarm robots have attracted growing interest as a physical interface for human–computer interaction, since a swarm can reshape its formation to fit the objects and surroundings it works with.
For a human operator, however, adapting the swarm’s behavior remains difficult. Most existing methods require the user to specify where the swarm should go, and they offer no intuitive way to change the collective’s behavior as each task demands.
We present Fluidic Body, a system that lets a person operate a swarm of fluid-imitating robots as an extension of the hand. The system places a virtual fluid between the hand and the swarm, and the user adapts the swarm’s behavior to each task by changing the fluid’s properties through simple hand movements.
When the user opens the hand, the swarm becomes soft enough to deform and flow around obstacles. Closing the hand turns it into a hard, cohesive body that can push objects.
We evaluated the controller’s performance and its operability in two simulation experiments and one demonstration with physical robots. First, our controller handled both obstacle avoidance and object transportation better than an existing method that behaves the same way in every task. Second, in a VR user study, 17 participants completed the combined avoidance-and-transportation task faster and more reliably than with that method. They also reported a lower workload and a stronger sense of agency. Finally, this experience carried over to physical robots in a real-world demonstration (88 participants).
These results suggest that treating a swarm as a fluid, a material people already understand, allows a robot swarm to work as a deformable extension of the human body.
introduction:
Swarm robotics studies how many robots can act as one, producing collective behavior beyond the reach of any single robot (Şahin, 2004; Brambilla et al., 2013; Bonabeau et al., 1999).
A swarm can form patterns and assemble into shapes (Alonso-Mora et al., 2011; Rubenstein et al., 2014).
It can also move through cluttered spaces as a group (Alonso-Mora et al., 2016) and transport objects larger than its individual robots through cooperative pushing (Kuroki et al., 2023; Igarashi et al., 2010).
The range of such tasks grows with the number of robots, and platforms of a thousand units have coordinated at that scale (Rubenstein et al., 2012).
Because a swarm can flexibly adapt to different tasks by reshaping its formation, it has drawn attention as a promising interface for human–computer interaction (HCI).
In HCI applications such as teleoperation (Ihara et al., 2023; Ichihashi et al., 2024) and tangible user interfaces (Le Goc et al., 2016), a swarm works among people and everyday objects, and the situations it faces vary widely.

For swarm robots to serve a human operator, the missing piece is no longer the swarm controller, which computes how the robots move, but the interface through which a person directs them.
Methods such as potential fields (Khatib, 1986), formation planning (Alonso-Mora et al., 2016), and reinforcement learning (Sui et al., 2021) already generate diverse collective behaviors automatically.
What remains is an interface that lets a person reshape that behavior during operation to match the demands of each task.
Research on human-swarm interaction has explored directing the swarm through gestures and embodying it as an extension of the body (Le Goc et al., 2016; Ihara et al., 2023; Ichihashi et al., 2024).
These methods, however, largely amount to specifying where the swarm should go, and changing how it behaves to fit each task is still unaddressed.
As a result, a person cannot yet fully draw out the potential of a swarm.

We propose Fluidic Body, a system that lets a person operate a swarm of fluid-imitating robots as an extension of the hand (Fig. 1).
To let a person shape the swarm’s behavior itself, not only where it goes, we place a virtual fluid between the hand and the swarm.
The person changes the fluid’s properties through hand movements, and the swarm produces the matching behavior as if it were that fluid.
Because such fluids are part of everyday life, a person already knows how they behave and can anticipate how the swarm will respond (Battaglia et al., 2013; Jacob et al., 2008).
An open hand softens the swarm into a deformable body that flows around obstacles.
Conversely, when the hand closes, the robots pack together into a hard mass that can push objects.
Through these simple hand movements alone, a person adapts the swarm’s behavior to representative swarm tasks such as obstacle avoidance and object transportation (Alonso-Mora et al., 2016; Kuroki et al., 2023; Igarashi et al., 2010).

Fluidic Body builds on smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH), which represents a fluid as a set of particles (Gingold and Monaghan, 1977).
Treating each particle as a robot turns this fluid simulation into a controller that makes the swarm imitate fluid behavior (Pac et al., 2007).
With this controller, the robots fill the region marked out by the hand and arrange themselves, and the person never has to address a robot individually.
We build on our previous SPH controller (Eguchi et al., 2025a; Eguchi et al., 2025b) and map the hand’s movements to the properties of the simulated fluid.
This mapping lets simple hand movements produce a range of fluid-imitating swarm behaviors.

We evaluate Fluidic Body along two axes, the controller’s performance and the operability it gives a person.
For performance, we run a technical evaluation in simulation without a human operator.
It compares our controller against a fixed baseline that keeps the same behavior for every task, to test whether changing the fluid’s flexibility helps across tasks.
Because no single behavior suits both tasks, the fixed baseline handles only one of them, whereas our controller adjusts the fluid to each task and handles both.
For operability, we run a VR user study and an in-the-wild demonstration in which participants operate the swarm themselves.
In the VR user study, 17 participants completed the combined avoidance-and-transportation task faster and more reliably than with the baseline and reported a lower workload and a stronger sense of agency.
In the in-the-wild demonstration, 88 participants operated the physical robots and agreed most strongly that their own hand movements drove the swarm.
This suggests that the sense of agency from the VR study carries over to real hardware.

We propose Fluidic Body, a control interface that exposes a swarm’s flexibility as a fluid property a person changes by hand to adapt the swarm’s behavior to each task.

At the core of this interface, we design a mapping from three features of the hand to the fluid’s viscosity and density and, through them, to the swarm.
The hand’s shape switches the fluid between soft and hard settings, and its height adjusts how far the swarm spreads.
Its outline defines the region the swarm fills.

We conducted a three-part evaluation: a simulation comparison against a fixed baseline, a VR user study (N=17N=17), and an in-the-wild demonstration with physical robots (N=88N=88).
Adjusting the fluid adapted the swarm to each task and let participants operate it more efficiently than with the baseline, with a lower workload and a stronger sense of agency.

title: Robots in the City: Persona-Based Perceptions of Urban Robots
authors: Keonhee Jang,Kanghoon Lee,Seokwoo Yun,Namwoo Kim,Yoonjin Yoon
subjects: Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Pedestrians increasingly encounter robots in urban public spaces without interacting with them, but how robots change the perceived safety of a street remains unclear.
We examine how robot presence and type affect perceived safety across urban contexts.
We generate 18 images of Seoul streets that vary in time of day, road class, and robot condition (no robot, a delivery robot, or a humanoid).
Two multimodal large language models (MLLMs), Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma4-26B, each conditioned on 500 synthetic personas, choose the safer image in each pair, and 25 human respondents complete the same task.
Both models prefer streets without robots and favor the delivery robot over the humanoid.
Robots are chosen more often at night and less often by older personas, whereas road class has smaller effects.
In the model rationales, the delivery robot appears as a physical obstacle, whereas the humanoid appears as either a threat or a source of protection.
Like humans, both models chose robots more often at night, but chose the humanoid over the delivery robot far less often, and Gemma showed a night effect for the humanoid about three times that of humans.
These results show that the effect of a robot on perceived safety depends on when it appears, and that persona-conditioned MLLMs capture only part of human judgments.
introduction:
Advances in embodied AI are bringing robots out of laboratories and into everyday urban public spaces.
People on the street often pass these robots without interacting with them directly, so robots must also be understood from the perspective of these pedestrians [30, 10].
Even without interaction, a robot becomes part of the street scene [30] and can change how safe the street feels, a long-standing topic in urban perception research [26, 11].
While prior studies has focused on the people who encounter robots without directly interacting with them [10], how robot presence and type shape the perceived safety of the surrounding streetscape remains unclear. Also, urban visual perception researches have rarely included robots.

Understanding this effect requires examining how people perceive a robot in a street environment: for example, an octopus on a farm would not fit its surroundings.
People recognize such an object less easily [5] and look at it longer [22], which suggests that it takes more effort to process.
Objects that require more effort to process tend to be judged less favorably [32], suggesting that an out-of-place object can make people feel uneasy.
A robot on a street is also an object in a scene, and whether it fits can depend on what it does and where and when it appears [29].
The same robot can thus fit one street or time of day but not another, changing how safe the street feels. To investigate this, we use street view images, a common stimulus in urban perception research [26, 11], and generate variants of each scene that differ in the robot and the time of day [38, 9].
This allows us to examine how the urban context of a robot shapes its perceived safety.

We evaluate these images through pairwise comparisons of perceived safety, which allow controlled variants to be compared directly without relying on absolute ratings [15, 35].
We conduct these comparisons at scale using multimodal large language models (MLLMs) conditioned on persona descriptions, building on prior work on simulated responses [2, 4] and visual reasoning in urban environments [34].
This allows us to examine whether the same visual changes are judged differently across personas.
We also collect the same judgments from human respondents to assess how closely the models align with human perception.
Because persona conditioning does not necessarily reproduce human heterogeneity [16], we use persona variation as an analytical factor rather than a direct proxy for human populations.

In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

We examine how robot presence and type shape perceived safety across urban contexts.

We compare human and persona-conditioned MLLM judgments, identifying where the models align with or depart from humans.

We analyze the rationales behind model choices and how they shift with context.

1. We examine how robot presence and type shape perceived safety across urban contexts.

2. We compare human and persona-conditioned MLLM judgments, identifying where the models align with or depart from humans.

3. We analyze the rationales behind model choices and how they shift with context.

title: Beyond Accuracy: Information-Theoretic Decoder Evaluation Under Latent Intent
authors: Tasha Kim,Benjamin Ballyk,Anson Lei,Ingmar Posner,Oiwi Parker Jones
abstract: A central challenge in assistive brain-to-robot control is decoding a user’s latent intent from complex and noisy brain signals. Prior approaches evaluate decoders as single-trial classifiers with accuracy-based metrics, but this neglects the inherently sequential nature of assistive control. Since a planner must integrate intermittent, noisy decoder outputs over time, single-step accuracy can only be a proxy when predicting downstream task performance. We formalize brain-to-robot control as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), and prove that there is a sharp phase transition: regret is uniformly bounded across the horizon as long as pairs of goals are all decoder-distinguishable, but grows linearly otherwise. We show that a single channel statistic, the worst-pair Chernoff information Γmin\Gamma_{\min} sets this boundary. Then, we derive a closed-form regret predictor Uid​(C)U_{\mathrm{id}}(C), that can be computed from any confusion matrix in O⁡(K2)O(K^{2}) time. Across two domains spanning orthogonal information channels, we show that UidU_{\mathrm{id}} predicts cumulative planning regret beyond what accuracy can explain. We then highlight a pathological accuracy trap, in which two decoders have identical validation accuracy 35.1% on real EEG data (BNCI2014001 subject 5) but result in a difference of 9.6×9.6\times in held-out regret, which UidU_{\mathrm{id}} predicts. Same-signal control confirms UidU_{\mathrm{id}}’s advantage with decoders that span independent feature channels. Ultimately, our work provides a drop-in diagnostic to evaluate and select sensors and decoders in sequential assistive control.
introduction:
Assistive control applications such as brain-to-robot control, gesture-conditioned interaction, often require agents to predict the user’s intent based on noisy and ambiguous observations. Recent methodological advances (Défossez et al., 2023; Xiao et al., 2025) and data curation efforts (Mantegna et al., 2026; Schwarz et al., 2020) have made significant progress towards decoders that can accurately infer latent user intent from complex brain and biosignal data from a wide range of sensor modalities. Here, much of the literature formulate intent inference as a supervised classification problem, and evaluate decoder efficacy using prediction accuracy metrics like top-kk accuracy and F1 score.
While this paradigm is well-suited to one-shot prediction settings (e.g. brain-to-text prediction (Défossez et al., 2023; d’Ascoli et al., 2025)), assistive control has an added layer of complexity as they are inherently sequential: decoder outputs are accumulated over time by a downstream planner. As such, standard single-step accuracy evaluations act only as a proxy that may fail to reliably predict downstream task performance.

We argue that this proxy is fundamentally insufficient.
We model assistive control
as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) (Jain and Argall, 2019), in which decoder outputs are treated as observations that inform downstream policies. Through this lens, we directly analyze decoder quality at the task performance level via its induced cumulative regret, defined as the gap between the executed policy and an oracle policy with access to the true intent. Using the decoder’s confusion matrix, we directly derive information-theoretic bounds on cumulative regret. By formalizing the communication channel between user intent and the policy, we explicitly characterize how decoder quality shapes downstream task performance.

Our central theoretical result gives a sharp phase transition on cumulative regret. That is, when all rows of a decoder confusion matrix CC are pair-wise distinct, regret remains uniformly bounded over the horizon TT. In contrast, regret grows linearly in TT whenever any pair of rows collapse, regardless of what the overall accuracy is. This means that overall accuracy does not provide the right measure of performance. Rather, what really matters is the hardest pair of goals to distinguish, which we identify as the minimum Chernoff information, Γmin\Gamma_{\min}. We also introduce a computable predictor, Uid​(C)U_{\mathrm{id}}(C) termed the cumulative identification envelope, which can directly estimate regret from the confusion matrix. Together, we show that two decoders with the same accuracy can still incur arbitrarily different regret downstream. Real decoders rarely confuse goals in a symmetric way. For example, in electroencephalogram (EEG) signals, motor imagery (MI) for left and right hands motor imagery are more readily confused than feet and tongue (Pfurtscheller et al., 2006).

We validate our theory empirically across multiple datasets and modalities. Through joint regression on the CIFAR-100 dataset that spans 17 decoders and 7 feature families, we show that l​o​g​(Uid)log(U_{\mathrm{id}}) explains around 89%89\% of the regret variance. Similarly on the NinaPro multimodal dataset, l​o​g​(Uid)log(U_{\mathrm{id}}) carried the signal, while adding accuracy did not make a significant difference. When the accuracy of two decoders are closely matched on the aforementioned datasets, UidU_{\mathrm{id}} correctly predicts which decoder will incur the higher regret in ∼77%{\sim}77\% instances. On a real EEG decoder pair (BNCI2014001 (Tangermann et al., 2012) subject 5) that has identical validation accuracy (35.1%), held-out planning regret gave a 9.6×9.6\times difference, and UidU_{\mathrm{id}} spots the right one. Finally, three same-signal negative control experiments with decoders using single-feature representation tests the theory’s predicted boundary. From this, we identify that accuracy captures most of the variation that is relevant to downstream performance when channels are not orthogonal. Despite this, UidU_{\mathrm{id}} outperforms precisely when channels are genuinely orthogonal, matching our theoretical results.

title: Representations of 3D Rotations: Mathematical Foundations and Comparative Analysis
authors: Aizierjiang Aiersilan,Haochen Liu,James Hahn
subjects: Graphics (cs.GR); Mathematical Software (cs.MS); Robotics (cs.RO); Algebraic Geometry (math.AG); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
comment: Keywords: Rotation representations, $SO(3)$, quaternions, continuity, gimbal lock, 3D shape registration
abstract: Rotation representations are foundational in fields such as computer graphics, robotics, and machine learning, where precise and efficient modeling of 3D orientations is critical. This paper comprehensively investigates diverse representations of the special orthogonal group S​O​(3)SO(3), such as Euler angles, axis-angle vectors, quaternions, rotation matrices, exponential maps, and emerging continuous and probabilistic methods, evaluating their mathematical formulations, continuity, susceptibility to gimbal lock, computational efficiency, storage requirements, interpolation properties, and composition operations, while integrating detailed algebraic insights with practical applications in fields like animation, pose estimation, inertial navigation, 3D shape registration, and neural networks. Empirical evidence highlights quaternions’ dominance due to their compactness and computational efficiency, while alternatives like 6D continuous representations and matrix Fisher distributions provide enhanced continuity and uncertainty modeling. Future research could explore hybrid methods and thorough large-scale evaluations to help build a solid foundation for improving rotation representation techniques.
introduction:
Rotations in three-dimensional space are pervasive in computational domains, supporting tasks ranging from robotic manipulation to viewpoint estimation in computer vision. Spatial rotations are characterized by the special orthogonal group S​O​(3)SO(3), which consists of all 3×33\times 3 orthogonal matrices with unit determinant:

Traditional rotation formulations such as Euler angles [8] and quaternions [16] have played a central role in computer graphics, robotics, and animation, especially after Shoemake introduced quaternion-based interpolation [34]. More recent work [18, 5, 37, 6] has highlighted the practical limitations of standard representations and emphasized that rotation parameterizations should be chosen with respect to application-specific requirements. Complementary algebraic perspectives have been developed by Goldman [14] and Voight [39], while Hart et al. [17] have discussed long-standing challenges in visualizing rotational structure.

This paper presents a consolidated overview of commonly used rotation representations, with an emphasis on their mathematical structure, practical considerations, and typical use cases. Instead of introducing new representations or theoretical results, we aim to synthesize existing knowledge into a clear and accessible form and to illustrate representative behaviors through small, reproducible numerical demonstrations. The main contributions of this work are as follows:

A concise and unified exposition of major rotation representations, detailing their mathematical formulations and highlighting common sources of ambiguity or numerical challenges.
